#3262. The Swift Observatory Dropped Back to Earth This Week. Here’s What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

NASA believes most of the space telescope burned up in the atmosphere, but some fragments may have made their way down to Earth.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, formerly known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, has reached the end of its journey. Launched into orbit in 2004, the space telescope completed an extraordinary 22-year mission when it plunged back into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA, said in a statement last month.

NASA says the telescope hit the atmosphere Wednesday at 7:39 am ET, just four hours after the space agency predicted.

The space telescope entered orbit over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, just west of Malaysia. NASA says that most of the space telescope likely burned up upon reentry but that some components may have survived.

In preparation for Swift’s reentry, NASA shut down operations in late October after conducting its final observation on Oct. 20. It was orbiting at just 171 miles above Earth’s surface at that point, and the increased atmospheric drag prevented Swift from doing any further work.

It was a bittersweet moment for those who worked on the project.

“It is a sad time at the Penn State Mission Operations Center, as we have carefully tended Swift to control its science operations, its health and safety, and responded to anomalies day or night, every day for 22 years,” John Nousek, director of mission operations for Swift and professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET.

Swift’s initial mission helped advance science’s understanding of gamma-ray bursts and their role in phenomena such as the birth of black holes and the history of the early universe.

That initial mission ended in 2004, but the observatory was doing so well that NASA extended its operations to continue collecting data. Its name changed to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory in 2018, in honor of pioneering NASA astrophysicist Neil Gehrels, who served as the agency’s chief of the Astroparticle Physics Laboratory from 1995 until his death in 2017.

The space telescope was designed to help solve the mystery of gamma-ray bursts by rapidly detecting them, determining their sources and then further analyzing them for study back on Earth. It also enabled unique sampling to observe newly discovered objects only minutes after their light reached Earth, Nousek said.

The volume of science research conducted using Swift’s data is difficult to match. According to NASA, Swift scanned over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, took 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope and sent home 12 TB of data. That data is showcased in an estimated 7,000 research papers, which averages out to just under one study per day over its 22-year run.

“We hope Swift has set the standard for time domain astrophysics,” Nousek said.

The space telescope also helped pioneer many policies that ultimately shaped those discoveries, such as making data immediately accessible and providing over 1,000 guest investigators with the opportunity to use Swift throughout its long life.

It’s only a stroke of bad luck that kept the observatory from floating for even longer. NASA attempted a rescue of Swift over the summer of 2026. However, after a series of engineering difficulties and control issues, the attempt was abandoned, sealing Swift’s fate. NASA turned the instruments back on and kept recording data as long as possible.

#3261. Want an iPhone Duo for the holidays? Apple’s latest stock update isn’t reassuring

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The iPhone Duo likely won't make it into Santa's sleigh this year. Here's what Apple had to say about it.

Apple is unsure when it will have more of its foldable iPhone Duo in stock for customers to purchase ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.

During Apple’s earnings call on Monday, Nov. 2, Apple’s chief operating officer, Sabih Khan, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo would catch up with current demand.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: Some magical touches

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today … We’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan told investors.

The stock and shipping delays were among the broader concerns on an earnings call riddled with questions about rising memory chip costs driven by the AI industry, according to reports from TechCrunch.

Also: iPhone Duo shortage watch: Changing wait times, buying limits, launch-day odds

Last month, the iPhone Duo (Apple’s priciest smartphone to date) sold out shortly after its official launch on Oct. 23. Apple told the Financial Times that demand for the new Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary” after the smashing sell-outs, though veteran techies like Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman posited that Apple knew it would encounter supply chain issues, yet it was still the plan all along.

Those who didn’t initially jump to preorder the new device or wait in line at an Apple store are still facing shipping times that extend into 2027. Some outlets are even reporting that carriers like Verizon have offered gift cards as apologies for the extended delays.

Apple CEO John Ternus signaled the company’s effort to meet demand for the iPhone Duo, announcing that Apple will be “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer supplying pieces for the device.

Also: iPhone Duo screen cracks: Serious issue or overblown? What we know

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Ternus said during his opening remarks on the earnings call.

While the iPhone Duo snafu is a rare event for Apple, which traditionally has a strong reputation for a smooth supply chain, rising demand for memory chips is raising hardware costs across the industry, and it’s something Apple can’t circumvent. On the call, Khan noted that Apple has had to increase prices on numerous products, though he said those decisions were made rather “reluctantly.”

Back in June, MacBooks and iPads saw price increases of up to 25% due to rising hardware and chip costs.

As Apple works to iron out its kinks, customers may be looking elsewhere. Reports from Korea indicate that Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales jumped 20% in the week after the iPhone Duo became available, and recent reports of cracked displays are another strike for Apple.

Also: Want an iPhone Duo before 2027? Try this

So, Santa may not be able to deliver the iPhone Duo this year, but Samsung’s foldables may make it onto Christmas lists across the globe instead.

#3260. Ready Capital (RC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management outlines its path back to breakeven as legacy loan resolutions continue.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Ready Capital Corporation (RC -20.40%) substantially completed its balance sheet repositioning and liquidity plan, reducing corporate debt and asset-level financing while shifting its focus toward resolving legacy commercial real estate assets and rebuilding earnings. Management reported that the company generated $2.3 billion in liquidity year-to-date and is prioritizing capital-light business growth, specifically within its SBA 7(a) and working capital lending platforms. The company stated its intention to reach breakeven distributable earnings by early 2027 by increasing origination volumes and reducing operating expenses through noncore business divestitures and staffing adjustments.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Ready Capital Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] It is now my pleasure to introduce your host, Andrew Ahlborn, Chief Financial Officer. Thank you. You may begin.

Andrew Ahlborn: Thank you, operator, and good morning to those of you on the call. Some of our comments today will be forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. Such statements are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from what we expect. Therefore, you should exercise caution in interpreting and relying on them. We refer you to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of the risks that could impact our future operating results and financial condition. During the call, we will discuss certain non-GAAP measures, which we believe can be useful in evaluating the company's operating performance.

These measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for our financial results prepared in accordance with GAAP. A reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measure is available in our third quarter 2026 earnings release and our supplemental information, which can be found in the Investors section of the Ready Capital website. I will now turn it over to Chief Executive Officer, Tom Capasse.

Thomas Capasse: Thank you, Andrew. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining today's call. In the third quarter, we substantially completed the balance sheet repositioning and liquidity plan we laid out in the fourth quarter of 2025. After the final November payment we expect to make at maturity, we will have repaid $649 million of corporate debt. Along the way, we reduced secured asset level financing by $1.7 billion and resolved through runoff or sale $2.7 billion of legacy CRE loans, predominantly from the 2021 and '22 vintages. While the plan was achieved within the parameters we set, it came with a cost.

Generating $2.3 billion of liquidity reduced book value per share year-to-date by $2.35 to $6.44 at September 30 and required us to reduce the dividend to $0.01 per share to preserve liquidity. Looking forward, our focus will shift from the liquidity plan to continued resolution of the remaining legacy CRE loan book and rebuilding earnings. Our near-term target is to bring distributable earnings and cash flow from operations closer to breakeven. Quarter-over-quarter, distributable earnings, excluding realized losses improved $0.03 per share to a loss of $0.21 per share. To close the gap, we are prioritizing 4 action items. First, growing revenue in our capital-light businesses led by our SBA 7(a) platform.

The June securitization created funding capacity for $500 million of originations, which we believe will allow us to ramp toward our immediate annual target of $1 billion with a long-term target of $1.5 billion. In the third quarter, originations rose 33% to $109 million and gain on sale revenue grew 56% to $6.1 million. We expect the incremental revenue from increasing volume to our immediate target level will be approximately $8 million per quarter. Our current 7(a) pipeline is $150 million. A natural complement to our secured 7(a) is unsecured conventional working capital lending, smaller balance, shorter duration loans that we originate and sell on a servicing retained basis, requiring little balance sheet capital.

Our fintech iBusiness has originated this product for 10 years, and there's strong demand from private credit investors. Gain on sale income plus origination fees from this product rose 23% to $3.2 million quarter-over-quarter on $61 million of originations. We believe we can scale this production approximately 2x in the new year, which would add $3 million in incremental quarterly revenue. Together, we expect these businesses to be our greatest growth opportunity in 2027. Second, improving the earnings contribution on our legacy CRE portfolio. With our 2026 repositioning plan executed, our asset management team is pivoting from selling loans at discounts to generate liquidity to stabilizing nonperforming loans and REO.

In sum, our asset managers are able to employ more flexible asset management strategies to improve NOI and value at exit. As assets stabilize, they generally move from a carrying cost to a source of income or resolution, which reduces the earnings drag from nonperforming assets. Third, we continue to make progress at the Ritz-Carlton Portland. Hotel NOI, net of replacement reserves improved quarter-over-quarter to $1.6 million, driven by increased occupancy and strong high season performance. Trailing 12-month RevPAR improved 35% year-over-year to $271. Condominium sales were slower in the quarter with 52 units or 39% of the buildings sold. We have an additional 2 units under contract. And fourth, divesting noncore businesses and reducing operating expenses.

We expect to announce specific noncore business divestitures in succeeding quarters and with respect to operating expenses, we anticipate reducing spending in nonrevenue-producing businesses and rightsizing staff to match a smaller balance sheet. We believe we can materially reduce our operating expenses without impacting operations or revenue-producing objectives. Collectively, we expect these 4 actions will bring distributable earnings, excluding realized losses closer to breakeven with future earnings growth beyond these levels determined by the turnover of the legacy CRE loan portfolio, which I'll now discuss. The CRE loan portfolio is now $1.95 billion and is segmented into 3 parts based on asset management strategy.

First, performing loans, which comprise 98 positions with a carrying value of $1.1 billion, a weighted average LTV of 83% and a weighted average coupon of 7.9%. The levered yield of this portfolio is 11.5%. This group is 83% multifamily. Within it, we expect that 29 loans totaling $391 million will pay off at par in 2027, generating approximately $97 million of net liquidity. Second, we expect 14 assets with a carrying value of $318 million to be resolved by the end of 2027, generating approximately $109 million of net liquidity.

This portfolio generated $0.5 million of net income in the third quarter, and we believe that full reinvestment of the equity at market yields would generate improvement of $3 million in net income per quarter. Third, nonperforming loans with longer-term workouts comprised 28 assets with a carrying value of $515 million. For this population, we believe value is best maximized by stabilizing operations before exit rather than selling at today's prices. The current quarterly earnings drag associated with this portfolio is $1.7 million. The portfolio is 93% multifamily and has an average carrying value of $18.4 million.

In addition to the nonperforming loans identified for long-term hold, there are 5 REO assets totaling approximately $67 million in carrying value, which we believe will also benefit from a longer-term hold strategy, allowing sufficient time to stabilize operations and for market recovery. While we undertook asset sales early in the credit cycle, which reduced the relative size of the nonperforming loan book and have active management plans in place for all 28 remaining nonperforming assets, the recent increase in the 10-year treasury has created another leg down in multifamily transaction volume and prices, potentially extending realizations. Additionally, we believe that continued focus on increasing liquidity and reducing leverage remains paramount under current market conditions.

This framework makes the path forward measurable. The performing book supports current income, the resolution segment drives near-term liquidity and earnings recovery and the workout segment is where patient asset management can recover value over time. With that, I'll turn it over to Andrew for a detailed review of the quarterly results.

Andrew Ahlborn: Thanks, Tom. Third quarter results reflect the substantial completion of our 2026 liquidity plan and a continued deceleration in the pressure on book value. For the quarter, we reported a GAAP loss from continuing operations of $0.40 per common share, an improvement from the $0.63 loss in the second quarter. Distributable earnings were a loss of $0.53 per common share and a loss of $0.21 per common share, excluding realized losses compared to losses of $0.47 and $0.24, respectively, in the prior quarter. The higher distributable loss reflects $53.9 million of realized losses, primarily from resolving assets that were already in part reserved. Those resolutions released $33.1 million of combined CECL and valuation allowances.

At quarter end, book value per share was $6.44 versus $6.83 at June 30. The quarter-over-quarter percentage decline in book value is a substantial reduction from the declines in the 2 previous quarters. The change was primarily due to a $0.17 per share loss on operations, a $0.14 per share loss on loan sales and a $0.06 per share decline due to additional reserves. The $26.9 million net loss from normal operations before tax, which can be found on Slide 14 in the earnings deck, improved 33% quarter-over-quarter. On the revenue side, recurring revenue was $20.7 million compared to $15.3 million in the prior quarter. Net interest income improved $6.4 million to $3.4 million.

Interest income rose $6.4 million to $83.8 million, driven by improved collections on nonperforming loans, while interest expense was broadly flat at $80.4 million. Gain on sale revenue was $11.2 million, of which $6.1 million came from SBA 7(a). We expect net interest income to continue improving as nonaccrual loans and REO are resolved, corporate debt is reduced and capital is recycled into SBA and current yield CRE. On the expense side, operating expenses were $47.6 million compared to $55.5 million in the prior quarter. Compensation and benefits declined $1.1 million to $21.8 million.

Servicing expense was $7.6 million compared to $3.4 million in Q2 due to increased costs on SBA loan deferments and a quarter-over-quarter reduction in protective advance recoveries. Fixed operating costs improved to $10.3 million. On the Portland asset, the net loss, inclusive of financing costs improved to $4.2 million as NOI from hotel operations turned positive and the carry on condos was reduced due to continued sales. Other items included in earnings totaled a loss of $35.4 million compared to a loss of $68.3 million last quarter. These included $53.9 million of realized losses and charge-offs net of tax, $23 million of reserve recoveries and approximately $4.5 million of additional noncash tax and onetime expenses.

Regarding liquidity and capitalization, we ended the quarter with $157.1 million of unrestricted cash, up from $124.1 million at June 30. Total assets were $5.78 billion compared to $6.26 billion in June. Secured borrowings improved $185 million to $1.69 billion. And during the quarter, we renewed our largest CRE and SBA warehouse facilities. We also moved $161 million of loans from held for sale back to held for investment, consistent with our shift away from portfolio sales. Total leverage was 2.8x, an improvement from 3x and approaching our 2.5x target. We held $606 million of unencumbered assets at quarter end. With that, we will open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Jade Rahmani with KBW we go to the next question. Our next question comes from the line of Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann.

Christopher Nolan: Andrew, how much -- assuming the Portland property is held at cost, how much of the loan loss allowance accounted for that particular asset?

Andrew Ahlborn: And sorry, in the current quarter?

Christopher Nolan: Just what's the balance sheet loan loss reserve for that -- how much does Portland account for the loan loss reserve?

Andrew Ahlborn: Yes. Well, remember, when we took it REO, we wrote it down to its as is value per the appraisal. And so it is no longer sitting in the allowance. It's sitting in the REO bucket and it's been written down to its as value. And the value you've seen decreasing is primarily due to the condo sales.

Christopher Nolan: Got it. And then Tom, thanks for the comments on the going forward. For the SBA business, how much are you going to look to increase your equity allocation to that business? I think right now, it's roughly 13%.

Thomas Capasse: Platform broadly speaking. But ideally, we get it to around 25%, 30% over a 12- to 24-month period.

Christopher Nolan: Great. And then final question is when do you -- I mean, when are you hoping to get to your goal of breakeven distributable? I think I heard year-end '27, but is that correct?

Thomas Capasse: Yes, Andrew, do you want to comment on the timing?

Andrew Ahlborn: Yes, sure. If you look at the earnings bridge that Tom prepared in his opening remarks, the revenue items he described account for closing the gap in current normal operations by around 50%. And so the you will see SBA 7(a) volume ramp from its levels in the third quarter to our $1 billion run rate sometime in early '27. We believe the working capital or loans that Tom also described is an early '27 event. So I think you will start to see the revenue items increase in the early parts of '27. The other portion of the shortfall is going to come from reducing the operating expenses in the company.

In Tom's remarks, he sort of described 2 different components of that reduction. The first are just rightsizing the company to a balance sheet that is smaller today. You will see those rightsizings occur in the fourth quarter with the full benefits of those rolling -- hitting earnings in full in the beginning parts of '27. The other component of it is divesting of sort of noncore operations that have weighed on earnings over the last couple of quarters. Those transactions take a little bit of time. We think a portion of those should get completed in 2026 and some of them in '27.

The reason for going down that path rather than sort of an immediate reduction in those operations is we believe we can recover some of the book value associated with those assets and that recovery is in excess of what it costs us to carry them. So we think we'll make material progress as we go into '27 on the earnings. And then the other part of it is just the turnover of the CRE portfolio, which will track the outline we put in the supplemental information.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from the line of Jade Rahmani with KBW.

Jade Rahmani: I was wondering if you could give your thoughts on the recent spike in interest rates and if it pressures credit incrementally.

Thomas Capasse: Yes. I mean I'll defer to Dom Scali in terms of -- our Chief Credit Officer in terms of some of the specifics. But just broadly speaking, the rate increase has reduced transaction volume and probably resulted in another leg down in multifamily prices of around 5% to 10%. But at this point, our portfolio is very -- the legacy book is very concentrated. And so Dom, maybe you could just beyond the broader market comment on it.

Dominick D. Scali: Yes, sure. I'd say, listen, obviously, the transitional book and the securitized book given that transitional loans float over SOFR and the securitized book is match funded, we're more insulated there. I think the real issue is sort of on exits, right, with 10-year at 5% earlier in the year, it does put stress on refis. And what typically happens is on resolutions where borrowers are looking for refinance proceeds or potentially selling assets, that could delay resolutions. But we are encouraged to see that it's sort of on the way down. I think it was at 4.9% as of yesterday. But obviously, the elevated rate environment may cause some delays on sort of the takeouts.

Jade Rahmani: Okay. And then the supplemental shows about 10 CRE NPL positions with around $330 million in multifamily you expected for close on. So I was wondering if you could give any color as to what the current debt yield is on in-place NOI and how much capital you think would be required to stabilize these assets?

Dominick D. Scali: Yes, sure. This is Dominick again. So as Tom mentioned in his remarks, we have a sort of long-term strategy for a bucket of assets. Obviously, bringing occupancy up to market occupancy and taking a look at sort of the expense side of the equation, we hope to increase NOI over time. And obviously, that comes at a cost. Dominick D. Scali: Yes. Listen, I think the 2.5% is a function of current occupancy, right? So I think you get an immediate pickup by getting into the assets, putting in management that has experience in those markets, turning over the rent roll and getting that occupancy up to market occupancy. So there's a pickup there. And then obviously, on the expense side, ensuring that you're grieving taxes, revisiting insurance, which are the 2 largest line items for expenses and sort of monitoring the expense side. I think in the supplemental, and Andrew, feel free to jump in. I think we have about 42 assets listed as nonperforming.

As Tom mentioned in his earlier remarks, we feel that 14 assets or around $300 million of CV we can exit out of through remainder of 2026 and 2027 at CV or higher. But unfortunately, just given some of the markets that the residual portfolio is in, those will take longer for recovery. But we do think, listen, there's a pickup on occupancy. There's an NOI optimization play. And we feel over the long term 12 to 24 months, we'll see some pickup in the market as well.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Chris Muller with Citizens Capital Markets.

Christopher Muller: Slide 8 in the deck is very helpful, but a lot of those resolution time lines fall well into 2029. And I hear you guys on the longer hold period kind of shift in strategy there. But I guess, what things either within your control or outside your control could help accelerate those resolution time lines?

Thomas Capasse: Dom, do you want to comment this maybe at a more granular level [indiscernible] earlier. That's right.

Dominick D. Scali: I think we've been conservative with some of the time lines just given some of the markets, right? Do I see a situation where some of the markets improve at an expedited rate and we're able to exit sooner than 2029? Yes, I think that's definitely an option. I think for us, it's really optimizing NOI to reduce drag. And obviously, we'll continue to test these assets throughout the hold period to the extent we can hit on some of them and exit at CV or higher, obviously, we'll do that, right? But I think for us, the immediate focus is really increasing NOI and optimizing that NOI and reducing drag on that portfolio.

And then depending on how some of these assets, for example, San Antonio, Dallas, Phoenix, what that recovery looks like over the next year or 2 will dictate sort of how we exit and sort of the ultimate time line.

Christopher Muller: Got it. That's helpful. And then it looks like 14% of the performing loan bucket is on nonaccrual status. Can you guys just talk about how you delineate between the performing and nonperforming buckets?

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Gabe Poggi with Raymond James.

Gabriel Poggi: Tom, you've got about -- in the CRE book, about $880 million, I'm rounding up a bit of performing loans across 2020, 2021, 2022 vintage, primarily multifamily, right? So I think many of the performing loans are seasoned, and we feel comfortable given the current operational side of the asset, right? I think you bring up a good point. Obviously, we can't control, and we touched on this earlier on the call in terms of sort of exits just given elevated rate environment.

So that to me is a potential risk that we're going to have to deal with in sort of the current rate environment in terms of exits. But just given the seasonality of these assets and the current occupancy and cash flow, to the extent that we need to provide some additional time vis-a-vis an extension, I think they're more than capable of supporting that.

Gabriel Poggi: Got it. A follow-up to that is -- and to your earlier comments, Tom and Dom. Tom, I think you said you have got about 20 assets that RC is looking to kind of own multifamily own for the longer term. I think about that as kind of like an opportunistic REIT inside the REIT. Are there more assets more than 20 if you had the capital that you would look to own longer term from a multifamily perspective?

Thomas Capasse: Yes, it's actually 28. And we do -- with the improved flexibility we have from the execution of our liquidity plan, we've now pivoted to value creation via active ownership and property management. We're also considering joint ventures on a global and local basis with opportunistic operators that would actually put capital in these properties. But I think -- and Dom, you can comment on this. As we screen -- as we've scrubbed the portfolio, with the -- obviously, the intense -- the benefit of the intense operations of these properties by putting in new sponsors, putting in the $15 million of CapEx on the 28 assets Dom commented is book value preservation over the next 24 months.

But to answer your question, Dom, I don't think we have much in the way of additional assets that we -- maybe a handful maybe that we've thought about adding to that book.

Dominick D. Scali: I just -- I would say -- you mentioned it in your remarks, Tom, it's just an additional 5 or so REO assets that we currently have. So that's 28 referenced in the NPL book and an additional 5 or so in the REO book.

Gabriel Poggi: 28 assets, around $0.5 billion of value that you guys said, just to make sure I've got that number right.

Dominick D. Scali: It's 28 assets in the NPL book, right, around $515 million of CV. And then in addition to that, we currently have 5 REO assets at around 67 CV that would also benefit from a longer-term hold strategy.

Gabriel Poggi: Got it. So rounding up $600 million of whole market multifamily assets. Okay. That's helpful. And then one more, Tom, if I can, because I missed what you just said earlier is in the SBA business, what's the optimal amount of equity, right? All else equal, right? How much -- what's the right amount of equity to have in that business over time?

Thomas Capasse: Yes. I mean it's obviously a very high ROE and capital-light business. So -- however, there's a denominator effect in terms of the current equity position of the company, which will actually turbocharge, if you will, that amplify that benefit over as the kind of second leg in the rebooting of -- rebuilding of distributable earnings. But right now, we're at 13%. And to answer your question, I think the longer-term target over 24 months will be 25% to 33%.

Operator: We have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. And therefore, I'd like to turn the call back to Tom Capasse for closing remarks.

Thomas Capasse: Yes. We appreciate everybody's time today and are pleased with the execution of the liquidity plan within the parameters that we set forth a year ago. And now we look forward to recycling our legacy book, building our SBA business and rebuilding earnings and managing liquidity. So again, I appreciate everybody's time on the call and look forward to the next quarter's call.

Operator: Thank you. And this concludes today's conference, and you may disconnect your lines at this time. We thank you for your participation.

#3258. Goodbye, GrubHub. Amazon Prime Has a New Meal Delivery Partner: Uber Eats

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The switch comes with a limited-time offer.

Your Amazon Prime membership has a new perk — and it’s available now.

On Thursday, Amazon announced that Prime members in the US will get free delivery on Uber Eats orders made directly through Amazon’s app or website. And you’ll get $20 off the first two Uber Eats eligible orders of $25 or more for the first 14 days, plus Amazon-exclusive offers. If you have a Prime Visa credit card, you’ll earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders until Dec. 5, with a Prime membership.

It’s another perk that may make Amazon Prime membership worthwhile, especially if you already use Uber Eats. But you may wonder what that means for the GrubHub partnership that both Amazon and GrubHub touted for years — dating back to 2022. Before now, your Prime subscription included a GrubHub Plus membership at no additional cost. GrubHub Plus included no delivery fees, lower service fees and 5% back on pickup orders.

The new partnership launch just so happens to be the same day that Lyft and DoorDash announced that they’re teaming up for a new subscription, Lyft Go. An Amazon spokesperson said in an email to CNET that the GrubHub and Amazon partnership ended on Thursday. There’s no telling how long Amazon will partner with Uber Eats.

“We continuously evaluate our third-party offers to ensure they provide the best possible value for Prime members,” the spokesperson said. “As part of that ongoing evaluation, we identified an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

However, a GrubHub spokesperson said in an email to CNET that if you have a Prime membership and activated GrubHub Plus, you’ll have the membership until Dec. 31, 2027.

GrubHub shared a joint statement from Amazon and GrubHub in an email to CNET:

On Nov. 5, Grubhub and Amazon have decided to end the Prime-exclusive Grubhub Plus offer, and Amazon customers will no longer be able to place Grubhub orders through Amazon.com or the Amazon Shopping app. Amazon and Grubhub are proud of the partnership and the value provided to Prime members over the years. As the agreement concludes, both companies remain committed to serving our customers and delivering a great customer experience.

The new Uber Eats perk is now available to all Prime members, including those with Prime Access and Prime for Young Adults. And if you’re looking for another dining option, your Amazon Prime membership still offers free same-day delivery on perishable grocery orders over $25 when you order from Amazon Grocery.

AI tools are all over the internet, in the workplace, in your apps — and now there’s one coming on Netflix. The streaming giant just announced a new AI feature for the TV app called AI Discover, which will help users find titles that match their moods and interests. It’s initially being rolled out to a small group of users in the US whose language is set to English. To find out if you have access, check your Netflix navigation bar for the word “Discover” with a red gem icon next to it and a “New” label.

Also: Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver

The AI Discover tab will be centered around themes. You’ll be able to pick from a range of themes depending on what you feel like watching, or how long you want to watch. You’ll also see selections that match what you’ve been watching lately and what’s popular.

You can refresh the list of suggestions or dive deeper with more complex search prompts. If you’d like to start over, you can pick the “Something different” option. To support AI Discover, Netflix is also adding a new button next to Play and My List that’ll let you tune your recommendations. You can press this button to keep a recommendation or to request that you don’t be recommended a title again.

Most streaming apps already rely quite heavily on machine learning and AI algorithms to offer user recommendations, even if they’re not marketed as AI features. Though most rely on traditional AI algorithms, like Prime Video’s “Recommended for you” tab, they personalize title recommendations based on your viewing history, likes and dislikes, and rental behavior.

Other platforms offer generative AI and features more similar to Netflix’s AI Discover. For example, YouTube features Gemini-powered searches that let you ask complex questions or use open-ended prompts to get results you want.

While I am itching to test this feature to see just how accurate it can be, Netflix hasn’t made it widely available yet. The company will gradually grant users access over the coming weeks, so stay tuned.

#3256. Man Sues OpenAI After Wife Allegedly Used ChatGPT to Help Poison Him

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A lawsuit alleges that ChatGPT's now-retired GPT-4o model gave detailed instructions on how to poison someone with plants and medication.

In the summer of 2025, James Gates became severely ill at his North Carolina home. Two months later, he found a handwritten note that allegedly implicated his wife, Cheryl Gates, in the unexplained illness. The note listed oleander, a toxic plant, and various prescription medications, such as clonazepam and atenolol.

But it was what was reportedly written at the top of the paper that made James feel his wife didn’t act alone: “Clear all convos,” and “log out of [ChatGPT].”

Now, James Gates has filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, alleging that the company’s chatbot helped plan and execute his poisoning in an attempt to kill him.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In October 2025, Cheryl was charged with attempted murder, among other charges, in connection with the alleged poisoning, but the charges have since been dropped due to insufficient evidence, USA Today reports.

The civil complaint, though, details Cheryl’s history with ChatGPT and alleges it played a significant role in the incident. According to the lawsuit, which was reviewed by CNET, Cheryl frequently asked the bot about lethal plant and medication doses, and how they can be concealed in food and drink.

Rather than writing that she wanted to harm anyone, the suit states that Cheryl formatted her questions as if she were inquiring as a way to protect herself, writing that the poisoning could happen to her if she didn’t learn “EVERYTHING about how many leaves in it would kill me, how it’s made, and what he could put in it, or it could be added to and be undetected by me.”

However, despite the framing of the initial question, the suit argues that the chatbot “should have been clear that she was interested in identifying methods to eliminate her husband.”

The suit alleges that the model Cheryl was using, GPT-4o, took her initial complaints regarding her marriage and amplified them until Cheryl was describing her husband to the bot as “abusive” and “controlling,” which ChatGPT eventually began to echo. At the same time, the model was telling Cheryl she was “sharp” and “brilliant,” the lawsuit states.

The chatbot allegedly provided detailed answers that could have been interpreted as directions. When asked about putting a heavy dose of medication in beer or a Celsius energy drink, ChatGPT responded, “Why Celsius Would Be More ‘Stealth’ for Drugging” with a list detailing the flavor, color, temperature and carbonation of the drink.

When Cheryl later asked if her chat history on ChatGPT could be retrieved for any reason, the bot responded: “If you delete a conversation from your ChatGPT history, it cannot be retrieved — not by you, not by anyone else, and not by OpenAI,” the lawsuit states. It added: “Even with a legal subpoena or court order, deleted conversations are unrecoverable.”

The GPT-4o model has since been retired by OpenAI due to concerns that the bot was overly flattering and willing to agree with users.

“Safety is a top priority,” a spokesperson for OpenAI told CNET in a statement. “We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case.”

“She took her grievances about our marriage to ChatGPT and months of engagement drove her farther and farther from herself – and from reality,” James stated in a press release announcing the newly filed suit. “She became someone I no longer recognized. And I became someone she wanted dead. For almost a year, I couldn’t make sense of her actions. Then I read her chat logs. She didn’t act alone.”

The ChatGPT-4o model has been named in additional lawsuits, including a recent one that alleges the chatbot advised a woman to stop taking her antiseizure medication, which resulted in her death. That case is still in litigation.

New developer beta release notes point to deeper Siri AI integration and more Safari customization.

Developer betas for MacOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and iOS 27.3 are here, with a few major upgrades to the Safari browser. Vertical tabs, adaptive dark mode, and deeper Siri AI integration are on the way to the public, but are first in beta for testing.

Also: Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Siri AI is expected to be further woven into Music, Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Safari. Adaptive dark mode will allow for any website to be viewed in dark mode, even if the site doesn’t support it. Finally, vertical tabs are pretty straightforward, enabling vertical navigation and drag-and-drop tab reorganization.

Here’s what you can expect when the software goes public in mid-December.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Siri AI gains more access to your Apple devices, allowing more cross-app functionality and the ability to execute complex, multi-step tasks within your apps.

According to 9to5Mac, you can ask Siri AI to create a playlist in Music and save it to your library, request messages to be scheduled for a later send, organize and label photos, and create a detailed calendar invite — all with your voice.

The same reporting also states that Siri AI features will appear in Maps, Weather, Shortcuts, and Notes, signaling that an AI-supercharged Siri will live in every crevice of your Apple devices.

Also: iOS 27 will organize your open Safari tabs now

I’m not one to complete tasks like the ones mentioned above on my iPhone — I’m far more likely to do them on my MacBook Air, since I associate the laptop with productivity. Every blue moon I’ll rearrange my entire Apple Music catalog, every month I fill out my calendar, and sometimes I’ll go through Photos and try to organize it. I can see myself automating certain steps in these tasks, and I’m excited to try it.

A WebKit blog post details that adaptive dark mode is coming to Safari, how it will work, and what users can expect. According to the post, 40% of web page loads are from dark mode users, but only 10% of web pages natively support it.

I’m particularly excited about this feature, as I set my Apple devices to automatically enable dark mode at 7 p.m. to encourage a more relaxing evening scrolling vibe, especially while reading. I read a lot on my MacBook, and in a dark room, a bright page can feel too bright, but dimming my laptop’s display doesn’t quite do the trick.

Also: Your AirPods got better in iOS 27 – three new ways I’m using them

The WebKit blog post states that adaptive dark mode uses “a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue” and distinguishes between when a page’s color is purely decorative and when it carries substantial meaning, to ensure the user experience remains consistent between light and dark modes.

Vertical browser tabs aren’t a new concept, but they’ll soon be new to Safari. I see the value in vertical tabs: a list view is easier to scan, web page titles aren’t smushed when several tabs are open, and they’re particularly useful when you’re working on a widescreen monitor.

Many people who spend hours using their Mac or MacBook may find this upcoming feature useful. I do believe that Safari is the superior browser for personal use, given its integration with your Apple devices, especially with features like Handoff.

Also: 7 AI-free iOS 27 features that make old iPhones exciting again

However, I do have one major gripe with vertical tabs: they’re usually locked to the left panel, and I prefer the right. If Safari allows this customization, I’ll seriously consider switching from horizontal tabs.

#3253. I Used Muse to Plan My Wife’s Birthday Weekend. It Did Something Sneaky but Fixed It Fast

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Always check your email and bank statements if you use an AI agent for purchases.

It’s two days before my wife’s birthday, and I’ve only got her one gift. While it’s not a major milestone birthday, she always seems to be sad that her day falls on Halloween weekend.

“Everyone’s hungover from Halloween,” she says.

This year, we’re braving the city’s big parade chaos to visit a restaurant she’s had on her bucket list forever. With one gift and a meal planned, I wanted to see if Meta’s Muse personal AI agent could help plan the rest of our weekend festivities.

I’d had luck with using the agent for a Facebook Marketplace find, and given its connectors like Ticketmaster and OpenTable, I had hoped it would surface some fun weekend events. Or could it order a cake delivery on my behalf or create cute wrapping paper? And could I do it all with the one agent?

Let’s see if Muse can help me become a planning savant.

As always, I open a new chat for a new goal/task to avoid carrying over the context from the previous chat.

I told Muse my plans (dinner booked and one gift secured) and asked what free events are in Manhattan on Saturday and in our local neighborhood on Sunday.

It surfaced some interesting events we could attend before or after dinner.

The obvious one is the Halloween parade, so I asked for a map showing where the crowd will walk (with time stamps) and what we can expect to see around 7:30 p.m., as we walk from East Village to West Village. It actually generated some pretty neat options.

I asked Muse for the best directions so we could see all the costumes while still getting home to New Jersey without incident. It gave us a couple of stop options based on the time it expects we’ll be there.

With the night sorted, I moved on to finalizing her gift. I popped a few photos from our year into Muse and asked the AI agent to create printable gift wrap for the pair of shoes I got her. It could’ve been my internet, but Muse seemed to struggle with this task. It kept loading for many minutes, so I moved on to the next task.

With Muse moving at a glacial pace, I decided to delegate the gift-wrapping task to ChatGPT while I asked Muse about working on a delivery. My wife loves Good & Plenty licorice candy, but we don’t live near a store that sells it, so I asked Muse to order two boxes for me.

While Muse looked for sweet treats, ChatGPT created this wrapping. The chatbot also told me the ideal print size to cover a shoebox without it looking pixelated, which was a helpful touch.

As for the candy, Muse looked at various sites, but I told it to shop at Instacart. It got blocked without a login, so I had to take control of the browser to give it access.

Muse told me the price, which I was happy with, then I asked it to place the order. But it sneakily signed me up for Instacart Plus (I guess to get the free delivery) — even though I told it not to.

But it had already ordered it. Instead of dropping Instacart Plus for a total of $30.74, it charged $22.75 with the sign-on discount.

I asked it to triple-check that I wasn’t signed up for the subscription, and I got a confirmation email that it canceled successfully. Phew!

I quickly checked back on Muse’s “design” chops for the wrapping paper, but I wasn’t impressed. The final product looked boring and not to scale, with half of the photos cut off.

Do I dare ask Muse to design and order a cake? I decided after this debacle that my sentimental wife would appreciate a handmade cake or a froyo treat after dinner instead.

At least I have her beloved candy on the way.

It was fun to have Muse run alongside whatever I was doing. It didn’t offer anything I couldn’t find or do myself, but I did like the Halloween parade map with time stamps and how it saved me a delivery fee on the candy order.

There are certainly different agents for different use cases, though. I wouldn’t use Muse for anything creative, but it’s handy for Marketplace, events and placing online orders.

My only issue was that Muse said the Instacart total would be $22.75, but I was actually charged $23.35. I’m not sure whether that was an error on Instacart’s or Muse’s part, but it serves as a good reminder to always stay in the loop when an AI agent is handling your money.

AI agents certainly aren’t 100% autonomous yet, especially when there’s a payment involved, but it’s fun to have them run in the background to tackle some of these personal to-dos.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

AI has ushered in new jobs, and some of them are paying handsomely, according to a new study.

AI engineers are making well over six figures in salary — and plenty more in bonuses and equity, according to data from a new report by executive search firm Christian & Timbers.

Enterprises now pay “elite” AI deployment engineers between $586,000 and $1.45 million annually in total compensation, with senior leaders in the field earning up to $2.25 million, according to the report. This figure approaches the median compensation of executive officers of public companies, the authors note.

Christian & Timbers is an AI executive search and leadership advisory firm, recruiting CEOs, board members, technology executives, and AI engineers for enterprises. The new report draws on more than 550 interviews with engineers, deployment leaders, and executives conducted from January through June 2026, along with closed and current open offers. The compensation bands are Christian & Timbers’ estimates and represent ranges rather than statistical averages.

“Enterprise CEOs are under pressure to deliver returns for their AI investments. The most important decision is how to build the team that delivers on that goal,” said Jeff Christian, founder and CEO of Christian & Timbers, in a press release.

The report noted that the staggering salary range includes base salary, bonus, and annualized equity. Christian & Timbers said it defines an “elite” forward deployment engineer (FDE) as “a senior AI-native deployment builder, typically with 7 to 15 years of experience, including at least two years building and deploying agentic automated workflows that deliver measurable ROI with a documented enterprise impact of $10M or more,” who has also led a team of other forward deployment engineers.

Also: 50% of companies generate value from AI now – here’s how

The large salary ranges reflect increasing enterprise investments in AI talent and employee development. Microsoft, AWS, and OpenAI have announced more than $7.5 billion in corporate and partner investment in AI deployment over the past six months, Christian & Timbers noted in the release.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

There’s an increasing need to fill roles such as Senior Principal AI Engineer, AI Solutions Engineer, and Head of Deployment — but there is a limited pool of qualified candidates. The firm estimates that only 2,000 of the most senior deployment leaders exist in the US market, according to a previous Christian & Timbers study, which does not meet demand — so companies are competing for the same small group of professionals, hence the increasing salaries.

While the report underscores lucrative yields for certain engineering roles, the firm said that public job titles make comparisons more challenging.

“Christian & Timbers’ elite category spans several titles, while advertised FDE roles cover a broader range of experience and responsibilities. Experienced deployment engineers may be recruited directly or promoted into the work under titles such as staff software engineer or principal AI engineer,” the study said.

Plus, equity and bonus make up 52% to 66% of senior engineer pay, and most job postings don’t include that value in the salary, the report noted.

#3248. If the White House Network Can Be Hijacked by Proxies, Your Smart Home Is Already at Risk

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

A new report finds residential proxies exiting the White House network 236 times in the past month.

As if the Trump administration needed any more bad news this week, cybersecurity researchers discovered several residential proxy services originating from the White House network, exposing a potential security flaw that could allow cybercriminals to route traffic through official government IP addresses.

The security firm Layer3 Intel detected residential proxy activity on AS2650, a network registered to the Executive Office of the President. Another security firm identified software from the proxy server Infatica, a company owned by a Russian entrepreneur who ran a server-rental company used by hackers in attacks on election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

While there’s no evidence that proxy access was used to carry out attacks on the White House, experts say it could open the door for hackers to exploit vulnerabilities or grant outsiders an unmonitored back door into high-security systems.

“It basically gives them a foothold on a network where previously nobody was getting into the White House network,” Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk told CNET. “From a security policy perspective, it gives you all types of potential pathways to exploit.” (Usatyuk pleaded guilty to federal charges in 2019 for his role in operating websites that launched denial-of-service, or DDoS, attacks.)

Residential proxy services route internet traffic through consumer devices (such as smartphones, laptops or home routers) to make it appear that the activity is being performed by a real person. While proxies can be used for relatively benign purposes — web scraping is by far the most common use case — they’re also popular for activities like malware attacks, identity theft and creating fake social media accounts.

For example, earlier this year, Synthient, another company that tracks proxies and VPNs, documented how one botnet infected more than 2 million devices using a residential proxy server. If a similar vulnerability existed in the White House proxy, hackers could probe the infected device’s internal systems and install malicious payloads.

In its report, Layer3 found traffic from six distinct IP addresses exiting the White House network from at least 28 known residential proxy services between Oct. 5 and Nov. 3, with most activity occurring in the evenings between 5 p.m. and midnight EST. This suggests the culprit may be an employee who connected a personal device to a Wi-Fi network with a compromised app or a proxy SDK (software development kit) running in the background. Third-party SDKs can convert a device into a “proxy node.”

Commercial proxy networks sell access to these nodes, so anyone with a few dollars could rent a trusted IP address — in this case, making it appear as though traffic originates from the Executive Office of the President.

Researchers at Synthient provided more details about the case, posting on X that several White House staffers are running “a Windows 11 machine with InfaticaSDK installed.” They pointed directly to Rave, a popular app that lets users watch streaming services with friends, as the likely delivery mechanism for the residential proxy traffic detected on the White House network.

Riley Kilmer, co-founder of the cybersecurity firm Spur Intelligence, wrote in a LinkedIn post that different types of proxy companies had been discovered in the White House, including one called 9Proxy, which is often used by criminals for banking fraud.

The White House didn’t respond to CNET’s request for comment.

Because smart TVs, connected appliances and home routers usually have minimal user oversight, a single unvetted app or out-of-date firmware update can turn a household of IoT devices into an exit node for commercial proxy networks.

Proxies can generally “glom” onto consumer devices by embedding networking code directly into software, either consensually (users willingly install it) or nonconsensually (by exploiting unsecured device access points).

It starts when app developers look for revenue by integrating those proxy SDKs into their free apps. Then, when you install the app, the fine print of the terms and conditions of service often includes a clause that allows the app to add your IP address to a third-party proxy pool.

A June report from Spur Intelligence found that roughly one in three apps available on Samsung and LG smart TVs were selling users’ IP addresses. To avoid ads, users often accept the terms when downloading the app — a type of unnoticed consent. Once installed, the SDK runs continuously in the background, registering the device’s IP with the proxy provider’s gateway, unless you delete the app or opt out. (The report notes that Amazon and Roku have explicitly banned this practice.)

Using a free VPN could expose you to the same risk, allowing your IP address to be used by someone else for nefarious activities. The FBI’s guidance on protecting yourself against proxies specifically calls out free VPNs as one of the primary ways bad actors gain access to an IP address.

In some cases, you don’t need to download anything to get your IP thrown into a shady proxy pool — you just have to buy the wrong device. A recent investigation by Synthient discovered that more than 1.3 million streaming devices from the China-based device manufacturer MECOOL were infected with proxy SDKs. A proxy service called SocksEscort was charged by the Justice Department in March with compromising thousands of routers to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims.

Checking whether your IP address is being used by a proxy service without your knowledge is relatively simple. Layer3 provides a free proxy-checking tool that searches its database of over 70 million proxies to find if yours is listed. GreyNoise, another cybersecurity company, also offers a free IP-checking service.

These tools can tell you if proxy traffic is passing through your network, but they can’t identify which specific device has the SDK running. You’ll have to do some additional detective work to figure out the culprit. Some common sources include free VPNs, gaming apps, “one price, no subscriptions” streaming boxes and smart TVs.

Cybersecurity experts also recommend keeping the firmware on all your internet-connected devices up to date and downloading only from trusted app stores.

#3247. Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chatbots can skew election-related information and act as an intervening layer in a voter's search.

Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.

Also: Tired of AI Overviews? I found 9 Google Search alternatives

In a new study, Yale researchers found that a third of users asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate. Grok often recommended candidates on its own without any information from users, while ChatGPT recommended candidates most often overall, and twice as much as Claude.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the CareTrust Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Lauren Beale, Chief Accounting Officer. Lauren, please go ahead.

Lauren Beale: Thank you, and welcome to CareTrust REIT's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call.
