During the call, the company will reference non-GAAP metrics such as EBITDA, FFO, and FAD.

A reconciliation of these measures to the most comparable GAAP financial measures is available in our earnings press release and Q3 2026 financial supplement, which are available on the Investor Relations section of CareTrust's website at www.caretrustreit.com. A replay of this call will also be available on the website for a limited period. On the call this morning is Dave Sedgwick, President and Chief Executive Officer; Derek Bunker, Chief Financial Officer; and James Callister, Chief Investment Officer. I'll now turn the call over to Dave Sedgwick, CareTrust REIT's President and CEO. Dave?

David Sedgwick: Thank you, Lauren, and good morning, everybody. Thank you for joining us. Normalized FFO per share is up 20% over last year. And year-to-date, we've set another record of approximately $2.9 billion invested across all 3 growth engines, setting up 2027 to be another strong year of growth. Let me put those figures in context. Over the last few years, since Q4 '22, health care REITs have grown assets by 27%. CareTrust's asset base has grown by 375%. And looking at FFO per share growth from '23 through estimates for this year, health care REIT FFO per share will have grown 30%. CareTrust will have grown 47%.

Looking at forward estimates, today, CareTrust trades at the lowest growth-adjusted multiple of all health care REITs. Rates have certainly moved against everyone this fall. If you've ever wondered why we have maintained extremely low leverage and stockpiles of dry powder while simultaneously growing at a record pace, it's precisely for a market like this. In times of rising rates and uncertainty, sellers prioritize the buyer who will close, and that's us. I'll remind you that our meteoric growth rate began and in no small measure was due to the Fed's aggressive rate hiking in '22 and '23, and during the subsequent higher-for-longer environment.

With last week's announced term loan and upsized revolver, Derek will walk you through how well positioned the balance sheet is today for today's market and for being able to comfortably close on a robust pipeline of accretive investment opportunities ahead. Now on October 1, we crossed the start line on a strategic relationship with LNT. This deal combines 2 growth engines, U.K. care homes and SHOP, with LNT acting as the multiplier. Let me say a word or two about LNT. The owner of LNT, Lawrence Tomlinson, has built more than 250 care homes in his career, and his team is now engineered to deliver around 30 care homes per year.

No other developer in the U.K. comes close to that pace. Standardization, vertical integration, and a talented and driven team are the special ingredients that make LNT one of one. When the ramp-up phase flips from triple-net to SHOP, our first-year NOI yield will be in the high 7% range with a strong runway of growth from there to conservatively achieve our target of double-digit returns. It will be the only portfolio of scale across the U.K. that is brand-new, high-quality, affordable private pay, purpose-built with 100% ensuite wet rooms competing with a market of much older, often converted buildings, 1/3 of which have ensuite wet rooms.

So in a season of fierce competition for SHOP assets, LNT provides us with a truly differentiated SHOP growth engine that will deliver double-digit returns with futureproofed real estate. In addition to LNT, the core growth engines continue to compound. In the third quarter alone, we closed approximately $740 million of investments at a blended stabilized yield of 8.3%, which James will talk to in a minute. This rate of growth can only happen with the right skilled nursing tenants and SHOP management companies. Lease coverage set another record this quarter. Skilled nursing EBITDAR lease coverage hit 2.62x and EBITDARM of 3.26x across the stabilized portfolio, up again from last quarter.

100% of the skilled nursing facility real estate that we own is licensed and run by independent operators under a triple-net lease. This financing structure gives 100% of the operating control to the tenant, which is why when they improve the financial performance of the facilities like you see here, 100% of every dollar above our fixed rent is retained by the operator. So what does this mean in light of our sector-leading lease coverage? It means our operators have the financial capacity to both reinvest into their people and processes and to adapt to an ever-changing operating environment. So here's where we stand as we begin to close out another extraordinary year. The CareTrust flywheel is delivering and accelerating.

The LNT relationship is just getting started and the pipeline continues to reload and our balance sheet has capacity to fund it all. And with that, I'll turn it over to James.

James Callister: Thanks, Dave. Good morning, everyone. As Dave mentioned, in the third quarter, we closed on investments totaling approximately $740 million at a blended stabilized yield of over 8.3%. The largest of these was the 20-facility skilled nursing portfolio in the Southwest that we announced in September. We sourced that transaction off-market and acquired it through a joint venture with a repeat partner. It is triple-net leased to an operator that we know well, and it is a strong example of our off-market pipeline at work.

In total, third quarter investment activity largely consisted of: one, the acquisition of the Southwest skilled nursing portfolio for approximately $399 million; two, approximately $269 million of senior housing triple-net investments, led by a 16-home U.K. care homes portfolio sourced and executed by our London-based team; and three, a 2-community addition to our SHOP platform in Utah for approximately $65 million. We have remained busy since the end of the quarter, closing on just over $1 billion of investments. Headlining that activity was the acquisition of the first 23 LNT homes for approximately $733 million, exclusive of transaction costs.

As previously announced, these homes are triple-net leased to LNT's operating company, Crystal Care, with the ability to convert to SHOP as this asset stabilizes. We also funded approximately $241 million of loans and preferred equity investments with existing operator relationships at a blended yield of approximately 10.9% and closed on the acquisition of 3 care homes in the U.K. for approximately $33 million. Taken together, our 2026 investments now stand at approximately $2.9 billion year-to-date at a blended yield of approximately 8.1%.

That includes $1.2 billion in U.K. care homes, roughly $1.1 billion in U.S. skilled nursing and seniors housing triple-net, approximately $481 million in loans and preferred equity, primarily secured by skilled nursing facilities and closed either concurrently with asset acquisitions or anticipation of them, and approximately $80 million in SHOP. Turning to what lies ahead. Our pipeline currently sits at just over $1.2 billion. Roughly 1/2 of that is the 21 remaining LNT homes under development, which we expect to close between January and September; roughly another 20% is U.S. SHOP; and the balance is skilled nursing, U.K. care homes, and loan activity.

As a reminder on methodology, our pipeline includes only those deals we have a reasonable level of confidence we can close within the next 12 months, and it does not always include larger portfolios we are reviewing. Looking ahead, we expect to keep growing the way we always have, underwriting with discipline, backing operators we trust for the long term, a committed focus on relationships, and structuring deals creatively and collaboratively so that both sides win. This same approach opens the door to more off-market opportunities, and we expect these principles to power our growth going forward. And with that, I'll turn it over to Derek for the financial results.

Derek Bunker: Thanks, James. For the quarter, normalized FFO increased 37% over the prior year quarter to $129.2 million, and normalized FAD increased 36% to $127 million. On a per-share basis, normalized FFO was $0.54, an increase of 20% over the prior year quarter and normalized FAD was $0.53, an increase of 20% over the same period. During the third quarter, we settled all of the 14.4 million shares outstanding under our May forward equity offering for gross proceeds of $578 million. We also issued 7 million shares under our ATM program at a weighted average price of $40.11 for gross proceeds of $280 million.

Subsequent to quarter end, we closed on a new $700 million unsecured term loan maturing in 2032, and we expanded our unsecured revolving credit facility to $2 billion. We use the term loan proceeds to repay borrowings under the revolver and to fund investment activity. We're grateful to our bank partners, existing and new, for their support on both the term loan and the revolver upsize. Together, they provide a deep, reliable source of capital, extend our runway, and position us well to keep funding our growth. In yesterday's earnings press release, we raised the low end of our full year 2026 guidance, which we last increased in October.

We're now projecting normalized FFO per share of $2.08 to $2.09, and normalized FAD per share of $2.04 to $2.05. At the midpoint, that represents growth of 18.5% in normalized FFO per share and 16.2% in normalized FAD per share compared to full year 2025 results.

Our guidance is based on a weighted average diluted share count of 240 million shares and includes the following key assumptions: first, no new investments, loans, or dispositions beyond those made or announced year-to-date; second, no new debt or equity issuances beyond those made year-to-date; third, 2.5% inflation-based rent escalators under our long-term triple-net leases; fourth, $147 million of loans to be repaid throughout the year, of which $111 million have been received so far to date; and fifth, no material change in the pound sterling to U.S. dollar spot exchange rate. Additional guidance measures are detailed in the press release yesterday. Looking forward, our liquidity remains strong.

As of today, it stands at approximately $2.3 billion, including approximately $100 million of cash on hand, $1.6 billion of availability under our $2 billion revolving credit facility, and $599 million of capacity available under our ATM program. Net debt to annualized normalized run rate EBITDA was 1.4x at quarter end. Pro forma, including all investments year-to-date, it's approximately 2.7x, still well below the low end of our long-term target range of 4x to 5x. Our fixed charge coverage ratio was 10.5x at quarter end, and we continue to have no scheduled debt maturities prior to 2028.

It's worth underlining that with the added capacity from our credit facility upsize, we have more than sufficient funds to close on our pipeline and keep leverage below our stated target range. We typically allow about 12 months to close on our stated pipeline. All else equal, if we were to utilize that capacity to fund the pipeline, by the end of 2027, we could be reporting another year of double-digit normalized FFO per share growth while keeping pro forma leverage still well below that range, all without accessing capital markets. And later next year, we expect to begin converting our LNT homes to a RIDEA structure by acquiring the opcos at a 20% yield on in-place EBITDA.

SHOP would then become a more meaningful portion of our run-rate FFO with multiple years of strong growth thereafter, given the quality and vintage of LNT homes. Simply put, our balance sheet is built for the identified and actionable opportunities ahead with flexibility to pull other levers for further accretive investments we source and close. And with that, I'll turn it back to Dave.

David Sedgwick: Great, thanks, Derek. Looking ahead to 2027, with all of its uncertainty, I think after today's update, you understand why we are as bullish as ever about our ability to deliver meaningful per-share growth for our shareholders. Our recent outsized growth in assets and FFO per share has been a result of a differentiated strategy. With LNT, we are again differentiating ourselves by partnering with the envy of the U.K. care home development sector. We look forward to sharing more of the progress as that and our other pipelines deliver. We're happy to take your questions now.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Farrell Granath with Bank of America.

Farrell Granath: About what makes LNT's development model different from other providers and how that's translating into better returns for CareTrust? And then is this an opportunity you could replicate with other partners? Or is it fairly unique to LNT?

David Sedgwick: You were, I think, muted for the beginning of that question. If you wouldn't mind, could you repeat it?

Farrell Granath: Could you just talk about what makes LNT's development model different from other providers? And is this an opportunity you could replicate with other partners?

David Sedgwick: Yes. Thank you. Thanks a lot for the question. I realize this is our first conference call since announcing the LNT deal. So allow me to take a few minutes to provide you maybe a little bit more color than you bargained for with that question, if that's okay. The way we view this deal, we've called it strategic for a reason. If you look at the going-in triple-net yield, that's not really how we measure the value of the deal nor why we characterize it as strategic.

That triple-net yield in 2 to 3 years will be in the high-7% to low-8% range for our first SHOP NOI yield, with plenty of room to run toward our unlevered double-digit returns. So we view the deal in a couple of ways -- we view this pricing in a couple of ways. We bought SHOP at -- if we bought SHOP at a 5.8% cap rate and underwrote year 3 at 7.8%, that's a 16% CAGR for those first couple of years. And essentially, we traded 2 years of growth for downside protection while retaining 28-plus years of upside. And the 7.8% yield is based on a trailing 3 annualized EBITDAR.

If we assume some growth in year 1 of SHOP, call it just 5%, that's actually an 8.2% year 1 SHOP yield. So if you compare that first-year NOI yield for a newly built home to how older assets trade in the U.S. today, I think you see how we view it. If we only measure the value of this acquisition of 45 LNT care homes by the same unlevered return targets we have in the U.S., we would do the deal all day long. But even earning those returns starting from a higher, safer yield is too simplistic of a way to measure the value of the LNT deal or why we characterize it as strategic.

So a little bit more specific to your question. LNT is really the most prolific developer of care homes in the U.K. Their proprietary, vertically integrated, fanatically standardized approach iterated over 30 years, builds homes to an unparalleled yield on cost in the mid-to-high teens, and they're currently capable of delivering around 30 homes per year. And their development pipeline beyond the next homes that we have under contract to buy stand at over 150 sites and counting. It's really why we call them one of one. So our deal with LNT delivers 45 newly developed care homes in initial lease-up phase without prohibitive lease-up risk or dilution.

And the relationship and current deal provide a path to lock up not only that massive and growing SHOP pipeline for ourselves for many years to come, but also to capture those yield-on-cost economics. So the bespoke structure that we have really solves the problem that traditionally prohibit REITs from developing or buying brand-new properties and lease-up. And so, that gives, I think, a lot more than you bargained for, but it describes why LNT is so strategic for us. Would we do other development? Sure, we could here and there, but on a programmatic way at scale, I think LNT is really one of one.

Farrell Granath: We certainly appreciate the additional color there. And maybe just to follow up, beyond the initial 45 homes, how do you see the relationship growing? And what drives the decision to keep acquiring completed homes versus maybe exercising the option to acquire the broader platform in the future?

David Sedgwick: Yes, I think some more color on it is, originally, we were working with LNT to figure out how to acquire the whole development company. And that's where we spent a lot of time this year for 6 months plus, we were trying to figure that out.

Ultimately, we decided that the more prudent approach would be to take this first step of doing an asset deal that will allow us to show our investors how they do deliver, in fact, on time, how they lease up, how the NOI performs, and all these other development metrics, so that as we see that proven to ourselves and proven to our investors, I think the decision to proceed and acquire all of LNT will become self-evident.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Austin Wurschmidt with KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Austin Wurschmidt: Maybe sticking with LNT. Given the basis that these assets have been developed at for all the reasons you cited, one, does that really put them at a competitive advantage from a RevPOR perspective relative to the quality of the assets? And two, does it give them a longer runway or ability to push RevPOR relative to where other developers need to set rate, I guess, to make the economics work for construction?

David Sedgwick: Yes. We believe that's exactly what it does. You answered the question in your question, but the product positioning here is really what we would consider the sweet spot. We entered the U.K. by acquiring a midmarket portfolio that performs very well. Incredibly high lease coverage, high occupancy, and there's certainly a market need for that. A lot of development in the U.K. and in the States targets that high-end luxury sector.

And what the LNT targets is that upper-middle class, so private pay only, but about 10% below that real high-end RevPOR that gives a ton of pricing power and super attractive, especially because it's competing with -- in a market that has about 1/3 of the U.K. care homes today have ensuite wet rooms. And of course, LNT with 100% and being brand new and priced as it is, I think there's going to be a ton of upside there.

Austin Wurschmidt: Maybe could you just frame what that RevPOR spread is versus market or what it would take to develop a new asset today?

James Callister: Yes. Austin, it's James. I think typical development we see in the U.K. runs about GBP 250,000 per unit or so. LNT develops for about GBP 100,000 less than that per unit, I would say. I think their average weekly fee is around GBP 1,500, which I think, like Dave said, is 10%, 15% below what we see in the luxury market above them, which is a great sweet spot, we think, that allows for room to grow in the future given the new nature of the asset, given that it's ensuite wet rooms that are in markets that are pretty significantly under-bedded when it comes to ensuite wet rooms.

Austin Wurschmidt: And then just last one for me, Dave or Derek. Appreciate the commentary about the balance sheet flexibility you've built. But how much does the shift in funding alternatives or how you're thinking about funding, does it change your ability to be competitive with any of the acquisition channels?

Derek Bunker: Austin, it's Derek. I don't think so really. If we look back at similar historical periods in a rising rate or higher-for-longer environment, we've been able to capture more of that market share and deal flow. And I think we came into the most recent higher-for-longer environment this year really well positioned, not just from the balance sheet but the other intangibles, the team in place, the momentum. And that all carries through and keeps that flywheel going. And I think the pressure, if we do face any, is probably perhaps more significant on other players and capital providers.

And we're starting to see, I think, a little bit of that generally, if you look at the HUD market, in particular, where rates are pretty sticky tied to the Treasury. And that's such a common takeout or exit for some of the bridge or alternative financing deal flow, allowing us to be positioned for that growth we feel is just as strong as ever. So we're still very excited. We like our positioning right now and feel like we can keep performing as we have over the past few years.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jamie Feldman with Wells Fargo.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Jesus ] on for Jamie. Just staying with LNT over here. Just sticking with LNT. Once the LNT home ramps towards stabilization, can you talk about the factors that determine whether you convert it immediately to SHOP versus continuing to collect the triple-net rent?

David Sedgwick: Well, I think we're going to be eager to convert. In fact, if there's opportunities to convert buildings that are well on their way to stabilization, we may have conversations with the LNT team about bringing them on earlier. So I think that's going to be our bias is to bring them on earlier rather than later.

Unknown Analyst: Great. And on the $274 million of the recent loan and preferred equity investments you guys made, just how should we think about the durability of that 10.6% yield? And any potential path to future ownership on those assets?

James Callister: [ Jesus ], it's James. So I think the durability is good. Those are great borrowers with great tenants running the buildings. So we really like those investments. Most of those were done with past relationships that we have where either we've already acquired assets with that group or have future deals with them anticipated already that the loans were done in connection with our lending with a purpose. So that's what I would say on the loan since the end of Q3.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Juan Sanabria with BMO Capital Markets.

Robin Haneland: This is Robin Haneland sitting in for Juan. I just wanted to touch on active asset management opportunities. Just given elevated lease coverage in SNFs and senior housing triple-net, do you see any opportunities to monetize some of that profitability and perhaps bring forward earnings growth from rent resets either via asset transitions or otherwise?

David Sedgwick: Yes, it's a great question. First, just philosophically, I think I would say that we have always believed that as far as skilled nursing lease coverage goes, the stronger the better. When underwriting new deals, we regularly sacrifice a little bit of yield for higher tenant coverage. We do not have a short memory about how often tailwinds can turn to headwinds for our tenants there. Having said that, not all tenants and leases are equally strong, and our asset management team is always actively evaluating the portfolio.

Last year we talked about proactively replacing a skilled nursing tenant whose coverage was slipping, and the replacement tenant came in the same rent and immediately brought us better credit and brought the facilities improved stability. And just last month, we again proactively replaced a Midwest SNF operator with a longtime CareTrust tenant who was willing to increase rent by 6%. And that's an example of a replacement tenant leveraging their strong coverage that they have with us to facilitate their growth while improving rent for us. So our asset management team will continue to look for win-win portfolio repositioning just like that.

And like you alluded to, given some of the extremely high covering master leases and evolving plans for some tenants, we expect there to be more opportunities like that in coming years.

Robin Haneland: And on the pro forma leverage, now closer to 2.7x, low but above prior trend levels. How are you thinking about equity to help fund the remaining LNT transactions at the close and/or other future opportunities? And then also the ability to maintain your financial flexibility despite a flattish share price year-to-date and then also being able to generate double-digit growth in '27?

Derek Bunker: Yes. I would just say that from our perspective, we look at where we sit today through the same lens as we have over the past year or 2. We try to look beyond short-term noise. We feel, like I said earlier, pretty well positioned from a balance sheet to flex it either way. And really part of the bank debt rework was to set the table and make sure that we extend the window for us to be opportunistic. So we'll always be price sensitive along with all the other factors that go into how we capitalize our deals. I'll say that if you look at our track record, we've been very active.

And so it would be hard to say that we wouldn't continue to be active in that regard, just to find the balance between really maximizing value for our shareholders while retaining as much flexibility and positioning to keep pursuing the pipeline and beyond because we still feel like we're in early innings of a multiyear growth phase.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Vikram Malhotra with Mizuho.

Vikram Malhotra: I guess just first on the LNT deal and thinking about if and when this converts to RIDEA, I think you've talked about roughly a high 7% yield on conversion or anticipated. And I'm wondering what's the likelihood of that yield being higher, perhaps higher RevPOR or higher margins because I think the occupancy on stabilization is more of a fixed number. But what's the likelihood of that yield being higher based on other top line parameters?

Derek Bunker: I'd say there's a good likelihood, it is. As Dave mentioned, that high 7% going-in yield when we do flip to RIDEA, which is what we're planning on and what LNT is planning on, is on trailing 3 annualized EBITDA. And so assuming no growth, that's year 1. Assuming very modest growth, you're getting into the low 8% yields. And at stabilization, it's really low-90% occupancy, still very, I would say, strong positioning from a RevPOR perspective, given their situation in the market being all private pay, 100% ensuite wet rooms. But at a cost that's 10% to 15% below similar higher-quality assets in the markets that they're competing in.

So we think there's a lot of organic growth beyond that. And I think to be able to step in on proven in-place high 7% yields for 2- to 3-year-old vintage assets at scale with a partner that's developing more and more, I think that is really where we start to get super excited about not just that yield but what the full portfolio, and then some, can do for us.

Vikram Malhotra: And then what about -- just can you clarify the tax impact, either what the rate is likely? Is there room to lower the rate or lower the dollar amount in the U.K. given that high 7s, maybe like a 7-or-something. But are there factors that can drive that tax rate lower?

Derek Bunker: Absolutely. We have opportunity to -- there's some leakage there that we can make some progress on that we're eager to. And I think that's something that we will spend some time focusing on over the next 12 to 24 months, not just for the LNT portfolio, but all of our U.K. assets as well. And so that's achievable. It might take a little time and a little bit of strategy, but we're able to probably capture or to protect about, call it, 1/4 of the leakage we're experiencing right now.

Vikram Malhotra: And then just maybe last one. there was a question asked about, I guess, rent step-ups given coverages in the triple-net SNF portfolio. But I'm wondering within U.S. SNFs, are there other ways to perhaps accelerate the growth, whether it is perhaps taking a position in an opco or perhaps like a RIDEA-like structure in certain select SNF relationships. Any color there, if there's a way to accelerate the -- or take advantage of the still improving operations in your tenants?

David Sedgwick: Yes. Thanks, Vikram. We don't have any plans today to take a RIDEA position with skilled nursing assets. But other things are certainly on the table. I think investing, taking a minority position in an opco could be interesting, as others have done. And I think at the end of the day, like I said a moment ago, we do not have a short memory about skilled nursing and things always tend to change, regulations tend to change, and we really do value our operators having a lot of cushion to be able to adapt to however the regulatory landscape changes.

Having said that, we are actively looking to answer that question, and there's multiple ways to answer it, and we have such massive lease coverage that in our portfolio, in particular, there's going to be interesting ways to tap into that in the coming year.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Dave Rodgers with Raymond James.

David Rodgers: I wanted to ask about the 150-plus sites and counting at LNT that you mentioned. And I think you've alluded to the idea that you guys could be able to get access to those sites. Can you talk about the agreement or any additional agreements that you might have or could structure with LNT that would get you access to those? And should we think about those looking similar to what you're doing now? Or would the time frame be different, negating the current structure?

David Sedgwick: Yes. I think what I would say is that we have a general high-level agreement that would lock up that pipeline in connection with locking up LNT Development Company, that would not just lock up that pipeline, but also as we incorporate LNT would provide a truly differentiated story, which is that we would then capture that mid-to-high-teen yield on cost for all of those for ourselves after we've paid for the company. So there's a really long-term strategic play there that we're considering. But the relationship is such that I think we're really pursuing with LNT a win-win approach.

And I think in coming quarters, we'll get closer to some more specifics that we'll be able to share with you.

David Rodgers: And then maybe one for James on the SHOP acquisitions. I think of that $250 million of the pipeline or so, plus or minus, sounds like it's in U.S. SHOP. Can you just talk maybe a little bit more about what you're seeing there, what you've been targeting, and where you're having success relative to what you've been doing in the U.K.?

James Callister: Yes. I think that when it comes to SHOP, Dave, I think that we really don't like boxes, I guess I'd say. I think that we want to look at everything, and we want to do the right deals. I think that what we're seeing, a lot of what everybody is seeing, and I think that -- we love to always see newer product in great markets. I think that there's a lot of that out there. We're focusing on those deals where we have particular relationships with the seller or with the operator going forward, or we have the right operator solution in place.

And I think we're seeing success in tying a number of those deals up, as you see in the pipe. I think that those deals are really priced pretty consistent with what you're seeing in the market and cap rates in the market, but because of relationships we have with the operator or the seller, we've had success in tying those up. And they create really exciting opportunities going forward. But again, I don't think we're really looking at any particular box.

I think that we recognize, given how much capital is chasing SHOP right now, that you're going to have more success when you can sharpshoot deals that are off-market or that you have a particular in to go and get, and that's what we're focusing on.

David Sedgwick: I think I would just add one little note to that. We're coming up on our first year in the SHOP space as a company. And given what's in our pipeline right now, there's some real near-term SHOP investments that I think will close in Q1. We'll have done about $400 million of SHOP in the U.S. in our first 12 months, give or take 1 month. And as active as it is right now and seeing what the funnel of deals look like that the team is pursuing, I would be really surprised if next year wasn't quite a bit more than that for U.S. SHOP. No pressure, James.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Carroll with RBC Capital Markets.

Michael Carroll: Dave or James, can you talk about what you're tracking on the portfolio side? I know in the prior press releases, CareTrust was pretty overt saying that the stated pipeline excludes portfolio transactions. It didn't seem to be as overt in this most recent update. Is the portfolio availability similar to what it was 3 or 6 months ago? Or was the portfolio that CareTrust was hinting at that LNT deal, and there's fewer out there?

James Callister: I think at the time, the portfolio we were hinting at was the LNT deal, but there's always 2 or 3 large portfolio deals, it seems like, particularly in the SNF space, circulating at a given time, Mike, that I think that we're always looking at. You can't control when those come to market. But I think that's the portfolio deal flow, I think, is pretty consistent with where it's been the last 6 to 12 months. There's always a few circulating.

Michael Carroll: And then, James, on the SNF portfolio transactions, how does CareTrust compete on that? Is that like the relationships that you've created that gives you the inside track on that? Or is the more, I guess, private buyers that are generally more aggressive on pricing that typically makes it harder to get those deals done? I guess what's the give or takes there on the ability to complete a larger SNF transaction?

James Callister: Other than my pretty face, Mike, I would say that...

David Sedgwick: Mike, that was a softball. You should know better.

James Callister: If you think about the fact that such a larger portion of SNF deals are off-market and are not marketed, unlike the SHOP space, that I think you really have to have a committed focus on relationships, and that's what drives a good portion of the deals. And I think also we benefit a lot from the fact that we have been involved in so many of the bigger deals that we do get more calls, I think, because of that. When you combine the relationships plus the track record, I think we're towards the top of the list of buyers for any of the larger or medium-to-large-sized transactions that come out. I think we've shown we've benefited from that.

And I think deal flow will continue to show us benefiting from that. But I would say it's predominantly a relationship-driven market on the SNF side, particularly with medium-to-large size deals.

Michael Carroll: I thought you were going to say it's predominantly because of your good looks.

James Callister: Well, that too. equally.

Michael Carroll: If I can switch on one more and to give to Derek. if I look at the purchase option disclosure in the supp, it looks like there could be roughly $340 million of transactions that could be exercised before the year-end in '27. Obviously, some of these is just the option window opens and still has several years before it closes. How many of those purchase options could be exercised, I think, by the end of next year? And does the recent jump in interest rates make it less likely that those get exercised here in the near term?

Derek Bunker: Yes. It's tough because we base it on not just at the inception of the lease or when the option was written, the feedback that the tenant provided, but basically on ongoing conversations with them. And those can change, as you mentioned, on interest rates, but also on other factors that they're considering. They've got diverse portfolios, they have other needs that drive sellers and operators. So it does change, period to period. I would say, generally, we like to view it, I think, conservatively and assume that most, if not all, would be exercised early in the window. Now, obviously, that's not always the case.

And I think looking back on the recent history, most have, but certainly, we've seen some that haven't. And we could point to interest rates or other considerations from those tenants and not exercising. I think certainly, logically, but also anecdotally, we've seen higher rates pressure a bit those tenants with those options. And I think we're well positioned there to either extend or to offer other solutions for their portfolio as they look to not just exercise this option, but how can they look at the portfolio in whole. So I think overall, we would probably assume most of those would be exercised.

Now as you could see, some of that is just -- some of those are multiwindow options, and our disclosure is really about the first of what could be several tranches. And so it's not 100%. And even within that subset, it's probably likely that at least some will consider their options at that point and decide to pursue a different path.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Omotayo Okusanya with Deutsche Bank.

Omotayo Okusanya: Congrats on the quarter. You guys put up massive numbers, 20% earnings growth, great rent coverage, everything is going in the right direction, but yet you have flat stock performance this morning. And I think the key question everyone's asking is how sustainable is this going forward. Derek, I think you gave a couple of really good points earlier on about what 2027 growth could look like, still in the double digits, just given what the pipeline looks like.

But again, the key question is just given cost of capital is going up, even with all the liquidity that you have, how do we get comfortable with this idea that this really is a multiyear growth story rather than growth dramatically slowing in 2028, for example. It sounds like '27 is going to be pretty good. But like in '28, how do we think about no risk of a huge step down in earnings growth?

David Sedgwick: Well, you can't predict the future. But one way to help predict the future is to build it. And I think the LNT relationship does provide us an opportunity to answer that question for many years to come. If, in fact, we lock up LNT and that seemingly endless pipeline, that's years and years of brand newly developed SHOP assets that you can bank on. But in addition to that, if you look at -- I think that question was, when we got that question in 2024, it made a lot of sense.

And in fact, I remember answering that question with some timidity because we had gone from doing $225 million a year for the first 9 years of our existence to $1.5 billion, and we got asked that question. In the middle of that explosive growth, is this a blip or not? And I remember being maybe a little bit too honest by saying, yes, I'm not sure. We'll see. And then we followed that up with $1.8 billion and then now $2.9 billion. The difference going forward from the growth that we've had is that today our team is bigger and better and more capable. The access to capital is fantastic.

The liquidity is there, and we are in -- we have more opportunities and engines for growth than we did a few years ago. So that's why I would say, unlike when I had to answer that question in '24, when this growth story really started kicking in, I don't have the timidity as I look forward in the next near-to-mid term, and we're very confident that we're going to be able to continue to grow in a meaningful way.

Omotayo Okusanya: There's a lot of swag in your LinkedIn post, I'll have to say that, Dave.

Omotayo Okusanya: And then one more follow-up, if you don't mind. On the SHOP side, I know a lot of your peers are out there giving a whole bunch of targets, who want to be 30% SHOP by this time or 40% SHOP by this time. Are you guys thinking along that same mindset? And if you are, could you just lay that out? And generally, what growth profile you also expect from SHOP on a going-forward basis, whether it's LNT or when you kind of think bigger picture?

David Sedgwick: Yes. We really love -- like I just said, we've positioned our company strategically, I would say, in a differentiated way from many of our peers. And I think, as you mentioned at the beginning, our results have been differentiated as well. We really like to be able to grow in skilled nursing, in SHOP, and in care homes, and now a fourth U.K. SHOP method with LNT. Having said that -- and so we haven't put out targets. We don't want to box ourselves in to not do great accretive deals in skilled nursing because it's going to hinder our ability to hit some stated goal.

Having said that, we fully expect SHOP in the U.S. and U.K. combined to become very meaningful parts of our portfolio in coming years. We just don't have a target that we're trying to hit.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Goldsmith with UBS.

Michael Goldsmith: Maybe following up on that last question, Dave and DB, you've got more levers to pull today than you've had in the past between U.S. skilled nursing, U.S. SHOP, U.K. care, LNT, and credit. So if you're allocating the next dollar of capital today, where are you seeing the best risk-adjusted return? And if there's -- is there any channel that you'd like to deploy more significantly to, but just pricing or availability is holding you back?

David Sedgwick: if you set them all side by side, ultimately, you get to very similar risk-adjusted returns. And that's why we love all of our kids the same. We really don't right now -- we're not in a position where we're having to choose between the 2 or 3 or 4. We take it 1 deal at a time, case by case, and we try to get the best risk-adjusted returns we can get. And they're all very similar based on our disciplined underwriting.

Michael Goldsmith: And then as a follow-up, James, on the SHOP, it really seems like you've stepped out of the shade and into the sun on the pipeline there. Just are you still underwriting the current pipeline to low-double-digit unlevered IRRs? And maybe you can frame the going-in yields and the NOI growth you're expecting in the first couple years? And then also just how would you characterize the mix between stabilized assets and deals you're underwriting were meaningful upside over time?

James Callister: Yes. So Michael, I think that as cap rates compress, you really have to have an increased conviction on the growth story of the assets that we're looking at. We still want to underwrite to that low double-digit unlevered IRR, 10-year hold. I think that what you're seeing in the market today really is some lease-up stuff that has higher year-over-year growth stuff, but most of what's out there is pretty stabilized stuff with occupancy in the 90s. So it becomes increasingly important to remain disciplined in the underwriting and have the right sharpshooter operator who's going to be able to drive growth going forward and having really the right metrics and indicators of growth for those assets.

I think that with cap rate compression, that's becoming more important. And the temptation to do volume for volume's sake has to be put in the back seat, and you have to focus on the right underwriting conviction and the growth story that you can get to that IRR.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Mike Mueller with JPMorgan.

Michael Mueller: Yes. Derek, I think you said you could generate double-digit growth in '27 without accessing the capital markets just by using the debt capacity you have to fund the pipeline. Question is, is that the plan? Or was it more of an academic statement and you're likely to continue to tap equity to at least partially fund it?

Derek Bunker: Yes. I think it was a little more of the latter, thought exercise. And I think we view that as a fallback and a sort of Plan C, if you will. We don't want to have to rely on certain sources of capital. But I think given where we have been able to tap capital over the past couple of years and where we sit today, we're super confident that we will be able to access capital markets. It was to suggest what it would look like without that. Although our stock price has come in, I think we're still seeing a ton of accretive opportunities even at these levels.

So I wouldn't be surprised to see us continue to participate somewhat in other forms of capital. But for us, the analysis is pricing, duration, and the multifactor approach we typically look at, that would only be what we see as an improvement over utilizing the revolver.

Michael Mueller: And then in thinking about the current interest rate volatility and looking back over time, what has it taken to get the going-in SNF yields to deviate materially from the 9% level that we tend to think of?

Michael Mueller: Either way. It just seems like rates could just jump or go down and you see 9s across the board.

David Sedgwick: I think that for the 25-plus years I've been in the business, they simply haven't moved much at all, regardless of political, regulatory, economic pendulum swings. And I think the reason for that is there's a constant tension between a bid for these assets and the stroke of the pen risk, headline risk that keeps it right where it's at. So skilled nursing has proven to be very, very sticky.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Rich Anderson with Cantor Fitzgerald.

Richard Anderson: So on LNT, how many beds are we talking about in the 45 homes? I'm guessing around 3,000. Is that right?

David Sedgwick: So when I talked about LNT, I said that they are hyper-standardized. They really have 1 building size that has like 3 different templates, and there's 66 units in each.

Richard Anderson: So that's about 3,000 units. And so if I'm doing my math right, you're buying them at $500,000 a bed. James, you said earlier, and using U.S. dollars, that development out there is $335,000 a bed. So that sounds like paying above replacement cost. Again, correct me if I'm wrong. I'm just spitballing here. And I coincide that observation with why would they be willing to pay you during the lease-up -- why would they willing to be taking that hit upfront? And perhaps the reason is because they're being compensated upfront with these purchase prices. Is that the right way to think about it?

James Callister: Yes, I think that is the right way to think about it. And I think the relationship drove that structure as well. And I think when you add [indiscernible] the scale together with -- you can definitely get caught up on the per unit price. But I think if you look at the opportunity in 18 months, 2 years, whenever it is, to convert to RIDEA at a high 7s, low 8, that per unit price, we'd do that deal all day here if we could. And so I think that it is the scale. I think that they are willing to cover the lease payment over this period because of the price that we paid.

And we view it as when we get in there and take over RIDEA, it's still an advantageous return to us, particularly given the lack of similar opportunities that we see at that scale and that vintage of asset here in the States.

Richard Anderson: Second question is, this is a higher quality ensuite wet rooms, as they say. And your Care REIT transaction was not that. And I'm wondering if that gives you comfort, like bookending the U.K. opportunity where on one side of the ledger, it's middle market quality triple-net, and this is higher quality, ultimately SHOP. Is that the way you're thinking about it? Are you trying to surround the opportunity in the U.K.? Am I saying that right? Again, not to put words in your mouth.

David Sedgwick: Yes, I think that is how we see it. I think we really like the triple-net business there because middle market, because the lease coverage is so strong and occupancy is so high. But as we think about our SHOP strategy in the U.K., like in the United States, we prefer newer, higher-end properties for our SHOP play.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Alec Feygin with Baird.

Alec Feygin: Dave and team, I appreciate you guys answering all our questions. I'll just do one. With your long memory in the skilled nursing industry, do you have any views going into maybe the next year or two with the big win in the midterms and the changing of the party in both houses of Congress?

David Sedgwick: Yes. Look, I've been personally in skilled nursing and senior housing for over 25 years. I've seen just about every type of government composition in D.C. And, during the Big Beautiful Bill debate, we reemphasized repeatedly that senior care is one of those very few issues that has bipartisan support. And we saw that play out in that bill as it got passed. And so I think that what we've seen over the years is that both sides really do believe that seniors deserve adequate funding, appropriate regulation, good care. And we welcome any opportunity to highlight the strong lease coverage, the star ratings, the quality metrics that our tenants provide for the sector.

So happy to work with whoever is currently in power.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time, and we have reached the end of the Q&A session. I will now turn the call back to Dave Sedgwick for closing remarks.

David Sedgwick: Thank you, everybody, for your questions and interest. You know where to find us if you've got follow-ups. We hope you have a great weekend.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

With October in the can, we can finally say goodbye to the Sunday scaries. Hoorah! Now that Netflix’s November 2026 schedule is set, we’ve got plenty of great new content to get stuck into. This week, I’ve gone for a trio of shows that contain mercifully few frights.

First up is the highly-anticipated second season of “Black Doves”, where Keira Knightley continues to shine as the wife of the British Prime Minister… oh, and she’s also a covert spy. Next is the debut of “Will Trent” on Netflix. If you’ve slept on this charming detective drama, you’ve got a whole lot of binge-watching ahead of you this weekend with all four seasons now available. Lastly, season two of “North of North” is streaming, and Siaja’s chilly Canadian misadventures continue to delight.

Whether you're pining for spy thrills or gentle laughs with a detective and his tiny pooch, here are three fresh Netflix releases you should definitely add to your weekend watchlist.

Talk about the best of British. “Black Doves” season 2 rocks an absolutely stellar cast of Blighty greats. Keira Knightley continues to impress as a covert agent who keeps leaking national secrets for the titular spy agency. Naughty Keira! She’s reunited with her handler Mrs. Reed (a typically charismatic Sarah Lancashire), who promptly goes missing, driving much of this season’s plot.

Our secrets-sharing protagonist also gets reacquainted with her best pal Sam (Ben Whishaw), who just so happens to be a professional assassin… and a bit of a drunk. This high-tension drama also benefits from the arrival of “Scream” legend Neve Campbell. Well plotted and stylishly shot, you can tell the Big N has chucked a huge amount at this thriller.

Watch "Black Doves" season 2 on Netflix now

The first four seasons of this detective drama are now available to stream on Netflix, and "Will Trent" really does feel like a love letter to “Monk”. Tipping its hat to Tony Shalhoub’s awkward but brilliant homicide cop, the titular star of this show (played by Ramón Rodríguez) also struggles in social situations due to his dyslexia. Yet there’s no other agent you’d want on your case if you suddenly found your corpse ditched down a drainpipe.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Much of the action of “Will Trent” focuses on whether our hero can Sherlock his way through various Atlanta-based crimes. But the real hook beyond your standard police procedural tropes? That would be Will’s relationship with a newly adopted chihuahua called Bluebell. This easy going show has serious “Turner & Hooch” vibes. I’m all in.

Watch "Will Trent" seasons 1-4 on Netflix now

Talk about a perfect show for these dark winter months. Focused on Ice Cove, Nunavut, this breezy comedy is set in Canada’s northernmost territory, meaning there’s a whole lot of daylight action. We’re once again back with Siaja (Anna Lambe), a young mother who’s still trying to figure out life post-divorce. In this second season, romance is back on the table, as our Inuk heroine enters the icy pools of the speed dating scene.

A big part of the show focuses on community, and Siaja now has to deal with new job demands under her boss Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub, who you might remember as the irrepressible Chloe from “24”). “North of North” doesn’t trade in Jack Bauer breakneck action, but the show’s gentle laughs are occasionally punctuated with low-stakes drama, like a mini water crisis. Easy giggles and gorgeous scenery. What’s not to like?

Watch "North of North" season 2 on Netflix now

Dave was a computing editor at Tom’s Guide who covered everything from cutting edge laptops to ultrawide monitors. Now he contributes to the site in a freelance capacity. When he’s not worrying about dead pixels, Dave enjoys regularly rebuilding his PC for absolutely no reason at all. In a previous life, he worked as a video game journalist for 15 years, with bylines across GamesRadar+, PC Gamer and TechRadar. Despite owning a graphics card that costs roughly the same as your average used car, he still enjoys gaming on the go and is regularly glued to his Switch. Away from tech, most of Dave’s time is taken up by walking his husky, buying new TVs at an embarrassing rate and obsessing over his beloved Arsenal.

#3243. Is Chrome’s settings menu getting a search bar? What we know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chrome might receive a much-needed addition.

I’m a longtime Chrome user, but I’ve never been a fan of the browser’s user settings menu, which has grown into a dense collection of nesting submenus that can be difficult to navigate. That may be changing soon.

Also: How Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

X (formerly Twitter) user, Leopeva64, posted a short video and several still images showcasing a potential new feature in Chrome Canary, which Google uses to test new Chrome web tools and features. The posts show the search bar pinned to the top of the settings menu for instant access. By entering the name of the submenu or feature you want to access, the new search bar could save a lot of time normally spent clicking around, trying to remember exactly where it’s located.

In Chrome Canary, Google is testing removing the scroll arrows that let you automatically scroll to reveal hidden items when you hover over them in the 3-dot menu. They also added a scrollbar, and the search box at the top and the footer are now pinned so they are always visible: https://t.co/Plx6BgKfJN pic.twitter.com/D7TxDkCtmP

According to Leopeva64, other possible new features include a visual update that groups similar menu options into tiles for faster navigation of your most-accessed settings, as well as pinning the menu footer to keep it visible as you click through.

Chrome Extensions is also up for a possible refresh with a move to a dedicated submenu called Manage Skills to help keep all of your installed extensions organized and make it easier to remove ones that are no longer needed.

Also: How to take full-page screenshots in Chrome on any device – it’s easy and free

Google Lens may get a new submenu, called “Ask Google about this page,” for searching for items you see across an entire page, not just in a single image.

There’s no official word yet on when these features will leave Canary’s testing environment and become available in the regular Chrome menu. I’ve reached out to Google for a comment, but at the time of writing, I have not received a response.

#3242. Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: New features and other upgrades to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

It starts with a surprise version number: Linux Mint 27 instead of 24. But the next release brings far more changes than that.

Linux Mint, my favorite Linux desktop distribution, is ready for a fresh start.

Its lead developer, Clement “Clem” Lefebvre, announced earlier this year that the team behind it was considering slowing Mint’s release cadence because the old twice-a-year release cycle was time-consuming and constrained their ability to make major changes. So it is that the next release, Linux Mint 27, will appear in your Christmas stocking.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for in 2026

The developers officially changed the designation on Oct. 13th when Mint changed both its release cadence and its numbering. Clem’s happy about the change: it “was a tough decision to make, but we’re really starting to see it pay off. We’re taking on projects and implementing changes which would previously have been considered too large or ambitious.”

The new Mint will use Ubuntu 26.04 Long Term Support (LTS) as its base. As before, it will offer Cinnamon, Xfce, and MATE desktops.

Earlier development snapshots had been labeled Mint 23 “Alfa.” That title was explicitly a placeholder while the team decided its release strategy. Its final name is Adrien. Moving ahead, release numbers will be based on the upcoming year. Clem said, “We’ll no longer use point releases, so the release after that will be 28. You’ll upgrade from 27 to 28 to 29, and so on.” Instead of girls’ names, Mint will use boys’ names for distro titles.

On Halloween, Clem announced the top changes in Mint 27. It starts with Mint bringing hibernation back into its supported desktop configuration through a dedicated Sleep Modes page in its System Administration tool. The page is intended to make enabling and configuring hibernation easier, including addressing its swap-space requirements.

It may not sound like much, but Clem explained it’s actually rather a big deal. “When you close the lid of your laptop, it goes into a sleep mode called “Suspend”. This mode is very useful… but it has a major limitation: It uses power.” People often forget it’s not really off and that your laptop will eventually run out of power. When that happens, “the outcome is worse than a normal shutdown. The session is gone, and the battery is empty.”

Also: Linux Mint vs. RefreshOS: I compared the two best distros for new users

That’s where “Hibernation comes into play. It saves the session to disk and completely shuts down the computer. No power is used. When you reopen the lid, the session is as it was, and so is the battery.”

Another new feature is Superlight. This fresh system-monitoring application replaces the older GNOME System Monitor. It comes with CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan-speed graphs. It also includes per-application and per-process resource views. Battery-equipped systems also get charge and power-flow history.

Its storage analysis is particularly interesting: it can break down disk usage into files and folders, Steam games, and Flatpak applications. That brings several common troubleshooting tasks — “What’s using the CPU?” and “Where did my disk space go?” — into one interface. I’ve been checking it out on a Mint virtual machine (VM), and I like it already.

The Nemo file manager is getting a media preview pane, toggled with F7 or a status-bar button. It supports pictures, audio, and video, and displays associated information — for photographs, that can include the capture date and camera model. I like this feature a lot. I’ve always done a lot of work from file managers going all the way back to the classic Norton Commander and its Linux successor, Midnight Commander.

I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again. You don’t need to ever touch a Linux shell via a terminal to use Mint. But if, like me, you’re an old-school Linux user and you like using the terminal, Velocitty, Mint’s new terminal application, looks interesting. Its announced features include:

The point is to make recurring projects and SSH sessions easier to find and reopen. If you like other terminal programs, my latest fave is the Rust-based WexTerm; you don’t have to use Velocitty.

Unfold is a new archive manager for viewing, creating, and extracting archives. It uses 7-Zip and 7zip-RAR and supports the encryption formats those backends handle, including password-protected archives. Its design goal is simplicity rather than a sprawling feature set.

The new Mint uses Ubuntu 26.04 LTS as its foundation. Mint is also moving from Ubiquity to the Linux Mint Debian Edition live installer for installing the operating system. This fresh installer comes with support for OEM bulk-produced installations, installation on both BIOS and EFI PCs, support for Secure Boot, and LVM/LUKS configurations.

Also: Linux Mint vs. Zorin OS: I’ve tried both Windows alternatives, and here’s my winner

For the Linux kernel, Mint 27 will use version 7.0. Which one exactly? Good question. We’ll see closer to Christmas.

Wayland compatibility remains the goal, but X11 isn’t disappearing. As Clem said in June, “In an ideal scenario, we manage to make Wayland work just as well as X11.” But they’re not there yet.

The central change is a cleanup of existing code. Mint’s longer cycle gives developers room to overhaul several parts of the desktop together, rather than squeezing individual improvements into six-month windows. As Clem put it in the September newsletter, “I don’t think I’ve ever seen so many changes and new features implemented for a single release.”

What that means for you and me will be better laptop power management, more capable built-in utilities, and a more complete collection of everyday desktop applications. For example, I expect the updated Mint will ship with GIMP 3.2.2 as its default photo editor, instead of Mint 22.3’s years-old GIMP 2.10.

#3241. A Wall-Mounted Smart Garden Is Peak Winter Decor (and a Great Gift)

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I tested Modern Sprout's handsome Growframe for a pop of green during fall and winter.

My pursuit of good houseplant tools means I’m always looking for shops and resources. That led me to Modern Sprout, a Chicago-based online store that sells plants and plant-care accessories. When they reached out offering a chance to test some of its high-design indoor garden tech, I decided to see what, if anything, is worth considering for your houseplant needs or as a place to get gifts for the plant parents in your life. I found a few pleasant surprises.

Whether I’m tending to houseplants in winter or gardening in summer, I’m always looking for tools to improve plant care. For houseplants in particular, this means watering, trimming, fertilizing, occasionally repotting and providing as much real estate in sunny windows as possible. When that’s not enough, I harness the power of full-spectrum LED grow lights, so I can have greenery in practically every room of my apartment.

A quick look at Modern Sprout’s website shows it sells most of what you’d expect from a boutique plant nursery: live plants, potting soil, gardening accessories, grow lights, grow kits, candles, bird feeders and gift sets. While Modern Sprout carries plenty of its own products, it also curates items from other small businesses instead of relying on large mainstream gardening brands. This is a nice bonus for folks who prefer to support smart business owners. Modern Sprout also offers wholesale accounts, so you might even see it at a nursery near you.

For my tests, I stuck to the Modern Sprout brand, which is also available on Amazon. Since I review a lot of smart home gear, I wanted to try out the Smart Landscape Growframe ($229) and compare it with other plant light options I use. I also wanted to see if Modern Sprout’s tools are any good, so I rounded out my experience with three essentials behind effective houseplant care: Pruning Shears ($20), a Glass Watering Can ($48) and Dissolving Plant Food Sheets ($20).

I don’t think anything could’ve prepared me for the size of the Smart Landscape Growframe: 32.1 inches long, 11.5 inches tall and 5.3 inches deep. For some context, that’s wider than my kitchen table and large enough to require a careful survey of my home to find a suitable location. I found a nice spot above my stairs next to the front door.

Additionally, its durable powder-coated steel frame weighs an incredible 8 pounds. That’s roughly the weight of a gallon of milk, which makes wall mounting tricky. I agree with Modern Sprout’s recommendation to place the mounting screws in studs, so you’ll need a stud finder, a level, and a power drill if you want it on the wall. You can use drywall anchors, but they aren’t included.

Make sure you visually line up the Growframe’s mounting holes with your marks before driving screws into the wall. This is easier with a second person, but I managed it alone. However, I relied purely on my measurements and had to redo the screws after one was slightly off. I suggest marking one stud first, then holding the planter and using a level to see where the other should go. Similarly, keep in mind that the 9-foot power cord needs to reach an outlet.

The app isn’t complex and is really easy to use. I really like that there are preset schedules for shade, partial sun and full sun light levels — these options always start at 8 a.m., providing 8, 12 and 16 hours of lighting at different intensities, respectively. The presets aren’t customizable, so you must use one of the app’s two other scheduling options to adjust the timing and other settings. I noticed that toggling a preset works as intended, but closing and reopening the menu shows an inactive toggle — a minor visual bug that doesn’t seem to affect the feature. (It might even get patched by the time you read this review.)

You can also set a schedule using specific times of day in the Growframe device menu. While this particular scheduling menu lacks an option to tie the lighting controls to sunrise and sunset, you can find that on the Scenario tab. (Sunrise/sunset automation isn’t necessary for most tropical plants and herbs people put in the planter, but it’s nice to have a temperate lighting option that changes throughout the year.)

The Scenario tab offers a few automation options based on device status, scheduling and weather changes, plus a way to set up manual Tap-to-Run automations. Beyond that, there isn’t much else to the app, which makes sense and aligns with the company’s goal of keeping things simple. However, folks wanting smart home integrations with a platform like Home Assistant or Samsung SmartThings might be better off using a smart plug with a different grow light brand.

Speaking of grow lights, the full-spectrum unit inside the top of the Smart Landscape Growframe can reach up to 1,480 lumens, which is very bright considering most plants in the planter will be within 6 inches or less. Given the size limit on the plants you can put in the planter, I doubt you’ll have any issues with giving your plants enough light. I want to note that the adhesive holding one of the grow light strips in my sample unit came loose during shipping, but it was easy enough to reattach.

Planting in the Smart Landscape Growframe is fairly easy. It comfortably holds up to seven potted plants (2- to 3-inch pots), though I ended up putting five 4-inch potted herbs in my setup. One pot in particular is a little taller than the planter box lip, but it doesn’t bother me.

Be mindful of pot size in the planter, as rims that press up against the side can cause water to overflow onto the floor, as it did with mine. The best solution is to remove a little soil from overfilled pots and to add a small notch or hole in a side of the pot that drains into the basin.

The potted herbs I got from my local garden center needed a little trimming before I could put them in the Smart Landscape Growframe, so it was a good opportunity to try out the Pruning Shears. I’m a huge fan of the all-metal design, which is easily one of the most comfortable pairs of gardening shears I’ve used. The nifty locking latch at the end of the handle isn’t metal — it doesn’t need to be — but it’s easy to use and doesn’t require any fiddling.

I also love the needle-nose blades, which are easy to maneuver into tight spaces when trimming dead growth off plants — they are great for trimming all of my herbs. Although I’ll admit that the densely packed chives tested my patience, that’s hardly the shears’ fault.

Of the items I tested, the glass watering can was my least favorite. For instance, the borosilicate glass may be more durable than other types of glass, but it’s still glass and still fragile. I’m not sure if I trust my clumsy self with it when I water my plants. Similarly, the 1-quart size is great for folks caring for a handful of plants, but it can’t keep up with the gallon-size watering can that I sometimes empty completely just to water my dwarf lemon tree in a large container.

Another issue I had with the glass watering can was the upper rim. While I like that the flared rim makes it easy to fill from my bathroom sink, it can get in the way when watering the Growframe. This is especially tedious when you need to tilt the watering can nearly vertical to get the last drops out. Fortunately, you can see when the water is almost gone, but that’s the only real advantage it has over my normal watering can.

I often put off fertilizing houseplants because it feels like a hassle. My main reason is that most of the carnivorous plants I grow don’t like fertilizer, so I skip it on other houseplants. (I get around this with plant food spikes, but I’m hardly consistent at that either.) A secondary reason is that keeping the fertilizer out where I’ll use it isn’t the best use of space in my apartment. While Modern Sprout’s Dissolving Plant Food Sheets don’t really solve the former problem, they’re very convenient for the latter.

Just like when I tested dishwasher detergent sheets, I really like how easy it is to toss Modern Sprout’s fertilizer into the watering can. A full sheet treats a gallon and has perforations so you can tear it into segments to fit your watering can. Since the glass watering can holds one quart, I needed only one-quarter of a sheet. The sheets dissolved a little slowly, and I had to stir them for a minute or two before no fragments were left.

I’m a fan of the seaweed sheets, which are a great option for plant food that isn’t entirely a collection of processed chemicals. Despite the seaweed ingredient, the sheets don’t explicitly state they’re certified organic, so keep that in mind if you use them for herbs or microgreens.

All of the Modern Sprout products I tested have a premium design and build quality that makes them easy to recommend for people who value form as much as function. I consider the Pruning Shears the best value in the bunch. They feel incredibly sturdy and capable for $20 and are a huge step up from my $10 Vivosun Gardening Scissors in every way. I haven’t tested Modern Sprout Bypass Hand Pruners, but I suspect they’ll easily rival the Fiskars Shears I use for thicker growth.

While $229 is a lot to ask for the Smart Landscape Growframe, keep in mind that premium heavy-duty steel planters without smart lighting already cost more than those made from other materials. Likewise, more affordable — and more powerful — grow lights are on the market, but Modern Sprout’s intuitive app includes every scheduling and customization feature I consider essential. Even people who don’t use other smart home gear should find it easy to navigate.

I think the Dissolving Plant Food Sheets are a fairly nice option for seaweed-based fertilizers, but the 20-pack will treat only 20 gallons of water at the normal dilution. This makes the sheets generally more expensive per feeding than liquid kelp fertilizers from brands like TPS Nutrients and Grow Queen. That said, Modern Sprout is more convenient to measure, and it won’t cause a liquid or powdery mess if you knock the package over. It’s a great gift, but not necessarily for an enthusiast with a large collection of houseplants.

I wouldn’t buy the Glass Watering Can, but I don’t think it’s a bad product. It’s undeniably attractive, but $48 is more than most. I’ll stick with my cheaper, larger plastic watering can. Overall, Modern Sprout suits folks with higher budgets or as an attractive gift option for your favorite plant nerd.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The wait is over for trying Siri AI on iOS 27. Here's what you need to know to get started.

Enabling Siri AI, Apple’s new generative AI-powered virtual assistant, on a compatible Apple device running iOS 27 used to prompt a message informing the user that the device would be added to a waitlist with varying wait times. Now, you can download Siri AI automatically as soon as you enable it on your compatible iPhone, Mac, or iPad. The one exception is that, if there is unusually high demand, Apple could temporarily reinstate its waitlist.

You’ll need a compatible device that runs Apple Intelligence, like an iPhone (15 Pro or newer), iPad (Mini A17 Pro or newer or an M-series chip), Mac (MacBook Neo or M-series chip), Apple Watch (Series 9 and Ultra 2 or newer), or Apple Vision Pro.

Instead of adding you to a waitlist, Siri AI will begin downloading right away.

Siri AI is Apple’s upgraded virtual assistant, now powered by generative AI. Instead of giving you canned responses to your questions, Siri AI will be able to answer complex questions, understand more natural-sounding phrases, and maintain context throughout conversations and across your Apple ecosystem.

ZDNET’s Lance Whitney recommends using Siri AI’s onscreen awareness feature to ask it for directions, explain something you see on your phone’s screen, or to add items from your screen to a list. He also uses Siri AI to edit his photos simply by asking for the changes he wants. But that’s just skimming the surface. You can read more about Whitney’s experiences using Siri AI here.

Also: I thought I had Siri AI in iOS 27 – until I found it hidden in my settings

For years, Apple has been working to gain relevance in AI to compete with major players like OpenAI and Google. While Apple Intelligence features like Writing Tools, Genmoji, and Image Playground have helped, Apple has lagged far behind in upgrading its signature voice assistant to generative AI.

iOS 27 delivered Siri AI in beta this fall, along with iPadOS 27, MacOS 27 Golden Gate, VisionOS 27, and WatchOS 27.

You need a compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, or Apple Vision Pro to use Apple Intelligence features like Siri AI. Not all Apple devices that support the latest iOS 27 (or other OS 27) will support Siri AI.

Here are the Apple devices that support Siri AI:

You also need to have your device in a supported language (English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, or Spanish) and to reside in a supported region (not available in mainland China or in iOS, iPadOS, or WatchOS in the European Union).

#3238. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.
