You’ll also get an in-stay credit when you book a vacation home through The Edit for four nights or more.

Starting in 2027, Chase’s The Edit collection of upscale hotel and resort stays will broaden to include more than 10,000 vacation homes. If you carry the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, that means you’ll soon have more ways to use The Edit credits on those cards.

This addition will significantly expand The Edit’s footprint — currently at more than 1,500 hotels and resorts — although its usefulness will depend on your travel style. The new properties are curated in partnership with Plum Guide, a vacation-rental booking platform.

Plus, when you book a stay of four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use at your vacation home.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming changes to The Edit.

Eligible Chase cardholders can currently book vacation homes through the issuer’s travel portal. However, those bookings are not eligible to receive The Edit benefits. That changes Jan. 1, 2027, with select listings.

If you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, here’s what you can expect when you book a vacation home through The Edit:

Up to $250 in statement credits on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardholders are capped at $500 in credits a year, while Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders get up to $1,000 (starting Jan. 1, 2027).

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

Compared to booking hotels and resorts with The Edit, you’re losing out on perks like a $100 property credit (which doesn’t have a four-night minimum), complimentary breakfast and room upgrades.

While cardholders will be able to redeem points toward vacation-home stays, Chase told NerdWallet that these bookings will not be eligible for Points Boost at launch.

You’ll also need to book vacation homes at least seven days in advance — a requirement that’s currently in place with standard vacation homes available in Chase’s travel portal. Chase said it plans to reduce that requirement in the near future.

Chase’s addition of vacation homes to The Edit follows American Express’ recent move to add Airbnb Luxe properties to its own lodging credit for eligible cardholders.

When you book a vacation home for four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use on services like massages, a private chef, dry cleaning and airport pick-ups.

Options vary by property, but you’ll see a list of available offerings prior to booking your stay. You won’t be able to see pricing, but you can reach out to a Reserve travel designer — a travel concierge who can help plan your trip — to get pricing estimates prior to booking. (You won’t be able to contact the vacation home host until after you’ve booked your stay.)

While it’s nice to get the credit, the four-night minimum could be frustrating for cardholders. When you book hotels through The Edit, there isn’t a stay minimum to get the $100 property credit (although you must stay two nights to use your eligible card’s $250 prepaid stay credit).

By comparison, AmEx offers a $250 Airbnb Experiences credit on the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express each calendar year when you book a prepaid Airbnb Luxe property through its travel portal. Terms apply. That statement credit is good for the rest of the calendar year in which the booking is confirmed. However, you can only unlock one $250 credit a year, even if you make multiple bookings.

Booking a vacation home through The Edit makes the most sense for longer group trips.

One of the best perks of booking a vacation home is that everyone gets to stay together in a shared space — something that’s difficult to do in a traditional hotel. If you’re able to get a larger group, you’ll also have more people to split the booking cost with.

Plus, you’ll want to stay at least four nights to benefit from the $150 in-stay credit.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

#3195. If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation

Merlin Bise is the CTO of Inbenta. He has built conversational AI since before generative AI.

​A lot of the AI deployed into the customer experience over the past three years isn’t performing. That’s just the reality. And the default response I hear, over and over, is to start all over again, evaluating and paying for a new platform.

In most cases, that’s an expensive way to rebuild the same problem.

I’ve been building AI for customer experience since before generative AI showed up. I watched intent matching give way to generative layers, and now we’re into agentic systems that can reason and act on their own. The platforms keep changing. But it isn’t the model that causes the deployment to fail—it’s the knowledge underneath it. I’ve seen that pattern in nearly every underperforming deployment I’ve looked at, going back years.

And look, none of this is a knock on the decision you made three years ago. You made it with the tools that existed then. Those were very different tools.

Here’s what’s new. Fixing the knowledge layer used to be a multiyear, hand-built project. That’s why re-platforming seemed faster, even when it wasn’t. AI now does the heavy lifting up front. It reads, structures and tags your content before anything goes live, so what customers hear is approved, not improvised. Work that used to take a room full of contractors a full year can now get done in weeks, not quarters. If you wrote off your knowledge problem 12 or 18 months ago as too slow or too expensive, it deserves a second look and, honestly, a lot more optimism than it would have earned back then.

Before you run another evaluation, check three things. You can diagnose all of them without a new vendor.

Content written for someone browsing a help site does a different job than content a model has to parse. A model can have the right document and still give the wrong answer. Why? Because two records that aren’t the same can look the same to a system reading them. If a customer asks about one product configuration and gets information about another, that isn’t because the company chose the wrong model or the customer botched the prompt. It’s a structure and authorship problem, and no new platform is going to fix it for you.

Count them. Most organizations have more duplication than they think. As mentioned earlier, a lot of platforms started with intent matching, then added a generative layer later and kept the original intent base underneath. So, now you’ve got two copies of your content, two governance surfaces and two possible answers to the same question. Contact center stacks do the same thing by channel—one store for digital and another for voice. The answer changes depending on which door the customer walked through. If a policy lives in more than one place, you have a consistency problem, not an AI problem.

This is the one that kills deployments. If the subject matter expert who spots a wrong answer has to file a ticket and wait on an engineer, corrections will never keep pace with the business. The person with the knowledge can’t act. The person who can act has no way to judge whether the answer was right. Give that six months, and the system has drifted away from how the company is supposed to operate, without a single error in the logs. You don’t get an alert—you get confused customers.

In the end, you should have one knowledge store instead of several, content structured so a machine can find the right answer and the people who own the policies in control of the answers. And there’s no need to replace your platform.

The economics back this approach up. A full platform replacement is a six-figure commitment before you even count internal time, and moving off an entrenched stack can run several times that. Fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of it. And you keep the asset, no matter what you run on top. If you want to switch platforms later, fine. You’ll be moving a structured, governed knowledge base, instead of hauling the same mess to a new vendor and paying them to discover it.

There’s a second-order benefit, too. A consolidated, governed knowledge layer gives you an audit trail. When a regulator asks about a specific conversation, you need to show the question, the answer, the source and who approved it. It doesn’t matter what platform was used. If you can’t see why your AI said something, you can’t defend it.

Here’s my takeaway. Before you run another evaluation, figure out whether you have a platform problem or a foundation problem. Most of the time, it’s the foundation. And it’s more fixable today than it was when you signed that original contract.

#3194. Essent Group (ESNT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Reinsurance premiums climbed sharply while persistency stayed elevated.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Essent Group Ltd. (ESNT -7.57%) reported third-quarter results characterized by stable mortgage insurance performance and continued expansion of its reinsurance operations. Management reported that elevated persistency, driven by low-rate mortgage portfolios, continues to support the insurance in-force base while purchase volumes remain constrained by housing affordability challenges. The company reported a significant increase in reinsurance premiums as it expands into property and casualty lines, seeking to diversify earnings and optimize capital through synergy credits. Management stated it remains focused on a balanced capital strategy, as evidenced by the authorization of a new $500 million share repurchase program and the maintenance of a quarterly dividend.

A complete description of these measures and the reconciliation to GAAP may be found in Exhibit Q of our press release and in our third quarter 26 earnings presentation posted on our website.

Now let me turn the call over to Mark.

Mark Anthony Casale: Phil, and good morning, everyone. Earlier today, we released our third quarter 26 financial results, which reflects solid credit performance, and the continued impact of interest rates on persistency and investment income. The cash flow from our core MI business remains strong. And gives us the flexibility to invest in the franchise while also returning capital to shareholders. For the third quarter of 26, we reported net income of $163 million or $1.82 per diluted share. Representing an annualized return on average equity of ~12%. Our book value per share was $62.58 as of September 30, and inclusive of common dividends has increased ~9% from a year ago.

Turning to our MI business, our insurance in force ended September 30 at $250 billion up 1% from a year ago. 12 month persistency was 83%, which reflects the current rate environment with over half of our in force portfolio having a mortgage rate of 6% or lower. We expect this dynamic to continue supporting elevated persistency while portfolio growth stays muted as affordability continues to impact origination volume. Over the long term, we remain constructive on housing as favorable demographics and pent up demand should provide foundational support to home prices and purchase origination volume.

The credit quality of our insurance in force remains strong with a weighted average credit score of 747 and a weighted average original LTV of 93%. Consistent with our expectations, the portfolio default rate increased to 2.75% reflective of seasonality and the aging of our portfolio. We continue to believe that substantial home equity embedded in our in force book should help mitigate ultimate claims. Additionally, 95% of our insurance in force is subject to reinsurance protection which provides capital relief and reduces tail risk. Turning to the Reinsurance segment, we expect written premiums of ~$320 million from our P&C reinsurance activity in 2026. With roughly half earned this year at a combined ratio in the high-90s.

We are currently focused on building Essent Re's P&C and remain disciplined with our underwriting. While mortgage risk and the related MGA business will drive the majority of the segment's earnings in the near term, we expect the P&C business to provide complementary earnings in the long term as well as capital synergy given diversification credit. Our consolidated cash and investments totaled $6.5 billion as of September 30 and are annualized aggregate investment yield for the third quarter was 4.4%. That yield includes income from other invested assets, a portfolio of strategic investments that now totals ~$450 million or 7% of our total portfolio.

While returns will vary from period to period, this portfolio gives us another way to deploy capital outside of our core business to generate income and grow book value. We continue to operate from a position of strength with $5.6 billion of GAAP equity, access to $1 billion of excess loss reinsurance, and $1 billion of cash and investments at the holding companies. With trailing 12 month operating cash flow of $857 million our franchise remains well positioned from an earnings, cash flow and balance sheet perspective. We remain committed to a balanced capital strategy that seeks to optimize shareholder returns over the long term while preserving flexibility for our strategic growth.

Year to date through October 31, we have purchased nearly 8 million shares for ~$475 million In addition, I am pleased to announce that our Board has approved a common dividend of $0.35 per share for the fourth quarter of 26 and has also authorized a new share repurchase plan of $500 million Now let me turn the call over to David.

David Bruce Weinstock: Thanks, Mark, and good morning, everyone. Let me review our results for the quarter in a little more detail. For the third quarter, we earned $1.82 per diluted share, compared to $2.8 last quarter and $1.67 in the third quarter a year ago. My comments today are going to focus primarily on the results of our mortgage insurance, and reinsurance segments. there is additional information on corporate and other results in Exhibits D and E of the financial supplement. Our mortgage insurance portfolio ended the quarter with insurance in force of $250.1 billion an increase of $342 million from June 30 and an increase of $1.3 billion compared to $248.8 billion at 9/30/2025.

Persistency at 09/30/2026 was 83.3% compared to 84% at 06/30/2026. Mortgage insurance net premium earned for the third quarter of 26 was $211 million. The average base premium rate for the mortgage insurance portfolio for the third quarter was 40 basis points. Consistent with last quarter. And the average net premium rate was 34 basis points down 1 basis point from last quarter. Our mortgage insurance provision for loss and loss adjustment expenses was $51.7 million in the third quarter of 26, compared to $29.4 million in the second quarter of 26 and $44.2 million in the third quarter a year ago. At September 30, the default rate on the mortgage insurance portfolio was 2.75%. Up from 2.53% at 06/30/2026.

Mortgage Insurance operating expenses in the third quarter of 26 were $31.9 million and the expense ratio was 15.1%. Compared to $31.9 million and 14.8% last quarter and $31.2 million and 14.4% in the third quarter last year. At September 30 Essent Guaranty's PMIER sufficiency ratio was strong. At 177%. with $1.6 billion in excess available assets. Turning to our reinsurance segment. Net premiums written year to date through September 30, 26 were $330 million, compared with $49 million over the same period of 2025. Net premiums earned year to date 2026 were $137 million compared with $46 million over the same period of 2025.

The increase in premiums reflects the growth in non mortgage business from our expansion in the P&C reinsurance activity. The reinsurance combined ratio was 84.7% in the third quarter of 26. Compared to 77.9% last quarter and 19.2% a year ago. The change in the combined ratio was as expected. Reflecting a difference in underwriting performance between the mortgage and non mortgage lines and the changing business mix of the segment's premiums. The pre-tax underwriting income for the reinsurance segment predominantly reflects the underwriting results of our GSE and other mortgage risk share business. While the contribution from our P&C activity was not material.

Consolidated net investment income was $63 million in the third quarter of 26 up $1.3 million from the prior quarter. Income from other invested assets was $10.7 million in the third quarter 26. Compared to $19.4 million last quarter and $1.8 million in the third quarter a year ago. Results this quarter again reflect the net favorable fair value adjustments on these investments. Investments. Total holding company liquidity remains strong and includes $500 million of undrawn revolver under our committed credit facility. At September 30, we had $500 million of senior unsecured notes outstanding and our debt to capital ratio was 8.3%. Year to date, Essent Guaranty paid $115 million of dividends to its U. S. Holding company.

At quarter end Essen Guaranty's statutory capital was $3.7 billion, a risk to capital ratio of 8.2 to 1. Note that statutory capital includes $2.7 billion of contingency reserves at September 30. As of October 1, Essent Guaranty could pay additional ordinary dividends of $324 million in 2026. On October 2, Essent Guaranty paid a dividend to its US holding company of $85 million. During the third quarter, Essent Group paid cash dividend totaling $31.1 million to shareholders and we repurchased 1.1 million shares for $74.5 million. In October, we repurchased 802 thousand shares for $50.8 million. Now let me turn the call back over to Mark.

Mark Anthony Casale: Thanks, Dave. In closing, Essent remains a well capitalized, high quality franchise with strong and consistent cash flow generation. We are well positioned to keep growing book value per share, returning capital to shareholders and investing in opportunities that strengthen our franchise for the long term. While continuing to support affordable and sustainable homeownership.

Operator: Now let's get to your questions. Please wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press 11 again. Our first question comes from Terry Ma with Barclays. Your line is open.

Terry Ma: Hey, thank you. Good morning. Maybe just to start off with persistency. Can you help us understand what you have been seeing in the mix of MI cancellations scheduled versus borrower initiated And then just looking ahead, how should we think about cancellation activity and the impact on persistency?

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah. Hey, Terry. It seems to be a popular topic this quarter. Amongst all the MIs not sure why. I would look at I think you are focused on the right Terry, because I do think, you know, there is not that many things that move the business. Persistency is 1 of them. So when you think just bigger picture, I know I-- you know, in terms of cancellation, a lot of it is going to be that 2021 book that just simply amortizes off over it started already, but it is probably going to be peak in, like, 2028, you know, 2029.

And then when you start thinking about growth, normal growth, you know, kind of consistent with this slow market, you know, I would think of persistency kind of in the 80% range. So it is fairly it is fairly muted, clearly lower than we have been. But remember, we have also experienced persistency of 60%, I believe it was, in 2020 and 2020. Parts of 2021. So bigger picture, really do think you have to focus it there. In terms of like MI cancellation, by, you know, actually had to look it up. Right? I mean, it is not something we track day on and day out. But, I mean, they give-- it is probably 37 thousand in the quarter.

15 of those was refinanced and the other 22 was cancellation, about 4 or 5 maybe, it is a little tough with the codes, was borrower initiated. The rest was just amortization. So, I mean, big picture again, Terry, the process works. it is a good. MI is a really good product. And it is been around for a long time, since, you know, really since almost 70 years. it is fairly priced. So on an average $400 thousand loan, it is like $1.2 thousand a year. And down payment, we are saving folks probably anywhere from $40 thousand to $45 thousand.

So and also remember, this is an industry that during the great financial crisis did not take any TARP. Probably 1 of the few financial services that did not. So a lot of credit to some of our peers who managed through that process, and an industry that paid $60-plus billion in claims over the years. So again, good product, I know there is a lot of kind of clearly emphasis on MI cancellation, and clearly, you want to make process. We are always what is best for the borrower.

So if there is ways in the future working with the GSEs and working with FHFA to kind of ease the friction, we are supportive, and we will work with them to do that.

Terry Ma: Got it. that is helpful. Thank you. And then maybe just a quick housekeeping question. Just on the current period provision for the quarter, the $81 million on MI, anything to kind of call out or unpack there? Is quite a bit harder than we were expecting. Thank you.

David Bruce Weinstock: Hey, Terry. it is David Bruce Weinstock. Really, I think when you look at our provision, I think 1 of the things that is really driving is that the average loan size is increasing. So when you look in our supplement, specifically if you look at Exhibit M, which kind of looks at reserves per bucket, We are reserving pretty much the same way we always have. Our reserve methodology has not changed. The loans that we are insuring have grown. I would say, in the past 18 months, they have probably grown from an average of like $300 thousand to now to about $400 thousand.

So that is going to be what is increasing the loan size and the risk in force, and it is going to increase the dollar of our provision. But overall, think that is what you are seeing.

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah. And I mean, sorry, again, I think it is a good question. And agree with David. The severity just the bigger loans are gonna hike the provision up. At the end of the day, it is really gonna be about unemployment. So, I mean, a lot of these still have to roll the claim. If they do, you know, clearly the pre-22 book has a lot of build in equity. It will be-- it is going to be, I would say, the post 2022 book is really the more normal So you are going to see. We are seeing higher severities. that is really the business.

I would not really look at 2021 as the business that was really an anomaly that is starting to work its way out. And it is, again, thinking longer term or from a modeling perspective, Terry, we have always said kind of we expect a 2% to 3% claim rate. that is what we price for And then in terms of combined ratio, kind of in that 35% to 45% ratio. So this is, you know, I do not wanna say it is always within our expectations, but it does not really surprise us.

And I still think just look at our cash flow over the past 12 months, in excess of $800 million So not a lot of cash is leaving the company yet. I mean, again, we will start paying more claims over time, but I do think what you are seeing is a normal MI business. And based on that, it is still I mean, it is still pretty good.

Terry Ma: Got it. Super helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Douglas Harter with BTIG. Your line is open.

Douglas Harter: Thanks, and good morning. Hoping you could just talk about your view on competition You guys continue to kind of be slightly below pro rata market share. And just kind of how you think or what that tells us about your view of you know, the risk adjusted returns in the market.

Mark Anthony Casale: Hey, Douglas. Welcome back. Nice to have you back on the calls. Would say the competitive market is still pretty similar. We have not seen much of a change. I think for us, we always do. We probably fall back a lot on the unit economics and we tend to, you know, look at our earned premium based premiums a little bit higher than the industry. We focus a little bit on that, and we like to do just-- it is a small market, Douglas, so we do not really look-- you know, we would love to be, you know, 1 of 6, so a little bit higher on the share.

But we are not particularly concerned given the smaller nature of the market. And we are kind of using this opportunity to test a lot of things. We will test pricing. You know, remember, SNEDGE, which, you know, is really our credit engine and does help us. So. And we can get into that a little bit more just in terms of Vantage. But, you know, it really helps us kind of, you know, we are really looking at, you know, kind of our estimated claim rates. So we will look and we will test geographies, we will test lenders, we will test certain tails. So it is working as well as we would like.

I mean, sometimes we know where you may sacrifice a little bit of volume for that. I think longer term, it is. You know, given the small nature of the-- we are not particularly concerned. In terms of the competitive environment, I would look at it as every MI seems to have their own buy box, right? Some like lower LTVs, some like higher credits, some like certain geographies, certain lenders, But I do think it kind of balances out in the end, so I would not read too much into our kind of take on the market because we are a little bit lower.

Douglas Harter: I appreciate that, Mark. Thank you. Yep.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Mihir Bhatia with Bank of America. Your line is open.

Mihir Bhatia: Hi, good morning. Thank you for taking my questions. Maybe I will just start with something you just mentioned there. Mark, about Vantage and EssentEDGE, Can you talk a little bit more about that?

Mark Anthony Casale: Sure. I mean, I think, you know, Vantage is coming into the market, and it is not very big right now. I mean, here, it is probably less than 5% of our originations. I do not think it is going to affect the MI industry that much. I think it is going to impact the MBS buyers in certain buyers of loans more, because they are so focused on FICO. But I think when we look at it, you know, FICO, FICO 10T, VS4, the GSEs are looking at, like, posting their scores. I think our advantage with Edge is we are looking at the raw credit data. So we are coming up with our own score.

So we are agnostic to kind of-- you know, we use it-- you know, it will impact those scores, but it is not really driving our ultimate claim rate. And anything we are on the card with, you know, clearly that is gonna go Vantage or FICO depending on the lender. We also run that through Edge on the back end. So I. We feel like we have a really good common denominator that we-- And we may start disclosing that over time. We will see we will see how it goes. But it will at least give investors what our view is on and the ups and downs.

I think from a bigger picture, I think with Vantage, you could see, a little bit of pricing compression if they start to pick, like, the best of all. You know? And I would be surprised if the industry does not respond and raise pricing a little bit. I mean, you are talking like a basis point or 2. it is not big dollars, but I would be surprised if the industry does not react. I think on the other hand, I do think you may see a larger market.

You know, I would believe, especially if there is some inflation you could see FHA borrowers migrate to conventional, which I think, again, if that is better for the borrower, that is good. So I think net, it is probably a positive, for the industry, you know, over the next year or 2.

Mihir Bhatia: Got it. The other question I had was just in terms of insurance in force growth at current market size. Right? I mean, if you think about 80% persistency, you have 50%. I guess, ~$50 billion running off each year. And IW is running about that same level. Should we expect insurance in force to be flat or even down next year?

Mark Anthony Casale: Well, it is hard. it is it is tough for me to say right now. I do say that it has been relative flat. I mean, we are entering 2027, kind of the fifth plus year of just a flat market. So-- and I think given where rates were, we were able to grow insurance in force a little bit over the past few years. I would not be surprised if it flattens out a bit. That being said, Mihir, I do think we are levered more for the up when you think about warehousing's been relatively stagnant, and then we can talk all day long about demographics, but I do believe there is a pent up demand for housing.

And kind of the longer this stays, this kind of slowness hangs around, the larger the snapback will be. So look bigger picture, you know, look at a $1.6 trillion of industry, enforced for the, you know, for the whole industry. I would not be surprised to see that grow to $2 trillion. You know, not next year, not but let's say over a certain period of time, again, take our share So I do think growth will resume. And I do not think, you know, and I do not think a lot of investors see that. And that is that is fine. Right? it is hard in this environment.

But I do think we have that kind of growth because housing will come back. It always does. It always resumes. It will grow in line with GDP. You have to think through why it is not growing. And part of it was 2021 was such an anomaly. We literally pulled 5 or 6 years' worth of growth into 1 year. Or 2 years. Home price is up 50% in 2 years. that is just not normal. So now what you are seeing more of the normalization. So we are flattening out.

We are fortunate, as a company that because of the persistent and the benign credit environment, we are still driving a lot of cash flow to the bottom line. But, you know, in some of the other participants, the transaction oriented businesses, it is us. So, but I do think we really. We kind of get-- we kind of look at it internally as we are paid to wait and the way we are kind of managing capital over time. Because remember, insurance in force, it does not grow, the capital needed to support it does not grow.

So that becomes you know, free cash flow, which again, we have used predominantly the last 18-plus months to repurchase shares, which we think that right now is a pretty good use of proceeds, you know, for the Got it.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Rowland Mayor with RBC Capital Markets. Your line is open.

Rowland Mayor: Mark, I think you said in response to a question that you price for a 2% to 3% claims rate. But then you still book new notices in a much higher figure than that. What would it take to close the gap?

Mark Anthony Casale: Well, remember, when we book new notices, that is not what our ultimate these things roll. So that is our initial claim rate, 2% to 3% roll ins at the end. So it is kind of apples and oranges. So think of it again as the ultimate claim rate. So just picture unit economics. Right? So premium rate, net premium rate, kind of loss rate, which is your claim rate. that is kind of your return on asset. Then you have your expenses and your investment income. it is relatively straightforward, but I do think claim rate for historically for us has been, like, less than 1%. That is just and we are pleased with it.

But I think, normally, you are gonna have to look in that 2% to 3% range. Hence, when you kinda run through the math, that gets you to that 35% to 45% combined ratio. And I do think that is a good guide. 35% to 45% combined ratio, kind of 80-ish percent persistency longer term is actually a good guide as you start to model this stuff out.

Rowland Mayor: Thank you. that is helpful. And then I guess from a competitive dynamic, we have seen a lot of multiyear quota share deals announced in the industry at fairly cheap cost of capital. You expect that to drive any change in pricing decisions as a result of the improved reinsurance dynamics?

Mark Anthony Casale: Great question. I do not know. We do not do I mean, we look at it. We price on an unlevered basis. We do not take the reinsurance cost and rotate that back into the front end. And part of it is just how the market works, right? I mean, there is only 6 participants, so if you use that to lower price, it is easily matched. I would be surprised if the other participants use it that way too because it is it is really just reducing premium in the industry.

So I think what we would do, the way we look at it is we will price for kind of an unlevered return and anything that is, you know, cheaper, so to speak, on the reinsurance side really benefits shareholders. And we took that and just lowered price, and shareholders do not really gain from that. And I think for, you know, reinsurance we generally have gone 2 years. We have seen some of the, we have seen a few participants go 3 years, which again speaks to 1, the demand for reinsurance in MI. there is really not a lot of GSE reinsurance, so we are kind of the only game in town. We like it, and we will.

I think we will continue. We think it is a great tool, but I would remind you that we do like capital too. Alright? I mean, I think reinsurance protects you, in the event of an, you know, kind of a lower, you know, call it higher unemployment, more losses, reinsurance clearly protects you. Capital lets you take advantage of those type of situations. And I give you the example. it is dated now, but in 2020, we talked earlier, we were the lowest in market share. You know? But in 2020, we were. We have only been number 1 in market share twice in our history, and both times were in 2020.

The second and third quarter when we had, we went out and had raised capital in May. We had a lot of capital. We wrote and I think we had a 20% handle on 1, and part of it was because some of the you know, there was not, you know, there was not as much capital around the industry, there is a little bit of a shock event. We took advantage of it. So again, I think you have to look at it both ways. Reinsurance is a great tool. it is really part of our, you know, when we think about buy, manage, distribute as a key piece of it.

But when you think about capital longer term, you also have to worry about the tail. Right? So when we think about how do we think about excess capital clearly insurance in force is not growing, we have a lot of excess capital. Could we use it for you opportunities outside of the core? Relatively small. We would love to plow it back into the core business. And then we look and say, how much do we need in an event? So remember, we hold first loss. We really hedge out against a mezz. You know, we reattach at the top.

So for our business role, and I know you cover the PNC market, a cat event for us is a severe macroeconomic recession. You know, what is the probability of that happening in the next 2 to 5 years? Probably pretty low, not zero. So I think we like, we have been through it. I have managed through the GFC. I have been through the subprime crisis of the late nineties. You know, we have seen the movie before, so we like-- you know, we think having dry powder to take advantage of an event And also when you think about just the, you know, kind of the price of the-- it is a call, Right?

I mean, so the price of holding on to that additional capital, we actually think is relatively cheap. Versus returning all of it to shareholders. I think for us, a capital return, we are gonna be in excess of 100% this year. We bought back 10% of the company last year. Would not be surprised if we are close to that this year. Again, I think we are fortunate in terms of how much capital we are generating. I think we are using most of it to buy back capital, so we think that is the best use of funds now. But we are still we are still retaining a little bit for-- we like to have dry powder.

Either for an opportunity that presents itself on the offensive nature or just being defensive.

Rowland Mayor: And then if I could just sneak in 1 more. We are coming up on 1/1 here Is there any interest in expanding the P&C appetite And can you discuss your premium expectations there?

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah. I mean, I think we are clearly in conversations now with Lloyd's around kind of our funds at Lloyd's commitments. We like our approach with Lloyd's. it is clearly different than some, but I think it is probably more it suits our style.

So you could see us grow a little bit, I would not expect a lot. And then on the, you know, the quota share that we did last year, that actually renews again for another year. And we will look to do potentially do some other retros or even some direct reinsurance with cedents. But, you know, we will see how it goes. We are seeing a lot of the submissions are coming in, but it is really the same unit economics kind of framework that we have, on the MI side. So we are looking at it.

We are we are building out the infrastructure, but I will give you a lot more color in February. it is a little early to tell because we are just starting to see it. But again, lots of capital floating out there. We do not need to kinda push on growth there for the sake of growth.

#3193. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

#3191. ​The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure

Bill Wong - AI Research Fellow, Info-Tech Research Group.

​​In my previous article, we examined the emergence of a new data center asset, the AI factory, which is optimized to run AI workloads. Compared to traditional data centers, AI data center campuses require up to 10 times the total facility power capacity, driven by GPU server racks that consume 12 to 28 times more power per rack and thermal density that requires advanced liquid cooling to handle five times the heat generation.

This new industrial revolution is driving an unprecedented demand for power, transforming the utilities industry from a relatively stable and quiet industry to a growth sector.​ Nations and organizations alike will need to optimize their AI energy strategy in order to flourish during and after this revolution.

After reviewing several national AI energy infrastructure strategies around the world, four distinct strategies stand out. These strategies will shape how nations are planning to build the required energy infrastructure for AI workloads.

• Sovereign Regulation-Driven: These jurisdictions introduce legislation to ensure that AI developers must fund their own power requirements, maintain the reliability of the grid and provide the supporting water infrastructure required for these data centers to prevent rising utility costs. In Canada, the country’s recently published AI strategy champions their grid’s 83% investment in clean power. Australia will require data center providers to generate as much energy as they consume. The EU has introduced a sovereign AI compute platform, EuroHPC JU, which aims to “develop innovative energy-efficient HPC software technologies tailored to exascale and post-exascale supercomputers.”

• Market-Driven: These countries rely on the private sector to drive the building of data centers and leverage easily accessible energy resources. The U.S. has begun by reinvesting into nuclear power plants and the use of small modular reactors. The UK has accelerated AI projects through its AI Growth Zones, fast track permits.

• Localization-Driven: Rather than adding additional workloads to the existing energy grids, some countries are locating new data centers near clean energy sources. Japan’s new collaboration strategy leverages nine designated green energy zones. South Korea’s new strategy directs the movement of 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul to regional nuclear and small modular reactor clusters.

• State-Driven: China’s government is planning to connect renewable energy resources from its western region to its computing hubs in its eastern region.​

In order to assess a nation or organization’s AI energy strategy, one must examine its energy value chain. This involves identifying the source of its energy, determining how power is generated, determining how power is managed and deployed, understanding the nation’s thermal management and understanding the sustainability strategy the nation or organization has implemented.​

Meaningful metrics in this area focus on the total volume, dependability and carbon footprint of the electricity required by the organization in question’s compute infrastructure. Countries and organizations using clean and renewable energy resources will be able to differentiate their energy infrastructure in a positive manner. On the other hand, countries leveraging fossil fuels, like natural gas, may have the short-term benefit of accessing low-cost energy resources, but they will also encounter long-term emissions problems, which expose them to carbon regulation and creates cost volatility.​

Metrics in this area focus on an energy infrastructure’s capacity and its ability to connect, control and optimize high-density energy flow between the bulk electric grid (external) and its computing facilities (internal).

From a macro-grid point of view, which focuses outside of the data center, leaders can use ultra-high-voltage transmission lines, battery storage and AI-driven load-balancing software to absorb the violent swings in demand from GPU clusters, which can dramatically improve power management.

From a micro-grid standpoint, which focuses inside the data center, leaders have a few things to consider. Today’s AI racks demand 130 to 600 kW, and pushing that much power through legacy wiring can generate wasted heat and requires multiple inefficient conversion steps. Modern operators can implement ±400V or 800V DC systems and solid-state transformers to reduce internal heat loss and conversion steps.​

Legacy air cooling can no longer dissipate the heat generated by today’s AI factories. How a company handles this heat is becoming a competitive advantage for any organization running its own sovereign AI infrastructure. I’ve observed some leading operators switching to direct-to-chip liquid cooling in closed-loop systems, which can slash operational water consumption.

Embracing robust environmental stewardship can help nations and organizations keep their data center expansion efforts sustainable, minimizing ecological disruption while preserving critical local environmental resources. Beyond conservation, some advanced operators are turning thermal management into a revenue stream. By establishing facilities in colder climates (like Canada, the Nordics or Hokkaido, Japan) and capturing the 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat directly from server racks, those operators can sell that heat to municipal district heating networks.​

Which AI energy infrastructure strategy is the best for a given organization will depend on several factors, and not all options are available for a given country or geographical location, especially those strategies that can leverage a country’s colder climate to reduce cooling costs.

Countries and organizations need to prioritize and align their energy infrastructure architecture with their nation’s sovereign AI strategy. For instance, sustainability initiatives will likely have the best success in countries like Canada and Nordic nations.

Finally, organizations need to learn how to address the current backlash from people regarding AI data centers near their communities. Builders and operators should be prepared to address questions and concerns surrounding the AI energy value chain they’re leveraging, along with its regional costs and benefits. Leaders should focus on sustainability, environmental impact and delivering an accountability framework for the operations of their proposed AI data center.​

#3188. ​Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows

Corey Ercanbrack is CTO at Vasion, leading the AI-native transformation of a cloud-native platform under FedRAMP High.

A state agency mails benefits notices to citizens, with personal data on the page and legal rights tied to what’s printed. When I asked the administrator responsible for its 30,000 endpoints what governs that output process, he said it runs elsewhere, on infrastructure owned by a different team.​

He wasn’t dodging me. That’s how these environments get built, and it produces a blind spot most leaders inherit rather than create. Information is governed where the data lives. Output is governed where the devices live. Those are two teams with different budgets, reporting lines and definitions of accountability, so the artifact carrying the heaviest legal obligation sits furthest from the controls protecting the information inside it.​

The same split appears across other organizations I work with. Major American cities operating under state public records law must produce any official communication upon request, whatever the medium. Their digital channels are instrumented. Paper isn’t. The specialist responsible for its endpoint estate acknowledged that if he sent a printed memo, someone would still have to find it.​

That gap has been survivable because a person stands in it. The employee who printed the memo knows he printed it, and if a request arrives two years later, someone can ask him. In audit terms, he’s a compensating control: what you document and test when the designed control can’t be implemented. Nobody documented this one. It’s been load-bearing for 30 years without appearing in a control matrix, which is why removing it looks costless.​

Agents remove it. Deloitte’s 2026 “State of AI in the Enterprise” report surveyed 3,235 business and IT leaders across 24 countries. Nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Among the capabilities Deloitte names as crucial are audit trails capturing the full chain of agent actions.​

When an instruction comes from a system rather than a person, there may be no human intent to reconstruct later and no awareness that a records obligation was triggered. Unless the workflow was designed to capture that context, automation can generate unaccounted output far faster than the informal human process it replaced. Leaders may be automating away a control they never knew they depended on.

Most AI governance programs are scoped to the application: which model acted, what data it reached, what it was authorized to do and what it produced. That work is necessary, but it is not sufficient, because operational documents don’t stay inside one application.​

I have watched a prior authorization request move from a medical record to paper, to a fax machine, to an insurer and return days later as an email. Each system recorded its portion and completed the step it was designed to handle, but none held the thread connecting them: the only view from which the organization could reconstruct the full event. The application finished its task. The business did not, and governance was scoped to the first while the obligation attaches to the second.​

An IT leader at a global distributor gave me a paperless example. More countries where his company operates now require documents to be deposited with a government authority. The regulation specifies where the document must be sent without specifying how it gets there. Treating the output boundary as a printing problem misses the broader obligation to govern the document throughout its journey.​

If an auditor picked up an AI-generated document tomorrow, what could you prove about it? Four questions help determine the answer.

1. Identity: Who or what produced it? Once a document is printed, exported or faxed, the chain of identity breaks. The artifact no longer shows which agent created it, who initiated the action or where the information came from.​

2. Authorization: Who approved its release? Knowing who generated a document is not the same as knowing whether release was authorized. A finished document proves neither.​

3. Audit: What happened between input and output? An agent extracts information, changes content and generates instructions. Record only the finished document, and you can’t show what it did. The record has to replay what went in, what changed, who acted and where it went.​

4. Retention: Can you find and classify it? Without the first three, you accumulate documents you’re obligated to protect and unable to trace, turning a governance gap into a storage liability.​

Miss one, and you don’t have end-to-end AI governance. Instead, you have a partial record of an action that continued without you. I recommend running these four against a live workflow before expanding agent authority. The gaps you find are the ones an agent will only widen.

The instinct is to connect every system, but these integrations are often fragile and require ongoing maintenance whenever one side changes.

Start with the work instead.​ Pick one operational document this week and follow it from creation to final disposition. Mark every point where somebody prints, exports, faxes, signs, scans or retypes information, and keep going after the data leaves the application. The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it. Test the four questions at each one. Wherever context breaks, you’ve found the real boundary of your program before an auditor does.​

The workflows that hold up often share one trait: The record was designed before the agent was deployed, rather than reconstructed after someone asked for it. That means someone decided where human review belonged and what needed to be recorded at every step, including the agent’s actions. You can’t deploy first and gather the evidence later. The record has to be created when the action occurs, or it may not exist at all. And the destination is rarely as modern as the agent. I’ve watched sophisticated automation end with a fax because that’s what the recipient accepts.​​

Governance has to follow the information through every handoff. The practical perimeter is everywhere the information goes.​​

#3187. Granite Ridge (GRNT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Production climbs as the company nears positive free cash flow in 2027.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Granite Ridge Resources, Inc. (GRNT +13.28%) reported a sequential increase in production and earnings, noting an inflection point as the company transitions toward generating positive free cash flow in 2027. Management indicated that 2026 represents the final year of investing ahead of cash flow, with future growth supported by a higher oil weighting and the expiration of lower-priced hedges. The company is expanding its operator partnership model through a new agreement in the Midland Basin and initiated a capital return program that includes both a recurring dividend and a share repurchase authorization. Management reported that the traditional non-operated business continues to generate steady cash flow across six basins, while the partnership platform compounds inventory and growth.

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.

#3185. Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes

Gayathri Kolandaisami | Doctoral Researcher | Human-centered digital and AI transformation in water utilities and critical infrastructure.

A technology investment can succeed on paper but still fail to solve the problem it was meant to solve.

I saw this happen long before the AI era. When I started my technology career in 2005, my job was to build and maintain the software used by my clients. Over time, I learned that building the technology was only part of the equation. We also needed to understand why it was needed and how the work was being done:

1. What problem were we trying to solve, or what improvement did we want in productivity, efficiency or service delivery?

3. What should the ideal process look like?

That way of thinking stayed with me as my career moved from software development into larger digital transformation projects. It left me with a principle I still believe today: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

I was in a position to observe an organization’s reaction when an AI coding assistant was introduced to its developers. The management had invested in this technology long before I got involved in the organization. However, they hadn’t understood or researched where and how that technology could help the developers, what the benefits of using it would be or whether the tool was apt for their environment. The outcome was a KPI introduced at an organizational level to measure the tool’s adoption. So, a developer was considered to have met this part of their KPI by simply showing that they’d adopted this tool.

This left me asking myself: Had we moved away from measuring the outcomes of the technology to simply measuring its adoption? That’s when I realized that we’d started working for the technology and not the other way around.

Make no mistake—every cell in my body screams technology. I want to develop new technologies that could solve a lot of global challenges. I’m a strong believer in new technologies, and I’m fascinated by how quickly AI is evolving. But I also think that we’re forgetting why we invented these technologies in the first place. Sometimes, we race toward adopting the newest technology without knowing what we were trying to make better.

Technology is a means to solve a problem, improve a process or create a better outcome. The technology itself isn’t the outcome.

I came across a 2025 study published in Management Science. The researchers estimated that using an AI coding assistant increased completed tasks by 26.08%. In contrast, another 2025 study that examined experienced open-source developers working on mature repositories found that developers took 19% longer when using the AI tools that were tested.

The lesson from these studies is that technology doesn’t produce the same result in different environments.​

Organizations can easily measure the wrong outcome.

Take software development, for example. Building new software or making a change to existing software can involve requirements gathering, design, programming, testing, bug fixing and implementation. Let’s say we implemented an AI coding assistant. We may think that this tool could cut programming time substantially. However, that isn’t the whole picture, is it? What happens if the AI-assisted code requires more testing? What if developers spend additional time reviewing and correcting it? What if defects increase, and some of the time saved in programming is consumed later in the process?

If we measure only programming time in this scenario, we may conclude that the technology has been highly successful. However, if we measure the entire journey from requirements to delivery, we may reach a very different conclusion.

The entire process matters when measuring the outcome of the technology. If the problem that the technology is addressing is slow delivery, measure the complete cycle from requirements to release. If the problem is quality, understand defects and rework. If the objective is greater capacity, determine whether the team can actually complete more meaningful work.

The metric should originate from the problem, the context and the process, not simply from the technology.

I prefer piloting the technology before widely adopting it. A pilot isn’t simply an opportunity to prove that a technology works. It’s an opportunity to discover whether it works for your people, your processes and your particular environment.

If employees aren’t using a technology, that should initially be treated as information rather than a performance problem. Perhaps they need training. Perhaps the technology doesn’t fit their workflow. Perhaps it works well for some tasks but not others. Perhaps the existing technology environment, including legacy systems or code, limits its usefulness. Or perhaps it simply isn’t solving a sufficiently important problem.

Adoption is only one part of the story. Technology can also affect employee and customer experience. It may remove repetitive work and allow employees to focus on more meaningful activities, but it may also create additional work when people have to check, correct or validate its output. Some outcomes are tangible, such as time saved, costs reduced, greater capacity or more work completed. Others are harder to quantify, such as employee satisfaction, customer satisfaction, trust and confidence in the service being delivered. They’re still outcomes.

As organizations embrace increasingly powerful technologies, the temptation will be to measure what’s easiest to see: licenses purchased, systems deployed, users onboarded or usage rates. Those numbers have their place, but they don’t answer the most important question: What became better because we introduced the technology?

Always remember: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
