#3184. Marcus & Millichap (MMI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Rate volatility is weighing on deal flow, but a looming maturity wave could reshape activity.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Marcus & Millichap, Inc. (MMI -3.17%) reported third quarter financial results that showed revenue growth across its core brokerage and financing segments, supported by increased activity in the middle market and larger transaction categories. Management stated that interest rate volatility remains a primary challenge to transaction velocity, as sharp fluctuations in treasury yields during the quarter triggered deal repricing and wider bid-ask spreads. The company indicated that it is prioritizing a series of long-term strategic initiatives, including the build-out of a retail leasing division and the implementation of AI-enabled enterprise systems to drive operational leverage. Additionally, the company noted that a significant volume of loan maturities scheduled for 2027 and 2028 is expected to act as a catalyst for future transaction activity as owners and lenders address assets that cannot be refinanced at current interest rate levels.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to Marcus & Millichap's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. As a reminder, this call is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, Jacques Cornet. Thank you. You may begin.

Jacques Cornet: Thank you, operator, and good morning, and welcome to Marcus & Millichap's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. With us today are President and Chief Executive Officer, Hessam Nadji; and Chief Financial Officer, Steve DeGennaro. Before I turn the call over to management, please remember that our prepared remarks and the responses to questions may contain forward-looking statements. Words such as may, will, expect, believe, estimate, anticipate, goal, and variations of these words and similar expressions are intended to identify forward-looking statements.

Actual results can differ materially from those implied by such forward-looking statements due to a variety of factors, including, but not limited to, general economic conditions and commercial real estate market conditions, the company's ability to retain and attract transactional professionals, the company's ability to retain its business philosophy and partnership culture amid competitive pressures, the company's ability to integrate new agents and sustain its growth and other factors discussed in the company's public filings, including its annual report on Form 10-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on February 26, 2026. Although the company believes the expectations reflected in such forward-looking statements are based upon reasonable assumptions, it can make no assurance that its expectations will be attained.

The company undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events, or otherwise. In addition, certain financial information presented on this call represents non-GAAP financial measures. The company's earnings release, which was issued this morning and is available on the company's website, represents a reconciliation to the appropriate GAAP measures and explains why the company believes such non-GAAP measures are useful to investors. This conference call is being webcast. The webcast link is available on the Investor Relations section of the company's website at www.marcusmillichap.com, along with the slide presentation you may reference during the prepared remarks. With that, it is my pleasure to turn the call over to CEO, Hessam Nadji.

Hessam Nadji: Thank you, Jacques. On behalf of the entire Marcus & Millichap team, good morning, everyone, and welcome to our third quarter 2026 earnings call. I'm pleased to report that MMI delivered a solid quarter despite a sharp increase in interest rates, which once again widened bid-ask spreads and pressured valuations of our inventory and transaction pipeline. Total revenue increased 7.5% to $208 million in the third quarter, bringing revenue year-to-date to $583 million, up 14% from a year ago. Brokerage revenue grew 7%, led by our middle market and larger transaction segments, which grew 17% and 20%, respectively. Private Client revenue rose 4%, reflecting the more pronounced impact of higher interest rates at lower price points.

It should be noted that the 10-year treasury yield moved by 80 basis points between late June and late September, which caused a fair degree of repricing. The year-over-year comparison for our Private Client segment was also particularly challenging given the 17% gain we registered in the third quarter of 2025. Despite the recent round of interest rate volatility, financing availability and lenders' appetite to compete and put capital to work remain favorable, albeit with elevated caution on underwriting and borrower qualification. I'm also pleased to highlight the company's improved profitability. Adjusted EBITDA increased 20% in the third quarter and reached $23 million year-to-date compared to a $400,000 loss during the first 9 months of 2025.

Our team remains laser-focused on improving profitability while continuing to invest in critical infrastructure, tools, and talent. This includes ongoing technology investments, some upfront costs associated with opportunistic talent acquisition, and outside resources engaged during the quarter to help us evaluate potential strategic acquisitions. As I've mentioned on prior calls, MMI's near-term profitability continues to reflect the expensing of investments in top talent retention and acquisition over the past 5 years. Market conditions have hampered revenue production for many of the leading sales and financing professionals we have invested in. Therefore, our strategy to achieve operating leverage is to control costs while maintaining essential investments, maximizing revenue growth per producer, and advancing key strategic initiatives.

The biggest challenge in delivering more robust and consistent revenue growth is interest rate volatility, a major headwind to our sales force's productivity. Over the past 4 years, the 10-year treasury yield has moved by at least 50 basis points in either direction, 16x. Each significant rate movement affects valuations, bid-ask spreads, marketing time lines, lender underwriting, and whether deals can even pencil up. Keeping transactions on track requires more time, leaving even the most experienced producers with less capacity to develop new business. This has been very frustrating for our entire team. This prolonged market volatility also makes it harder for new producers to reach acceptable production levels.

As I've shared on previous calls, this is the underlying driver of our elevated new agent turnover, making quarterly tracking of net hires more volatile. We're also shifting new talent recruiting to rely more heavily on alternative channels, including our very successful internship and fellowship programs. These initiatives have developed higher-quality new producers who are gaining momentum, but will take time to translate into more measurable net additions to our sales force. Despite these near-term challenges, I want to point out several trends that remain very encouraging. Significant repricing of real estate has already occurred with further adjustments underway as the market adjusts to interest rates remaining elevated longer and much more so than previously expected.

Sellers' motivation to transact is increasing as the likelihood of interest rates returning to prior levels becomes a distant hope. More sellers are listing properties at realistic prices and showing greater willingness to transact as buyers seek more of a return premium. However, price adjustments vary widely by property type, market and asset quality, which is where Marcus & Millichap sales and financing specialists truly stand out through local expertise, deep relationships, and real-time market intelligence. Situational distress from weak operations, lower-than-expected rent growth over the past several years and the $1.2 trillion of loan maturities expected in 2027 and 2028 should result in higher transaction activity.

Lenders are better positioned to address underperforming assets and maturing debt that cannot be refinanced at current interest rate levels without the injection of significant fresh equity. Over the next 2 years, multifamily and retail loan maturities will account for nearly 50% of the total volume, positioning MMI ideally to provide solutions for affected owners and lenders in our leading business segments. Looking ahead, our long-term strategy for scaling the business, maximizing revenue growth, and achieving operating leverage centers on 6 key initiatives that are timely for me to refresh given our current business planning process underway for 2027. Our first priority is to further expand our market-leading Private Client platform across geographies and property types.

Despite our market dominance in this segment, as I've shared with you before, the vast and fragmented nature of the microcap and middle market commercial real estate market offers substantial room for growth. More effective hiring, training, deployment, and producer development will play a pivotal role in capturing this opportunity under the guidance of our local market leaders and divisional Chief Revenue Officers. We are very well positioned to leverage this talent for further growth. The second expansion strategy is to further build out our IPA platform, which is designed to bring advisory and brokerage capabilities to major accounts and institutional investors.

Adding IPA teams in multifamily, retail office, and industrial complements our Private Client business and has proven to be a scalable growth opportunity. Third, we're building on the progress we've made in expanding our finance division, MMCC. This includes developing and recruiting leading loan originators and growing our IPA Capital Markets platform. Collaboration between our financing specialists and sales teams has proven to be highly effective and, again, points to the opportunity for scaling. We're actively expanding our financing division through experienced hires and targeting boutique mortgage banking firms for acquisitions. We're also exploring complementary ways to broaden our financing capabilities. Fourth, we're expanding our auction division, which we launched organically 3 years ago.

Since then, our auction specialists have successfully integrated the service into our core brokerage offering. Collaboration across our auction, investment sales, and finance teams has proven effective and, again, scalable. In recent months, we added auction specialists in strategic regions to enable more internal collaboration with our sales force and generate incremental new business. For our fifth strategy, we're scaling our leasing capabilities in key markets. The integration of leasing and investment sales offers a strong advantage in our Private Client and Middle Market segments, where MMI can bring significant platform level advantages to owners and investors we have relationships with.

Retail leasing is our priority given our existing footprint and the opportunities for collaboration between leasing specialists and our retail investment sales force. We expect to grow leasing through a buy-and-build approach, enabling us to acquire boutique firms and groups as well as recruiting experienced teams in select markets. During the third quarter, 2 seasoned leasing executives joined senior management to help develop the strategy, systems, and support infrastructure for this initiative. Given the required planning and ramp-up time necessary to offer best-in-class support, we do not expect a meaningful revenue contribution from this initiative in 2027. However, we believe the long-term strategy will be extremely accretive to MMI's growth plan.

Last but certainly not least, over the next 12 to 18 months, we plan to upgrade a number of enterprise systems and implement a series of AI-enabled tools. Our strategy blends a series of proprietary tools, enhancements to legacy proprietary technology as well as the leveraging of commercial systems, all integrated into the MMI ecosystem. MMI is well positioned to leverage its market-leading brand and footprint to enter new revenue channels and offer more services to our core clients. We've worked hard to maintain a strong balance sheet and a balanced capital allocation strategy. Since launching the plan in 2022, we have returned $132 million to shareholders through dividends and $120 million through share repurchases.

The company's growth initiatives will take time to produce meaningful, sustainable incremental revenue growth, and will moderately increase costs over the next 18 to 24 months. However, we are confident that each initiative's close alignment with our core business will drive efficiencies, cross-selling opportunities, repeat business, and greater operating leverage over the next several years. With that, I will turn the call over to Steve for more details on our financial results. Steve?

Steve Degennaro: Thank you, Hessam. Total revenue for the third quarter was $208 million, an increase of 7.5% compared to $194 million in the third quarter of last year. Year-to-date, total revenue was $583 million, up 14% compared to $511 million a year ago. Looking at revenue by segment. Real estate brokerage commissions were $174 million for the quarter, an increase of 7% year-over-year and accounted for 84% of total revenue. We completed 1,584 brokerage transactions, essentially flat with last year for total volume of $9.4 billion, an increase of 13%. The volume increase, along with a 9 basis point decline in the average commission rate is reflective of a shift in mix towards larger transactions.

For the 9-month period, brokerage commissions were $479 million, an increase of 12% compared to the prior year. Within brokerage, for the quarter, our Private Client business grew 4% year-over-year to $106 million against a very strong third quarter last year. Our Middle Market business grew 17% to $31 million and our larger transaction segment covering deals above $20 million grew 20% to $31 million. Revenue from our financing business was $27 million in the third quarter, an increase of 3% compared to $26 million in the prior year quarter, which itself was a 28% year-over-year increase. For the 9-month period, financing revenue was $84 million, an increase of 19% compared to the prior year.

Other revenue was $7 million in the quarter compared to $5 million in the third quarter of last year. For the 9-month period, other revenue totaled $19 million compared to $13 million a year ago. Turning to expenses. Total operating expense for the quarter was $209 million compared to $196 million a year ago. Cost of services was $133 million or 64% of revenue, an increase of 160 basis points compared to the same period last year, primarily due to the increase in year-to-date revenue over the prior year and a greater mix of revenue from large transactions in both brokerage and financing that are typically generated by more senior producers on higher commission splits.

Selling, general and administrative expense for the quarter was $73.5 million or 35.3% of revenue compared to $72.5 million or 37.4% of revenue in the same period last year. For the 9-month period, SG&A totaled $216 million, slightly above the prior year. The increase in SG&A reflects our investment in enterprise technology development as well as strategic headcount additions related to new business initiatives, partially offset by reductions elsewhere. Let me expand on each of these major initiatives. Enterprise technology development includes standing up a new HRIS system while also implementing a new ERP system as well as various upgrades to our business analytics, reporting, and security applications.

New business initiatives, as Hessam outlined, include senior level opportunistic hires in leasing, retail, and auction as we look to expand these areas. We expect our investment in these strategic initiatives to represent incremental spend of approximately 1% to 2% of revenue over the next 18 to 24 months. These investments will drive long-term scalability and contribute to operating margin improvement and higher operating leverage as revenue grows. Net income for the quarter was $1 million or $0.03 per share compared to $240,000 or $0.01 per share in the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA was $8.2 million compared to $6.9 million a year ago.

For the 9-month period, earnings were $0.05 per share compared to a net loss of $0.39 per share in the prior year, and adjusted EBITDA was $23.3 million year-to-date compared to a loss of $400,000 in the same period last year. Our effective tax rate for the quarter was approximately 61% compared to approximately 84% in the third quarter of last year. As a reminder, our tax rate may fluctuate from quarter-to-quarter. Moving to the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with $373 million in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities.

That's up $28 million from the end of the second quarter and down just $9 million from the end of the third quarter last year in spite of having paid $20 million in dividends and repurchasing shares worth $42 million in the last 4 quarters. The year-over-year and sequential increases reflect continued operating cash generation. And as always, we have no debt. In early October, we paid a semiannual dividend of $0.25 per share. We remain committed to a balanced long-term capital allocation strategy, which includes investing in technology, recruiting, and retaining best-in-class producers and returning capital to shareholders. Turning now to the fourth quarter.

While we anticipate quarter-over-quarter sequential revenue growth due to usual year-end seasonality, interest rate volatility and uncertainty are challenges relative to prior year, and therefore, we remain measured in our near-term expectations. In addition, Q4 last year benefited from a shot in the arm when bonus depreciation was first made permanent, and we don't expect the effect this year to be quite as significant. Cost of services as a percentage of revenue in the fourth quarter is expected to follow the usual trend and be sequentially higher than Q3. On a dollar basis, SG&A is expected to be comparable to the third quarter, reflecting ongoing investment in technology enhancements and the addition of new talent added for strategic growth.

The income tax rate in the quarter should be in the range of 45% to 50%. With that, operator, we can now open the call for Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is from Blaine Heck with Wells Fargo.

Blaine Heck: Hessam, you pointed to debt maturities that can no longer be postponed as a potential catalyst for sales, but also a widening bid-ask spread that's keeping activity under pressure. I guess can you talk about what you're seeing that suggests lenders are becoming less willing to extend and whether those situations are turning into executable listings at realistic prices or just more conversations that haven't yet translated into closings?

Hessam Nadji: Happy to address your question. Two-fold answer. First, the direction that we're getting from active dialogue in multiple markets directly with lenders is the basis of expecting more transactions because the tone has changed in those conversations directly with the lenders related to properties that they're going to have to take back or upcoming maturities and being proactive about discussions on what to do with them.

This is very different than what we were witnessing directly from the field being sort of collectively observed than a year ago and especially 2 years ago, where the appetite for an actual execution of a transaction or much more decisive action upon loan maturity or significantly underperforming properties hardly ever included a discussion of an immediate decision or action. The loan modification, buying more time, expecting rates to come in, dominated the conversations in the last couple of years. That shift is the reason we believe that going into '27 and '28, there will be a lot more actual transactions that clear the market. They're going to have to be priced in order to clear the market.

And that's another area where our team is reporting a lot more realism, both by lenders of this category of potential sales and the current owners that are having some distress. The other component of that forecast, Blaine, is tied to what happened with interest rates over the quarter in that this last round of an unexpected spike in rates really challenged the underwriting and the notion of any hope for value recovery because interest rates would go back down. It actually put a lot more properties into the red zone of not being able to really have any recapitalization or any hopes of a refinance than previously.

So that was a little bit of a wake-up call for the market in a way that pushed more decisions to want to engage with us more actively on listings that we believe will come to market in the first half of 2027. And so those are the combination of factors that leads us to expect more transaction activity from that group of kind of pipeline discussions.

The other more near-term challenge, Blaine, has a direct implication of what we've seen several times since this elongated downturn began, and that is the direct impact of higher interest rates, especially when they're unexpected on active listings and properties that have been negotiated, they're about to go under contract or go hard with nonrefundable deposits. And all of a sudden, you now have an unexpected change in the underwriting because of the cost of debt or a lender wants to change the parameters of the net proceeds or the interest rate. That's always disruptive, especially in the private client market, as you know, because of the lower price points being more sensitive to the cost of debt.

And there is the kind of tug of war between the near-term pressure, but also seeing that the pipeline going into '27 is likely going to have a lot more sales in it because of maturing debt and because of a different attitude by lenders and owners of underperforming properties.

Blaine Heck: And I guess just digging into that line of questioning deeper on transactions. Are the bigger constraints just fewer new listings coming to market or a lower conversion rate on deals already under contract? And then have the recent rate moves primarily pushed the closings into 2027 or caused buyers and sellers to just abandon those transactions altogether?

Hessam Nadji: Yes. It's -- our biggest challenge really is more around the sellability of the current inventory that's on the market. It's not as much of a challenge to see new inventory come to market in '23, '24 and really much of '25, we still had a large cadre of our client base that we've been in dialogue with for multiple years about selling. They really weren't ready to pull the trigger in the hopes of something changing that would bring interest rates back down and restore values. As that hope has faded, more and more of our client base that we've been in active dialogue in is now bringing inventory to market.

And another positive trend is that, that initial price -- list price is more realistic. But then when you have the kind of interest rate about that we just had in the third quarter with a 70, 80 basis point movement in just a few weeks, even the more realistic price gets challenged once the property is on the market. So we have near record inventory going into 2027. We're very confident that, that inventory within a 10% or 15% price range is sellable, but that's where the rub is in that the bid-ask keeps moving because of the volatility in interest rates. So the second part of your question was around delays versus deals that have fundamentally died.

We're seeing very few deals that have fundamentally died. There is a lot of motivation to sell. There's plenty of capital on the sidelines to want to transact. It's a question of bid-ask and it's a question of kind of regrouping and putting deals back under contract once we rediscover alignment between the buyer, the seller, and the lender. The good news is that within the last few weeks, interest rates have retreated. We would hope that, that is going to have a positive ripple effect going into Q1.

But right now, we're still kind of recovering from the ripple effect of the higher interest rates in the quarter because there's always a several month lag between the occurrence of interest rates going up or down and what ripples through the repricing of our inventory and the impact on our pipeline. There's always a few month lag. But fundamentally, the market is ready to transact. And fundamentally, there's capital that wants to come into commercial real estate.

But we're seeing a lot more demand on the buy side for the risk premium that real estate has typically required above the 10-year yield -- 10-year treasury yield that kind of went away for a while, where investors were willing not to demand that premium over the 10-year treasury. That premium is absolutely back in the market. It's not any more than the long-term averages. It's typically 200 basis points, if you look at historical data. But the market is still having to adjust to the fact that the risk premium is a requirement now in an environment where you have inflation and you have higher interest rates.

Blaine Heck: Last question, you didn't repurchase shares this quarter. I guess, can you talk about whether that reflects the timing and pricing of opportunities to buy stock, desire to preserve liquidity through the current environment, or greater visibility on external investments? And what would make repurchases the preferred use of capital again?

Steve Degennaro: Yes, Blaine, this is Steve. I'll take that. Our capital allocation strategy has, more recently, over the last several years, been focused on, obviously, internal investments and more geared towards dividends and repurchases. That did slow in the last couple of quarters. As we look at other areas to deploy capital, whether that's more enhanced investment internally in technology to allow us to scale. But also, Hessam alluded to the fact that there, at the moment, are more opportunities out in the market for M&A on the brokerage and the financing side, in particular, as well as some other areas that we're looking into.

So this is a point where we're, as we always do, assess where best to deploy our capital. And at the moment, we're keeping a little bit more in the quiver here for some potential opportunities.

Operator: Our next question is from Mitch Germain with Citizens JMP.

Mitch Germain: So I wanted to just dive in a little bit deeper to some of the commentary from you, Steve, in terms of strategic acquisitions. And you say the pipeline is a little bit more constructive today. I'm curious, is this kind of growing your core capabilities? Or as you mentioned, leasing, is it kind of moving into new ventures? How are you approaching this process?

Steve Degennaro: Yes. Great question, and you're picking up on some of the commentary that we made in our prepared remarks. Certainly, on the leasing side, as Hessam mentioned, we have brought on a couple of senior level executives to begin the build-out of that opportunity, which we're really excited about. We're tempering expectations in terms of top line growth. It will take a bit to build that out, but highly complementary to our investment sales and business in particular. So opportunity is there. But then other opportunities on the financing side, in particular, that still -- it's too early to get into any specifics, but there are, just suffice to say, more opportunities presenting themselves in this environment.

Mitch Germain: The 10-year was 5.3%. It's now 4.85%. We had been given indications or been told indications from a couple of different industry people about repricing on the way up, and now we're back down -- moving back down again. So Hessam, how do your clients -- how do you navigate this environment with your clients? Are you doing more outreach? Or is there a way to compare it to historical trends? I'm curious in terms of how you're marketing the business through this volatility.

Hessam Nadji: The volatility is the absolute toughest headwind for producer productivity. As I mentioned, the tenure has now moved in either direction by 50 bps or more 16x in the last 4 years. Each one of those periods requires repricing of both inventory and deals under contract. It's taken us significantly longer to market an average listing. It's taken us significantly longer to oversee the various stages of contingency removal, due diligence, and closing process. And that leaves less time for developing new business, even for our most senior producers.

So this volatility is more of a challenge for our business than just the overall higher interest rate environment, frankly, because if higher interest rates had occurred and had stabilized at whatever rate the market felt was sustainable, the industry would recalibrate after some time and we would be able to kind of move on into a new cycle. The disruptive nature of this truly elongated downturn is very different than any cycle that I've been in really since the early '90s with the RTC, which took 4, 5 years through process, and that was much more of a macro breakdown of commercial real estate due to massive overbuilding and overleveraging.

This isn't the same kind of drivers, but it's creating an environment where an end to a down cycle has been very difficult to reach and to define because last year was the effect of tariffs. This year, it was the effect of the Iran war and higher inflation and then various reasons that the volatility has continued. Our approach, Mitch, has been to stay very close to our clients throughout this entire period of uncertainty starting in fall of 2022.

The number of times we've had to go back to the same client and revalue the real estate and do broker opinion of value 2 to 3 times a year and advise them on whether it was the right time to bring the property to market, what it would likely trade for is at a record high, especially when those conversations have not been translating into closed transactions unlike what we normally see. So we still believe in the client relationship. We still believe in investing, in being there as many times as it takes to guide the client on what to do with an asset, both at a portfolio level and at an asset level.

We are investing heavily on being in touch with our clients, both institutional, by the way, and private client is no different. Even a small $5 million to $10 million owner that is trying to figure out what to do with their portfolio or asset of that private client type of business needs as much guidance as a major institutional client does. And so we take it very seriously, and we've deployed all of our resources to enable our sales force to be there for them without consummation of transactions. So we believe that will come to us at some point in the future.

And in fact, a lot of the inventory that's come in the market now or I'm fairly confident will come into play in 2027, almost in every case will be tied back to multi-year conversations with our team on what to do with that asset. And that's what sets us apart. It's an investment in the relationship over the long term. At the same time, we have taken several measures to just increase the touch point of our sales force with owners. It's a vast and fragmented market, as I've always said.

There are literally hundreds and thousands of owners that probably don't know what to do and have been trying to navigate this last 2- to 3-year period of uncertainty that we don't have relationships with and we should be in touch with. So while we're kind of nurturing the existing relationships and being in front of existing clients and those that we've worked with in the past, we're equally putting pressure and really pressing the gas pedal on new relationships. That's where our research comes in, the industry events come in, the branding comes in and local -- at a local level, marketing campaigns, outreach campaigns, contests for the salespeople and so on.

Operator: We have reached the end of the question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the floor back over to Hessam Nadji for closing comments.

Hessam Nadji: Thank you, operator, and thank you, everyone, for joining our call. We look forward to seeing many of you on the road and to have you back on our next quarterly call. This session is adjourned.

Operator: This concludes today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.

#3183. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3182. The AI Control Gap: Companies Adopting AI Must Learn What Wall Street Learned The Hard Way

Samuel Kaluvuri, CEO of ApyHub, works on API infrastructure and runtime policy enforcement and holds a PhD in security assurance.

Somewhere inside a large bank, an AI agent has a name, a login ID and a manager who has to write its performance review.

This is less eccentric than it sounds, and it’s one of the more rational things I believe banking has done this year. These are institutions with serious risk functions and long memories for things that lose money quickly. Looking for a way to control software that acts on its own, they reached for the instruments they trusted: an identity, a reporting line and someone answerable for it.​

They are developing ways to manage a new kind of software, and the questions they are working through are ones other companies adopting agentic AI will increasingly need to address.​​

Enterprise software has always come with controls: permissions, approval chains, segregation of duties and audit logs. That worked for 30 years because a person asked for something, another looked at it and the system did exactly what was approved.

All three assumptions have stopped being true. The requester is now software operating at machine speed, and approval no longer describes the action. When someone signs off on “handle customer onboarding,” nothing in that sentence says which systems get touched, what data leaves which jurisdiction or what the agent does when it meets a case nobody thought about. The approval covers intent, but the risk lives in the path.

Put an approval workflow in front of a system taking thousands of autonomous actions, and you have not built oversight. You have built a very fast queue of things you already agreed to.

Finance learned this the hard (and expensive) way. Sign-off on trades worked until trades stopped happening at human speed. In 2012, Knight Capital pushed faulty code into production and lost more than $460 million in 45 minutes. By the time a conventional approval process notices a problem like that, the money is gone.

The response was not a better approval workflow. Control moved into the execution path: limits enforced before an order left the building, kill switches and real-time surveillance. Regulators then went further, and this is the part I believe is worth borrowing. Under the Securities and Exchange Commission’s market access rule, those controls must sit under the firm’s direct and exclusive control.

A broker may buy the risk technology from a third party, but it must keep the ability to monitor and adjust the controls in real time and cannot simply rely on the provider’s assurance that they work. The point of intervention moved to where the machine acts and stayed with whoever carries the liability.

So where does control over an agent actually live?

Not in the model. It sits below where these products are demonstrated and sold, in the software that determines which systems an agent can reach, what it may do with them, when it stops and what gets written down. Change the model, and the agent gets cleverer. Change that control layer, and it can no longer touch your payments system.

Three capabilities determine how effective these controls are: the ability to limit an agent’s actions before they happen, stop them while they are underway and independently reconstruct what the agent did afterward.​​

Running infrastructure that sits in the path of these calls gives you a different view. Human traffic arrives one action at a time. Agent traffic arrives in bursts: dozens of calls in a few seconds while the thing works through a task. Everyone can check whether the task completed, but few see what it read on the way or where it sent what it found.​

This is where the buying decision becomes important. A company does not necessarily have to hand this layer to its vendor. An enterprise can retain control over its access policies, gateways, transaction limits and logging, as many already do for systems used by employees. But those controls need to be deliberately extended to cover agents. Otherwise, buyers may inherit runtime rules configured by engineers focused on task completion or rely on defaults that are rarely revisited. These settings may also fall outside the governance documents boards and compliance teams regularly review.​

An employee’s limits are typically enforced through systems the bank controls and can adjust as needs change. An agent’s limits depend on the systems governing its actions, which may be managed by the buyer, the vendor or both. If the buyer has not established who controls that layer, important decisions may effectively be made elsewhere. The purchase is therefore not just software that performs tasks; it also involves a set of operating rules, some of which may already be in place before the buyer evaluates them.​

Platforms should be assessed not only on what an agent can do in a demonstration but also on where controls are enforced and who can change them. If a platform does not provide the necessary oversight, building a replacement layer may be one option, but it is not always practical or sufficient. In some cases, the better decision may be to keep a workflow under human supervision until the organization can establish controls appropriate for autonomous operation. That may be a less appealing sales proposition, but it can be the more responsible choice.​​​​

The regulatory direction is visible. In June 2026, the Financial Stability Board warned that the autonomy of AI agents can amplify risks that materialize at great speed.

Supervisors are no more likely to accept “our vendor handles that” than they were for outsourced trading infrastructure. Meanwhile, the platforms are sold on handing the work off entirely.

Every autonomous system runs inside rules that determine what it can do, and those rules exist whether or not the board has seen them. The question for a vendor is not merely who wrote them but whether you can inspect them, change them and, when the machine is already moving, enforce them yourself.​

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3179. Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies

Anuj Goel is CEO and co-founder of Cyware, a company focused on intelligence-led cybersecurity and operational resilience.

Every threat intelligence feed shares a blind spot: It knows the threat but nothing about our specific environment.

The feed carries threat data; only our environment provides context. The industry has spent a decade refining data when it should have focused on environment-specific context.

As a practitioner, the hardest conversations were never about explaining suspicious activity. They were about explaining why it reached us when the best intelligence available had already flagged it. We had the indicators. We just weren’t connecting them to the assets they might reach. What surprised me then, and still does, is that the problem was never a shortage of intelligence or its accuracy. It was the missing step between knowing about a threat and knowing, in real time, that it applied to us. That experience shaped how I think about this space, and it is why I believe context, not volume, is where the real work is.

Intelligence has no universal version; “good intelligence” depends on sector and geography, not sheer volume.

Financial institutions require fraud-focused reporting, while industrial operators need OT intelligence built around controllers and plant-floor realities. Neither is “better,” but they aren’t interchangeable. Relevance is inherently specific to who we are and where we operate.

No feed can see inside our walls, and that’s where we decide which known threats matter to our environment.

Relevance is derived from the assets we actually run. The identities and access paths that connect them. What is business-critical versus incidental? Where our controls are strong and where they are thin. This is the ground truth every external indicator has to be measured against. An indicator evaluated against our environment becomes elevated to a prioritized, actionable risk. The same indicator, without an environment behind it, is just a rumor about someone else’s network.

Relevance is the product of the two: the intelligence our sector trusts, correlated with the infrastructure, data and assets we have. Neither input alone produces it. The best feeds in the world, unmeasured against our environment, cannot tell us what to do first on Monday morning. A perfect map of our environment, with no sector intelligence flowing into it, has nothing to act on either.

Consider when identical intelligence arrives at two different organizations.

For one, the indicator maps to a critical, internet-facing application reachable by elevated identities. This context resolves to a high-urgency risk, requiring immediate isolation and escalation.

For the second, the same indicator maps to a decommissioned service or a segment with existing controls. This context resolves to a low-urgency risk requiring only logging.

Same feed. Same indicator. Same morning. Two entirely different answers, and two entirely different actions determined by adding the context.

This is what customer-specific context means in practice. It is not a cleaner presentation of the same data. It is a different computed result for every organization, because the inputs on the other side of the equation differ for every organization. It determines not only whether to act, but what action is warranted, in what order and with how much confidence. Any system that skips this step applies one global severity score to environments that share almost nothing in common.

One line is worth drawing sharply, because the industry constantly blurs it. Tagging an indicator as malicious is enrichment, attaching a known attribute to a piece of data. Knowing that the same indicator belongs to a campaign actively targeting our sector, that a machine on our finance team touched it three days ago and that the identity behind that machine is exposed, that is context. Enrichment adds metadata. Context fuels risk reduction.

This is also why dozens of feeds never added up to an answer. More raw indicators, unmeasured against our environment, is a larger pile to triage, not a clearer picture. Most security leaders have a graveyard of unused subscriptions to prove it.

Increasingly, the systems making security decisions are not human analysts reading a feed. They are platforms and agents consuming intelligence to prioritize, correlate and act, and a decision engine is only as good as what we put into it.

Feed a system raw, one-size-fits-all intelligence and it inherits the problem we started with: It cannot tell a live risk from an irrelevant one, because the feed never carried that distinction. The input has to be measured against that specific environment, already resolved into what is relevant, exposed and worth acting on.

This reframes what “having threat intelligence” should mean. A feed is not the same as threat context, and a raw feed piped into a decision-making tool does not become context on arrival. Intelligence has to be made relevant before it becomes an input, per sector, per environment, per organization or every tool consuming it is reasoning from a rumor.

The organizations—and increasingly, the systems—best positioned for what is coming are not the ones holding the most feeds. #3178. Lincoln (LCLN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management stated that the company is benefiting from structural changes in the private markets, including the increasing participation of retail investors and the demand for more frequent independent valuations. The firm noted that its diversified platform, which includes capital advisory and valuation services alongside mergers and acquisitions, provides stability across different economic cycles. The company reported that its global footprint and sector expertise have led to increased market share among private equity sponsors, particularly for larger and more complex mandates.

Both investment banking and valuations and opinions delivered robust year-over-year revenue growth, demonstrating the breadth of our capabilities and our ability to capitalize on opportunities cost across the private capital markets. Our M&A business continued to show strength, particularly across industrials and business services. For the second consecutive quarter, we generated the largest transaction fee in our firm's history.

This underscores the continued evolution of our franchise and our ability to compete successfully for larger, more complex mandates. Beyond M&A, our capital advisory practice achieved record third quarter and year-to-date revenues. This performance was supported by increased demand for financing solutions, particularly refinancing activity. Our private funds advisory practice continues to see strong demand for general partner-led advisory and fundraising. The growth in these businesses reflects the investments we made in senior talent to enhance financing solutions for our clients, broaden our addressable market and increase productivity. Our valuations and opinion segment generated record quarterly revenues. Within our portfolio valuations business.

This was driven by continued execution of the strategy to deepen existing client relationships, expand the breadth of asset classes valued and increase the frequency of valuation services delivered. In addition, our transaction opinions business delivered solid growth in the quarter we saw particular strength in secondary transactions. With these results into context, I want to spend a few moments discussing the broader market dynamics and some of the trends we're seeing. The improving M&A environment we discussed in the second quarter continued into the third quarter, while buyers clearly remain selective and the pace of recovery varies across the sectors. We remain encouraged by the momentum in transaction activity, including increasing engagement from private equity sponsors.

The high-quality businesses with compelling growth opportunities continue to attract significant interest and drive competitive processes. At the same time, we continue to see greater transaction activity among companies that previously faced more challenging market conditions, which we believe suggests a broadening recovery. It is not new news that private equity sponsors remain under pressure to generate liquidity, driven by extended hold periods, selective fund rating environment and increasing demand for distributions from limited partners. Combined with substantial capital available for deployment and largely good company performance, which we can see in our valuation data, we believe these dynamics provide instructive foundation for a continued improvement in M&A activity.

From a financing perspective, our capital advisory practice is benefiting from several durable demand drivers, including elevated borrowing costs, growing demand for liquidity and the debt maturity of portfolio companies acquired in 2021 and 2022. Capital clearly remains available for high-quality transactions. At the same time, we are seeing foreclosure activity increasing as lenders tighten operating constraints and financial sponsors are increasingly unwilling to provide additional capital where there is no path to equity returns. With this backdrop, private equity sponsors are actively seeking creative capital structures to preserve liquidity or generate distributions. Beyond the recovery in transaction activity, we continue to see important structural changes reshaping the private markets.

First, the growing participation of private wealth and individual investors is expanding the investor base. This trend is increasing demand for transparency and frequency of independent valuations. Second, the continued expansion of alternative investments into a broader range of products and investment structures is also driving higher demand for increasingly complex valuations. These trends are particularly pronounced in private credit including both direct lending and asset-backed finance and are increasingly evident across private equity and secondary funds. We believe these developments create meaningful long-term growth opportunities for our valuations and opinions business. Our ability to capture these opportunities reflect years of deliberate investment in our platform to broaden our capabilities, sharpen our sector expertise and strengthen our competitive position.

Transaction opinions activity also remained strong. with an increase in the number of opinions completed during the quarter. And the margin -- the increase of interest rates on the margin is not impacting a sponsor running hard after an A asset. The opportunity cost of not putting those dollars to work is far greater than -- or putting them to work far greater than not putting more. I think also importantly, the strategic buyers that are coming to our processes and competing in our processes, there's often significant synergies that are outlaying any marginal increase in the cost of capital.

So in theory, you would think that the rise in interest rates would decrease in values, but we're just not seeing it in our marketplace. It is predictable, if it's small in interest rate increase, it's just not going to impact it.

Robert Brown: Yes. James, I think you alluded to something. I think if you have a rapid rise where people don't know where it's going to end, then that gets back to creating instability. It doesn't seem like that the interest rate increase environment that we're in. And we'll continue to monitor it because, obviously, conventional wisdom is a higher cost of capital, lower values. But I think what's driving transaction activity, and we've mentioned this in the comments as well as the questions. We'll continue to monitor it. But right now, we're not overly worried about it.

In fact, there's some thought that the interest rate increase could be the catalyst for some sponsors to maybe mark down some of their businesses that are overvalued and could result in more activity, but that remains to be seen.

James Yaro: Fascinating. Okay. Well, that actually brings me to my second question, which is on valuations opinion part of the business. So hoping you might be able to just talk a little bit about trends there that are not related necessarily just to the market backdrop. The first is the impact of the continued shift to more frequent valuations out of a monthly or daily and how this has evolved over, let's say, the period since the IPO.

And then number two, the impact of some of the newer products that you've built in this business, the senior debt indices and the private market index being the 2 that I'm thinking about and how the growth of those 2 products has gone.

Robert Brown: Yes. Good questions. And in terms of the frequency evaluations, James, we just see that continue. I think when we were on the road show, we quoted that over 30% of our valuations are now done more frequently than quarterly and largely driven by the retail money that's coming in. And when you have to have redemptions on a more frequent basis than quarterly, you need valuations. We're seeing that number has gone up. And I think the last I heard in talking to Brian was it's kind of mid-30s now. So we are seeing that continue. You've got some large asset managers come out and say, we're just going to value everything daily because we want to.

And so part of it is the redemptions. I think part of it is there's just a shift for more transparency. So that trend is continuing. And there's no indication that's going to stop. And also on that point, the question on how do we see the midterm effect and to the extent there are more regulations for this business, regulations tend to be good. So we'll see what plays out there. In terms of the product, as we previously communicated, we, earlier this year, announced the S&P Lincoln Senior debt index. We brought that to market. We signed up contracts.

We continue to feel that this index will become and if it's not already, kind of the benchmark of choice over time. In Q3, we launched the monthly and sub-industry indices for this with a very favorable market reaction. Nobody else is doing that on a monthly basis. So we're still not modeling any of this in a material way into our revenues gains, but we think that this is a product that's a branding element to it, and we think, ultimately, this has the ability to have an impact on earnings.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Devin Ryan with Citizens Bank.

Devin Ryan: I want to come back to the opportunity that you guys highlighted several times around kind of larger fees. I'm just trying to understand what's driving that and kind of mapping this out into the future? I mean I'm curious, is that mainly you just pay off from building relationships over a long period of time. And so Lincoln just getting involved in larger assignments as you kind of win those customers over trust? Or is it about expanded capabilities and so now you're kind of opening up maybe a different part of the market that wasn't there for you before.

And then connected there certain verticals here where you feel like you have more of a right to win at least initially here?

Eric Malchow: Good questions. I would say to you that it's an evolution of our business. And if I go back to my prior comments, which is, we have built a platform over time with one, diversified, but two full-service products and building value for those portfolio companies over their hold periods. Our goal is to serve the entire life cycle of that company and have round trips. So perhaps sell that business when it's $15 million of EBITDA and then $40 million or $50 million of EBITDA and then maybe $100 million or $200 million of EBITDA. And you're seeing that. And to your sector question, there are different maturation levels of our industry groups.

And we had particularly strong success this quarter, for example, in data centers and power and those -- we've got the leading position there. So we're taking advantage of the structural trends in that market. But also the expertise that we have in that market but no different across other groups like services or health care or even technology where we've had multibillion-dollar deals. And it really goes to the long-term investments that we made that are now paying off because of the expertise that we have, the deals that we've done in that space, the value we're adding to the private equity groups and the portfolio of companies that we are tracking. Anything you'd add?

Robert Brown: I would just say none of this is a change in our strategy. None of this is, hey, we have a strategy to go up market. I think both Lincoln, and I think many of our peers, I think our clients are realizing that firms like us, our expertise in M&A, the industry expertise that we've built up over decades the disciplined processes that we run can be really, really effective at all sides of business. So I completely agree with Eric. I think it's just it's advising companies over decades and deals to get deals. And when you've announced larger deals and more complex deals than more of those tend to compete.

So I think it's been a function of a lot of building blocks over a long period of time that have put us in a position to continually advise on better, larger and more complex transactions.

Devin Ryan: Appreciate that great color. And just a model question. I don't think I missed this, but on non-compensation costs, the outlook last quarter, I think you framed for full year growth in the high single digits off of the -- I think the comparable base was $157 million from 2025. The third quarter of $43 million was better than we had modeled. So that would seemingly imply something in the low $50 million range in 4Q, if that's still the right framework. So just checking to see if that's still the right framework and any modeling help would be appreciated.

Theodore Heidloff: Yes, Devin thanks for the question. Yes, we continue to expect high single-digit growth for noncomp on a pro forma basis once you had MarshBerry,. Q4 tends to be a little bit seasonally higher as you work through some of the year-end billing for firms like consultants, things like that and tend to come through in the fourth quarter there. But yes, consistent expectations with high single digits for full year.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the conference back over to Rob Brown for any closing remarks.

Robert Brown: Really just thank you all for the engagement today. And hopefully what came through is that we believe we're well positioned to capitalize on the momentum that we have. And we look forward to updating you on our fourth quarter and full year results early next year.

Operator: The conference has now ended. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

#3177. 2027 Tax Brackets and Federal Income Tax Rates

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3173. Franklin (BEN) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record AUM growth and raised 2029 targets signal momentum

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Franklin Templeton Inc. (BEN +4.72%) reported a return to positive long-term organic growth driven by expansion in alternative assets, exchange-traded funds, and customized tax-efficient wealth solutions. Management reported record assets under management across several segments and increased its multiyear strategic targets for fundraising and operating margins. The company is integrating recent acquisitions while utilizing artificial intelligence to enhance investment research and operational productivity across its global distribution platform.

Operator: Welcome to the Franklin Templeton's Earnings Conference Call for the year ended September 30, 2026. Hello. My name is Shamali, and I will be your call operator today. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, Selene Oh, Head of Investor Relations for Franklin Templeton. You may begin.

Selene Oh: Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss our quarterly and fiscal year results.
