#3111. Lyntris (LYNX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Backlog doubled this year as international demand reshaped the growth outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Lyntris Inc. (LYNX +28.66%) reported third quarter results characterized by significant revenue growth and a more than twofold increase in total backlog since the start of the fiscal year. Management reported that expansion is occurring across all mission domains, particularly within the Air & Missile Defense and Space ISR & Resilient Communications segments, which both saw triple-digit revenue growth. The company stated that its merchant supplier model allows it to support multiple prime contractors while maintaining high ownership of design intellectual property, which accounts for 85% of product revenue. Following its August IPO, the company has reduced its net leverage ratio to 1.2x and established a new $300 million credit facility to support future working capital needs and strategic initiatives.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Good afternoon, and welcome to the Lyntris Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note that today's conference is being recorded. I will now turn the call over to Nathan Rutledge, Senior Vice Senior Vice President and Head of Investor Relations. Nathan, please go ahead.

Nathan Rutledge: Good afternoon, and welcome to Lyntris Third Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Call. Please turn to Slide 2. Before we begin, please note that certain information presented on this call contains forward-looking statements. Forward-looking statements are based on current expectations, forecasts and assumptions that involve risks and uncertainties, including, but not limited to, economic, competitive, governmental, and technological factors outside of our control. These factors may cause our business strategy or actual results to differ materially from forward-looking statements.

For further information on these risks, please review the risk factors discussed in our registration statement on Form S-1 filed with the SEC as well as the Form 8-K filed today, the associated earnings release and the safe harbor statement contained therein. All forward-looking statements should be considered in conjunction with those in our earnings release. The company undertakes no obligation to revise any forward-looking statements in today's remarks or to update them to reflect events or circumstances occurring after this call. We will also discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures. Definitions and reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in our earnings materials.

We have also posted a slide presentation at investors.lyntris.com in the News and Events section. The information discussed on this call is time-sensitive and is accurate only as of today, November 4, 2026. Joining me today are Brian Morrison, our Chief Executive Officer; Matt Alty, our President; and Tim Paulin, our Chief Financial Officer. With that, I'll turn the call over to you, Brian.

Brian Morrison: Thank you, Nathan, and welcome, everyone. I'm excited to share Lyntris' third quarter results. Our quarter was driven by strong performance, growing customer demand, and an expanding role on programs that matter to the future of defense and space. Let's look at Slide 4. I'll start with our third quarter highlights. Tim will review our financial results, and then Matt will discuss the capabilities and programs driving our growth. I'll then return for our outlook and priorities before we take your questions. In August, Lyntris made its debut on the New York Stock Exchange. That IPO strengthened our balance sheet and increased our capacity to invest in the business and support future growth.

Our focus now is to build on the strong business momentum we experienced leading up to the IPO and which we have continued to see since the listing. We'll continue to execute as these programs advance, translating today's opportunities into sustained long-term growth. Our purpose is straightforward. We help customers connect the modern battle space from sense to act. Our engineering talent and proprietary technology help detect threats, share and interpret information, and enable a response. We bring these capabilities together to meet demanding mission requirements, working with government agencies and military customers as well as both established and emerging primes.

Our track record of delivering for these customers positions us to grow as their programs advance and will take on a larger role as their needs evolve. In the third quarter, we delivered total revenue of $194 million, a year-over-year increase of 90% or 89% organically. Adjusted EBITDA grew 91% to $28.5 million, representing a margin of 14.7%. Adjusted net income was $17 million or $0.15 per share, and free cash flow for the quarter was $79 million. These results exceeded our expectations, demonstrating strong momentum in our business as we continue executing against our strategic priorities. Our third quarter performance reflects strong customer demand and the increasing relevance of our technology to evolving mission requirements.

Customers need to detect threats at greater distances, operate across more frequency bands, and respond with greater speed and accuracy. Those requirements closely suit the capabilities we brought together at Lyntris, from sensing and communications to software that connects information to command and control. We see broad-based growth across a number of programs, particularly in Air & Missile Defense and Space ISR & Resilient Comms, supported by the modernization of U.S. and allied radar systems and the growing need for resilient space-based communications. International customers are also investing in sovereign defense and space capabilities, creating additional opportunities for our technology.

Much of this increased activity supports well-funded high-priority programs with room to grow as programs move through the development life cycle. This work includes upfront engineering and initial production that generate revenue and adjusted EBITDA today but also establish the technology and manufacturing foundation for follow-on work. The first system requires more engineering effort, subsequent systems build on that work, creating the opportunity for higher margins as production expands. These program positions are an essential part of our long-term growth strategy. Engaging with customers early on allows us to embed our technology in their solutions and expand our role as programs mature. Our merchant supplier model also allows us to apply that technology across multiple customers and programs.

We welcome the additional revenue and adjusted EBITDA dollars from this work while continuing to focus on driving execution and profitability for the long term across the portfolio. That customer demand is also reflected in our backlog. We ended the quarter with a total backlog of just over $1 billion, up about $100 million sequentially and 113% compared with $476 million at the end of fiscal 2025. Our book-to-bill in the quarter was 1.5. Even with the strong revenue growth we delivered this quarter, orders continue to significantly exceed revenue, strengthening our visibility into future activity and supporting our confidence in the continued growth of this business.

Orders during the quarter included both initial awards and follow-on commitments that move programs from development into low rate production. International demand continues to support our growth. While international customers have historically represented about 15% of revenue, their share of our backlog has grown substantially in the fiscal year, accounting now for nearly 1/4 of our total backlog. These trends strengthen visibility into future activity and support our confidence in sustained growth. Slide 5 shows how that growth is taking shape across our core missions.

Air & Missile Defense revenue increased 154% to $83 million, reflecting accelerated activity on a major radar program where we are supporting initial fielding and low-rate initial production, along with contributions from programs across the production life cycle. Across this mission area, our positions span initial fielding, low rate production and programs preparing for higher production volumes. The absolutely essential modernization of U.S. and allied radar systems creates opportunities to build on these positions as customers demand greater range, accuracy, and sensitivity in response to a rapidly evolving threat environment. In Maritime Domain Awareness, revenue grew 29% to $54 million. Our work there spans naval radar, command and control, defensive cyber and integrated maritime sensor networks, including unmanned systems.

These capabilities help customers understand activity across their waters, protect mission networks, and coordinate a response. In Space ISR & Resilient Comms, revenue grew 108% to $57 million as we met rapidly growing sensing and communications demand. Here, we're expanding from integrated antenna solutions into full-up satellite payload solutions. Our recently announced role as a prime payload integrator on PTS-G illustrates that broader capability. We also see a substantial international opportunity in sovereign ground antenna and satellite payloads as allied nations seek resilient space-based communications capabilities tailored to their own requirements. Our space heritage across geostationary and medium earth orbits, together with our expertise in multi-frequency antennas gives us a strong foundation to address this emerging demand.

As requirements become more complex and deployment time lines compress, we see opportunities to bring these capabilities together into broader payload solutions and apply our technology across additional customer programs. Across all of our core mission areas, we are seeing opportunities to advance positions we've spent years establishing. Our engineering expertise and track record of delivery give us the foundation to support customers as their programs advance and requirements expand. This quarter demonstrated what that can mean for Lyntris. Customers asked us to do more, and we met the moment, driving growth in revenue and in our bottom line. Tim will now walk through the financial results in some greater detail.

Tim Paulin: Thank you, Brian. We're now on Slide 6. Our third quarter results reflect both growth in customer demand and faster pace of activity on existing programs. I'll walk through the financial detail on Slide 6, and then we'll cover free cash flow and our balance sheet. As Brian mentioned, revenue was $194 million, up 90% year-over-year or 89% organically, reflecting increased activity in Air & Missile Defense, integrated satellite payload programs and allied maritime programs. Adjusted EBITDA increased 91% to $28.5 million with a margin of 14.7%.

Higher revenue and cost actions offset the program mix, including more upfront engineering and initial production on programs where we are embedding our proprietary technology as well as growing investment in public company capabilities. As these programs move into higher rate production, we expect to benefit from the engineering work already completed and greater manufacturing scale. On a GAAP basis, we reported a net loss of $5 million or $0.04 per share compared to a net loss of $3.5 million or $0.03 per share in the prior year period. Adjusted net income was $17 million or $0.15 per share versus $1.7 million and $0.02 per share in the prior period.

Our adjusted net income measure excludes acquisitions and integration-related costs, stock-based compensation, amortization of acquired intangibles and certain other items together with related tax effects. The year-over-year improvement in adjusted net income was primarily driven by stronger results of operations, lower interest expense and adjustments for onetime items such as share-based compensation and loss on debt extinguishment. Turning to our results for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026. Revenue increased 55% to $435 million, reflecting stronger growth on new and existing programs. On a GAAP basis, we reported a net loss of $18 million or $0.17 per share compared to a net loss of $13.2 million or $0.14 per share in the prior year period.

Adjusted net income was $30.6 million or $0.28 per share versus $2.4 million and $0.03 per share in the prior period. The increase in our net loss is mainly attributable to nonrecurring stock-based compensation expenses and a loss on refinancing debt, partially offset by stronger operational performance and lower interest expense. Adjusted EBITDA grew 65% to $66.3 million, supported by top line growth and effective cost controls, yielding an adjusted EBITDA margin of 15.2%, a year-over-year increase of 90 basis points. Reconciliations of adjusted EBITDA, adjusted net income, adjusted diluted earnings per share and free cash flow to the corresponding GAAP measures are included in our earnings materials. Turning now to free cash flow.

Operating activities generated approximately $84 million of cash in the quarter, while capital expenditures were $5 million, resulting in a free cash flow of $79 million. Free cash flow excludes IPO proceeds. Through the first 9 months, operating cash flow was $119 million, capital expenditures were $11 million, core free cash flow of $108 million. Lyntris delivered strong free cash flow this quarter, supported by earnings and favorable customer payments. Across our portfolio, we received payments at different points in program execution, including upfront funding, progress payments and payments following delivery. We work with customers to align payment terms with program requirements and reduce the working capital required for growth.

Our mix of payment structures, disciplined working capital management, and low capital intensity support an attractive cash flow profile. Cash flow will vary from quarter-to-quarter as receipts and program spending move through the business. We expect continued strong cash generation as we execute our backlog, further strengthening our balance sheet and financial flexibility. We also took important steps to strengthen our balance sheet during the quarter. In July, we entered into a new $200 million term loan plus $100 million revolving credit facility, which came with materially lower interest rates than our prior facilities. Additionally, we used about $60 million of IPO proceeds to repay debt and ended the quarter with no balance on our revolver.

We ended the quarter with $88 million in cash and $198 million in debt, bringing net leverage to 1.2x, down significantly from 4.2x at the beginning of the fiscal year. Looking ahead, we expect net leverage to continue declining over time, although working capital requirements may lead to some quarter-over-quarter variability. Our strengthened balance sheet provides greater financial flexibility to support customer commitments, fund working capital needs, and invest in future growth. With that, I'll turn it over to Matt to discuss our capabilities and progress we're making across key programs. Matt?

Matthew Alty: Thank you, Tim. Let's now turn to Slide 7. I'd like to start by taking a step back and examining the mission environment because it explains why customers choose Lyntris. Warfare has changed in three fundamental ways. Firstly, our adversaries are adapting faster and the threats we encounter are more complex and numerous across every domain. We operate in a spectrum that is now congested, contested and weaponized. And detecting, tracking and responding to these threats require sensors with more range, sensitivity, and accuracy. Second, the data. Following the proliferation of sensor networks, data often remains siloed by service and platform, which is a problem when decision time lines are compressed.

Commanders need a clear integrated view of the battle space that enables faster, more informed decisions. Third, connectivity. Adversaries of industrialized electronic warfare and legacy architectures, satellites and waveforms can become single points of failure. The United States and its allies need secure, resilient links. And many allied nations are building sovereign capabilities to protect their own borders. Together, these dynamics are reshaping mission requirements and creating significant opportunities for Lyntris. Turning to Slide 8. Lyntris' capabilities cover the full path from sensing to action. Our sensors are used to detect threats and communicate data in highly contested environments. Our sensor architecture shapes how those sensors behave and prepares their output to be fused with other sources.

Our data and mission software then turns that information into an integrated picture that supports faster, more informed decisions. Our solutions are modular by design. We build proven hardware and software building blocks that can be adapted for different platforms and missions so a customer can start with a single component and scale to a fully integrated subsystem. That modularity is why our technology appears in every domain from integrated satellite payloads and into subsystems to radar on next-generation fighters, multiband ground terminals and maritime systems. The platforms differ, but the same core technology carries across each one.

Together, these capabilities support the 3 missions that Brian described earlier, Maritime Domain Awareness, Air & Missile Defense, and Space ISR & Resilient Communications. Slide 9 shows how we bring those capabilities to market. Our merchant vendor supplier model gives us multiple paths to participate in customer programs. We work with both established defense primes and newer entrants and our technologies often support more than one team competing for the same opportunity. We also work directly with end users, including the U.S. services and allied governments. Engaging early helps us understand their requirements and build our proprietary technology into the solutions that can advance with the program. Proprietary technology is central to that approach.

Approximately 85% of our product revenue comes from products built on design IP that we own. And the vast majority of our business comes from sole, single or directed source positions. As of the end of last year, we supported more than 200 programs. Those IP-derived positions provide continuity as programs advance and they are the foundation for the program momentum on the next slide. Let's turn to Slide 10, where 3 programs show how our capabilities address the needs we described earlier and how our role can grow over time. We'll begin with Air & Missile Defense.

LTAMDS is a program that we've supported from concept, and the program has recently transitioned into production and deployment phase under a U.S. Army contract valued at over $1.7 billion to the prime. In September, we announced production orders under a long-term purchase agreement with Raytheon, supporting demand through 2028. LTAMDS has been developed to provide the Army with 360-degree integrated Air & Missile Defense capabilities. The precision thermal management assemblies that we build at Lyntris help the radar's high-power electronics maintain stable temperatures and directly support the radar sensitivity, accuracy and range. Detecting and tracking the threat, however, is only the first step.

In Maritime Domain Awareness, our customers need to interpret data faster so they can make informed decisions, develop a plan and coordinate a response. Our command-and-control solutions bring information from multiple sensors into a shared operational picture, enabling faster, more informed decisions. For the Navy's Maritime Tactical Command and Control Program, or MTC2, we deliver a command and control platform that combines data integration, visualization and mission planning. It helps fleet planners at sea and at shore to understand the operating environment, plan missions, and coordinate operations. In Morocco, we adapted our Garda C2 technology to connect distributed sensors, operational sensors, mobile systems and ships, creating a common operating picture tailored to the Morocco Navy's requirements.

In Egypt, we are applying that approach to an awarded Maritime Domain Awareness program that brings together coastal sensors, operational centers, and command and control software. Each is an example of an established technology reaching another customer through an architecture tailored to its needs. In Space ISR & Resilient Communications, we're taking on a broader payload role. Earlier this month, we announced our selection as the prime payload integrator supporting the U.S. Space Force's Protected Tactical Satellite Communications Global Program or PTS-G. Our work spans radio frequency architecture, pointing systems, antenna and full payload integration and testing at our antenna center of excellence in Longmont, Colorado.

Building on 20 years of space heritage, this program expands our role from integrated antenna solutions to integrated satellite payloads. The same RF and antenna capabilities apply to sovereign payload opportunities that Brian described earlier. Many international customers need increasingly complex satellite systems that can operate in contested environments, often on compressed schedules. Building on established technology allows us to reduce technical risk and quickly adapt designs to their specific mission requirements. Together, these programs show how we leverage established technology, expand our role in mission-critical programs and create additional paths for growth. Slide 11 shows how those positions can develop through 4 stages: develop, deploy, expand, and sustain & upgrade.

The stages can overlap and we participate at different points across programs. In develop, we help establish the architecture and solve technical challenges on well-funded, high-priority customer programs. This upfront engineering work embeds our proprietary technology in the customer system and positions us for repeat production, incremental content, and margin expansion as the program scales. In deploy, we integrate and field the solution drawing on established designs, manufacturing processes and software. The LTAMDS program I shared a moment ago is a prime example where we are scaling production of thermal management technology to directly support a high-growth program. In expand, we bring that technology to additional customers or missions or take on more of an existing system.

Expansion can also mean leveraging the same proprietary technology to address a similar requirement on an adjacent program. For example, our thermal management IP supports multiple AE or radar programs and our RF and precision pointing technologies support multiple SATCOM programs, both domestically and internationally. Because we're a merchant supplier, we can support multiple customer teams at the same time. So an investment in our IP extends well beyond any single program award. Leveraging established technology and increasing production volumes can improve program economics over time.

In sustain & upgrade, we support fielded systems and add capabilities as requirements change or the system is upgraded to adapt to an emerging threat or emission requirement, including internationally, as we are doing with the Captor-E Mk2 radar upgrade for the U.K. Typhoon fleet. We support customers with programs at different stages of this life cycle. Programs entering production today often reflect years of earlier engineering work. At the same time, the development work we undertake today helps establish positions that can support growth for many years to come. Participating early allows us to help customers solve demanding technical requirements and incorporate our proprietary technology into the solution.

Successful execution then gives us a foundation to support subsequent deployments, production orders and upgrades. The mix of activity across these stages may affect margins from period to period. Our objective is to improve the profitability of established programs while building the next generation of growth opportunities. Back to Brian.

Brian Morrison: Thanks, Matt. That life cycle progression that Matt talked about is fundamental to our long-term growth strategy. We see opportunities to expand our role on existing programs, broaden the solutions we provide, and bring our technology to new customers and missions. Our priority is to translate those opportunities into sustained growth and strong financial performance. We're focused on aligning engineering, suppliers and production capacity with the commitments we already have in hand. We're also bringing more capabilities together around customer requirements. Our task now then is to turn product improvements into consistent execution and measurable financial results. Turning to Slide 12. I'll start with our fiscal 2026 outlook.

For full year 2026, we expect revenue of $623 million to $630 million, representing approximately 61% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. Adjusted EBITDA of $95.5 million to $97 million or expected growth of about 54%. We expect growth to come from increased activity on established Air & Missile Defense programs, continued integrated payload execution and delivery against already awarded maritime programs. Backlog conversion and follow-on orders support that opportunity with customer schedules and award timing influencing the pace of revenue. Our margin assumptions reflect higher volume, improved operating efficiency and a greater contribution from our technology, partly offset by continued initial fielding activity and investment to support growth.

With more design and initial deployment work than we had initially anticipated, we now expect adjusted EBITDA margin expansion to occur over a somewhat longer period than initially anticipated, although that work is helping us to overdrive EBITDA and revenue today. We remain confident in our long-term margin improvement strategy. Our work embeds our IP and customer solutions and creates opportunities for higher margin repeat production as programs expand. And as I suggested, we welcome the additional revenue and adjusted EBITDA dollars associated with this increased volume. We're building Lyntris around differentiated technologies, strong positions on critical programs and the ability to deliver integrated solutions across connected missions.

Our priorities are clear: execute consistently, expand our proprietary content, and drive greater efficiency as we scale. By doing so, we believe we can strengthen our competitive position, capture a greater share of our customers' evolving needs, and translate that growth into higher earnings and stronger cash generation over time. I want to thank our employees for their expertise and commitment, which helped us drive these results. I want to thank our customers for their trust and our shareholders for joining us on this next chapter. We look forward to updating you on our progress. With that, I'll take your questions.

#3106. Doc Rivers talks Giannis Antetokounmpo leaving Bucks, challenges of coaching superstar

Giannis Antetokounmpo is one-of-one. He doesn't play in the style of other superstars, which makes coaching the NBA champion and two-time MVP a particular challenge.

Doc Rivers, the former Bucks coach turned NBC Sports studio host for NBA broadcasts, pulled no punches when talking about how he found it difficult to coach Antetokounmpo in an appearance on the Bill Simmons podcast.

"I liked Giannis a lot. I liked him more as a dude. He's interesting. He's not easy. He's not easy because he plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy....

"He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have this super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing, and he really has one way: downhill, force, force. Every play, he wants to force it. I wish he learned how to execute better. He's one of those guys... that have never needed to execute because they can do it on their own. But that doesn't help the team. And I told Giannis this, the thing he needs to still learn is the value of execution. How important it is when you're in practice and shoot-arounds to lock in on execution. And now he has a coach [Erik Spoelstra] who is as good as there is in execution."

Rivers came in at the end of Antetokounmpo's time in Milwaukee, taking over in the middle of the 2023-24 season, and the team never found a consistent identity under Rivers' leadership. Part of that was the personnel around Antetokounmpo at the time: Jrue Holiday was gone, Kris Middleton was battling injuries and not the same player as his peak, and Damian Lillard was supposed to be the "fix."

Rivers also was there for Antetokounmpo's exit from Milwaukee, and he talked about that as well with Simmons.

"Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. And he didn't want to be the bad guy. He wanted [GM Jon Horst and owner Wes Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

That take is not controversial, that's how pretty much everyone saw Antetokounmpo's exit from Milwaukee.

His comments on Antetokounmpo's play are going to draw pushback out of Miami.

#3103. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3099. Raptors look to claim first NBA Cup win

The Toronto Raptors are looking to secure their first win in the Emirates NBA Cup this season as they take on the Milwaukee Bucks on Friday, November 6.

The Raptors, who are currently 0-1 in the competition and are coming off of a 128-109 loss against the Denver Nuggets. Toronto has not been on great form, losing 3 of their last four and currently sit at 4-4.

For the Bucks, their start to the season has been poor as they enter this contest with a record of 1-7 and are on a four-game losing streak.

The Raptors have had many issues to start their season off, mainly surrounding slow starts to games, while not being able to finish games. Perimeter defence has also been a problem.

There has also been massive vulnerability in the frontcourt and rebounding. While they're strong on the offensive glass, their undersized or banged-up frontline has struggled to contain dominant opposing centres. With no true centre, the Raptors have struggled. They should be looking to make a trade for a well renowned centre to help them fix their issue there.

Not having Kawhi Leonard has also seemed to affect the Raptors, as there is now more pressure on Scottie Barnes, Immanuel Quickley, and RJ Barrett to carry the load.

For the Bucks, life without Giannis Antetokounmpo has been difficult. They are fielding a younger squad and are in a transitional period.

The core now features players acquired in recent moves, such as Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr., and Kel'el Ware from Miami, alongside veterans like Myles Turner and coach Doc Rivers (with assistant Darvin Ham) trying to install a new system.

General execution and youth consistency have also been issues early in the year, the young and reshaped rotation (including rookie Brayden Burries and Ryan Rollins) has struggled with late-game execution, shooting efficiency, and closing out tight contests.

BOSTON, MA – NOVEMBER 4: Tyler Herro #11 of the Milwaukee Bucks handles the ball during the game against the Boston Celtics on November 4, 2026 at TD Garden in Boston, Massachusetts. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Babineau/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

The key to this matchup lies in the battle for possession, where Toronto's elite offensive rebounding and low turnover rates are heavily favoured to exploit Milwaukee's 27th-ranked defence.

To stay competitive, the Bucks must rely on Myles Turner and Kel'el Ware to control the glass and prevent Scottie Barnes and RJ Barrett from dominating the paint, while forcing Toronto into a perimeter shooting contest where they currently hit just 31.9 percent from deep.

Ultimately, if Milwaukee's Tyler Herro and AJ Green can capitalize on high-efficiency looks from three-point range to offset Toronto's relentless downhill physicality, the Bucks can mask their defensive deficiencies and stall the Raptors' high-volume possession game.

This is a great time for the Bucks to win their second game of the year, as they face a Toronto side that has really struggled as of late.

For the Raptors, they poses as a great get back game as they try to get back on track this season and avoid falling under .500 for the first time.

#3092. Giannis Antetokounmpo is ‘difficult’ to coach: Doc Rivers

Retired NBA coach Doc Rivers is never afraid to speak the truth, and Giannis Antetokounmpo is on his mind these days.

Rivers explained on the "Bill Simmons Podcast" that Antetokounmpo is a "difficult guy" after having coached him for a season and a half before retiring in April 2026.

"He's not easy," Rivers said of coaching Antetokounmpo. "He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy. He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't have super IQ at the same time. He really has one way. Every play, he wants to force it."

Giannis Antetokounmpo of the Miami Heat shoots a free throw during a game against the Golden State Warriors in San Francisco on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Antetokounmpo is an ultra-rare physical specimen, earning the nickname "The Greek Freak," standing 6-foot-11 and weighing 250 pounds.

His time in Milwaukee is mostly considered a success, as he won an NBA title in 2021, but the end of his career with Rivers was frustrating. The Bucks had nearly no assets to acquire new players and Antetokounmpo himself was a constant source of trade conjecture.

"I wished he learned how to execute better," Rivers said. "The thing he needs to still learn is the value of execution. How important it is when you're in practice and shoot around to lock in on execution. Now he has a coach who's as good as there is in execution."

The Bucks finally did trade him to the Miami Heat this past offseason and he's hooked up with coach Erik Spoelstra, though early returns have not been good with a 3-6 record.

"For the team to work, you have to learn how to execute," Rivers said.

Rivers has always been honest when talking about players he's coaching, including when he's still with the team.

Head coach Doc Rivers and Giannis Antetokounmpo #34 of the Milwaukee Bucks look on against the Brooklyn Nets during the game at Barclays Center on December 08, 2024 in New York Getty Images

As the 76ers coach, Rivers had a blunt answer to a reporter after Ben Simmons passed up a wide-open layup in Game 7 of a playoff game against the Atlanta Hawks in 2021.

The reporter asked whether Rivers still believed in Simmons to be an elite point guard on a championship-winning team.

"I don't know that question or the answer to that right now," Rivers replied after they lost to a clearly inferior Hawks team that went on to not be a contender in the years following. "So I don't know the answer to that."

Simmons refused to show up the following year and was eventually traded to the Nets for James Harden before falling out of the league in a detrimental chain of events for his career.

Simmons later said Rivers' comments infuriated him.

Doc Rivers has never been one to clam up when talking about his players. USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con

"How did I feel? I was like, 'What a piece of s—t," Simmons said of Rivers' blunt comments in a recent documentary "Ben Being Ben". "When times get tough, people start panicking. People throw people under the bus, and that's just what happened."

Antetokounmpo and the Heat face the floundering Kings on Sunday after losing to the Warriors on Thursday.

#3088. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#3085. Report: Warriors expected to trade Kristaps Porzingis by December 16th

The Golden State Warriors Kristaps Porzingis saga is expected to come to an end before the end of the year, according to a report by Brett Siegel of ClutchPoints. Porzingis, who re-signed with the Dubs last season on a partially guaranteed two-year, $40 million deal, opted not to join the team for training camp and has accepted not receiving payments, seemingly deciding to retire. However, hoping to make the best out of an unexpected situation, the Warriors are hoping to use Porzingis' salary essentially as a trade exception. While that was all known, Siegel's reporting suggests the front office is expected to trade Porzingis by December 16th.

"For starters, Porzingis' time with the Warriors is over," Siegel wrote. "He will not be playing another game for this franchise, as ClutchPoints reported on Oct. 23 before the team's first game of the season, and it's almost a given he will be traded, likely within the next 30-40 days… Much like how the Warriors traded for Dennis Schroder in the middle of December during the 2024-25 season, only to re-aggregate him in a bigger deal for Jimmy Butler at the trade deadline, league sources are anticipating a similar strategy this time around with Porzingis."

Siegel notes that players who signed free agent contracts this offseason will all become trade-eligible on December 15th, which will also give teams more options on that day. Moreover, December 16th is the deadline for a player to be traded and still be eligible to be aggregated in a deal at the trade deadline in February. So while it's definitely possible for a deal to be made sooner, that effectively becomes the deadline for the Warriors front office if they would like to make a smaller move with Porzingis that would leave them flexibility to still go looking for bigger fish at the deadline.

Siegel's reporting does not even engage with a scenario where the Warriors do not trade Porzingis in December. It's worth wondering if they would simply hold onto him until the trade deadline if they did not receive an offer that enticed them enough before. With the Warriors 6-3 and looking like a legit playoff team, though, the front office should be less inclined to slow play adding depth to the roster.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Federal Reserve Board today published feedback letters for resolution plans submitted in October 2025. The agencies did not identify any shortcomings or deficiencies in these resolution plan submissions.

Resolution plans, also known as living wills, describe a banking organization's strategy for orderly resolution in the event of material financial distress or failure. The agencies conducted a joint review of the 2025 resolution plan submissions from 15 banking organizations with over $250 billion in assets.

In addition, the agencies determined that the shortcoming previously identified in the 2021 BNP Paribas resolution plan has been satisfactorily addressed.

#3075. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#3073. Taylor Swift called the 'fakest' celebrity fan by Knicks player

During a TikTok stream where the pair were playing NBA 2K, New York Knicks guards Tyler Kolek and Miles "Deuce" McBride were asked a question: who was the "fakest" celebrity fan they encountered during the Knicks' championship run? Kolek didn't hesitate to name a major celebrity.

Kolek promptly named pop superstar Taylor Swift, who made headlines for her courtside appearance at Game 4 of the Knicks' series against the San Antonio Spurs on June 10, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Swift was spotted in a custom blue-and-orange T-shirt with the pun "Stevie Knicks," accompanied by her longtime friends Mariska Hargitay, Alana Haim, and Este Haim.

"I don't know if I've seen her at any other games. … It's a little performative," Kolek said during the live stream.

McBride, laughing, agreed with Kolek's assessment but was quick to warn his teammate: "I would agree. The Swifties aren't going to like that answer."

Saving himself from the potential backlash, Kolek quickly clarified his remarks. He suggested that her busy schedule might simply prevent her from attending more often.

McBride teased Kolek for trying to backtrack and from the wrath of Swift's loyal fanbase.

Later Friday, the Knicks released a statement showing support for Swift.

"Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization," a representative for the Knicks told ESPN.

This story has been updated with new information.
